The qualitative characteristics include the relevance, reliability, and comparability over time of financial information that is reported about the different groups of products and services of an enterprise and about its operations in particular geographical areas, and the usefulness of that information for assessing the risks and returns of the enterprise as a whole. 12. The predominant sources of risks affect how most enterprises are organised and managed. Therefore, the organisational structure of an enterprise and its internal financial reporting system are normally the basis for identifying its segments.

13. The definitions of segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities include amounts of such items that are directly attributable to a segment and amounts of such items that can be allocated to a segment on a reasonable basis. An enterprise looks to its internal financial reporting system as the starting point for identifying those items that can be directly attributed, or reasonably allocated, to segments. There is thus a presumption that amounts that have been identified with segments for internal financial reporting purposes are directly attributable or reasonably allocable to segments for the purpose of measuring the segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities of reportable segments.

14. In some cases, however, a revenue, expense, asset or liability may have been allocated to segments for internal financial reporting purposes on a basis that is understood by enterprise management but that could be deemed arbitrary in the perception of external users of financial statements. Such an allocation would not constitute a reasonable basis under the definitions of segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities in this Standard. Conversely, an enterprise may choose not to allocate some item of revenue, expense, asset or liability for internal financial reporting purposes, even though a reasonable basis for doing so exists. Such an item is allocated pursuant to the definitions of segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities in this Standard.

15. Examples of segment assets include current assets that are used in the operating activities of the segment and tangible and intangible fixed assets. If a particular item of depreciation or amortisation is included in segment expense, the related asset is also included in segment assets. Segment assets do not include assets used for general enterprise or head-office purposes. Segment assets include operating assets shared by two or more segments if a reasonable basis for allocation exists. Segment assets include goodwill that is directly attributable to a segment or that can be allocated to a segment on a reasonable basis and segment expense includes related amortisation of goodwill. If segment assets have been revalued subsequent to acquisition, then the measurement of segment assets reflects those revaluations.

16. Examples of segment liabilities include trade and other payables, accrued liabilities, customer advances, product warranty provisions, and other claims relating to the provision of goods and services. Segment liabilities do not include borrowings and other liabilities that are incurred for financing rather than operating purposes. The liabilities of segments whose operations are not primarily of a financial nature do not include borrowings and similar liabilities because segment result represents an operating, rather than a net-of-financing, profit or loss. Further, because debt is often issued at the head-office level on an enterprise-wide basis, it is often not possible to directly attribute, or reasonably allocate, the interest-bearing liabilities to segments.

17. Segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities are determined before intra-enterprise balances and intra-enterprise transactions are eliminated as part of the process of preparation of enterprise financial statements, except to the extent that such intra-enterprise balances and transactions are within a single segment.

18. While the accounting policies used in preparing and presenting the financial statements of the enterprise as a whole are also the fundamental segment accounting policies, segment accounting policies include, in addition, policies that relate specifically to segment reporting, such as identification of segments, method of pricing inter-segment transfers, and basis for allocating revenues and expenses to segments.

Identifying Reportable Segments

Primary and Secondary Segment Reporting Formats

19. The dominant source and nature of risks and returns of an enterprise should govern whether its primary segment reporting format will be business segments or geographical segments. If the risks and returns of an enterprise are affected predominantly by differences in the products and services it produces, its primary format for reporting segment information should be business segments, with secondary information reported geographically. Similarly, if the risks and returns of the enterprise are affected predominantly by the fact that it operates in different countries or other geographical areas, its primary format for reporting segment information should be geographical segments, with secondary information reported for groups of related products and services.

Transfer of employees between group entities

B59. The fourth issue relates to group share-based payment arrangements that involve employees of more than one group entity. For example, a parent might grant rights to its equity instruments to the employees of its subsidiaries, conditional upon the completion of continuing service with the group for a specified period. An employee of one subsidiary might transfer employment to another subsidiary during the specified vesting period without the employee's rights to equity instruments of the parent under the original share-based payment arrangement being affected. If the subsidiaries have no obligation to settle the share-based payment transaction with their employees, they account for it as an equity-settled transaction. Each subsidiary shall measure the services received from the employee by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments at the date the rights to those equity instruments were originally granted by the parent as defined in Appendix A, and the proportion of the vesting period the employee served with each subsidiary.

B60. If the subsidiary has an obligation to settle the transaction with its employees in its parent's equity instruments, it accounts for the transaction as cash-settled. Each subsidiary shall measure the services received on the basis of grant date fair value of the equity instruments for the proportion of the vesting period the employee served with each subsidiary. In addition, each subsidiary shall recognise any change in the fair value of the equity instruments during the employee's service period with each subsidiary.

B61. Such an employee, after transferring between group entities, may fail to satisfy a vesting condition other than a market condition as defined in Appendix A, e.g. the employee leaves the group before completing the service period. In this case, because the vesting condition is service to the group, each subsidiary shall adjust the amount previously recognised in respect of the services received from the employee in accordance with the principles in paragraph 19. Hence, if the rights to the equity instruments granted by the parent do not vest because of an employee's failure to meet a vesting condition other than a market condition, no amount is recognised on a cumulative basis for the services received from that employee in the financial statements of any group entity.

This Standard does not require, but does not prohibit, a 'matrix presentation'.

23. In some cases, organisation and internal reporting of an enterprise may have developed along lines unrelated to both the types of products and services it produces, and the geographical areas in which it operates. In such cases, the internally reported segment data will not meet the objective of this Standard. Accordingly, paragraph 20(b) requires the directors and management of the enterprise to determine whether the risks and returns of the enterprise are more product/service driven or geographically driven and to accordingly choose business segments or geographical segments as the primary basis of segment reporting. The objective is to achieve a reasonable degree of comparability with other enterprises, enhance understandability of the resulting information, and meet the needs of investors, creditors, and others for information about product/service-related and geographically-related risks and returns.

Business and Geographical Segments

24. Business and geographical segments of an enterprise for external reporting purposes should be those organisational units for which information is reported to the board of directors and to the chief executive officer for the purpose of evaluating the unit's performance and for making decisions about future allocations of resources, except as provided in paragraph 25.

25. If internal organisational and management structure of an enterprise and its system of internal financial reporting to the board of directors and the chief executive officer are based neither on individual products or services or groups of related products/services nor on geographical areas, paragraph 20(b) requires that the directors and management of the enterprise should choose either business segments or geographical segments as the primary segment reporting format of the enterprise based on their assessment of which reflects the primary source of the risks and returns of the enterprise, with the other as its secondary reporting format. In that case, the directors and management of the enterprise should determine its business segments and geographical segments for external reporting purposes based on the factors in the definitions in paragraph 5 of this Standard, rather than on the basis of its system of internal financial reporting to the board of directors and chief executive officer, consistent with the following:

(a)

if one or more of the segments reported internally to the directors and management is a business segment or a geographical segment based on the factors in the definitions in paragraph 5 but others are not, sub-paragraph (b) below should be applied only to those internal segments that do not meet the definitions in paragraph 5 (that is, an internally reported segment that meets the definition should not be further segmented);

(b)

for those segments reported internally to the directors and management that do not satisfy the definitions in paragraph 5, management of the enterprise should look to the next lower level of internal segmentation that reports information along product and service lines or geographical lines, as appropriate under the definitions in paragraph 5; and

(c)

if such an internally reported lower-level segment meets the definition of business segment or geographical segment based on the factors in paragraph 5, the criteria in paragraph 27 for identifying reportable segments should be applied to that segment.

The data place of the ψsixty-fifth percentile is = 7*0.65 = 4.55.

The arm's length range will be beginning at 8.2% and ending at 10.57%.

Therefore, if the transaction price of the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction has OP/OC percentage which is equal to or more than 8.2% and less than or equal to 10.57%, it is within the range. The transaction price in such cases will be deemed to be the arm's length price and no adjustment shall be required.

The data place of median is calculated by first computing the total number of data point in the data set * (50/100). In this case it is 7 * 0.5 = 3.5.

Since this is not a whole number, the next higher data place, i.e.; the value at the fourth place would have at least fifty per cent of the values below it (median).

The median is the value at fourth place, i.e., 9%. Therefore, the arm's length price shall be considered as 9% and adjustment shall accordingly be made.

SCHEDULE II - Form X (see regulation 36)

Outsourcing of Activities

1. Core Activities

(a) The Insurance broker shall not outsource any of the following activities in any manner whatsoever:

i.

the functions of the direct/ reinsurance/ composite broker as given in Schedule I - Form A under Regulation 4.

ii.

risk management services unless the broker does not undertake this activity at all.

iii.

claims consultancy services unless the broker does not undertake this activity at all.

2. Responsibilities of the Board of Directors - 1) The Board of the insurance broking company shall be responsible for the following functions under these Regulations:

The Board of Directors shall put in place an Outsourcing Policy covering the following:

(a)

Framework for assessment of risks involved in outsourcing, including the confidentiality of data, quality of services rendered under outsourcing contracts.

(b)

Parameters for determining materiality of outsourcing contracts for the purpose of determining enhanced oversight by the Insurer.

(c)

Parameters for determining the cost-benefit analysis for each Outsourced activity.

(d)

Guiding principles for evaluation of the Outsourced Service Provider including its ability and capability to provide the required services.

(e)

Conflict management policy that ensure adherence to the provisions on related party transactions as envisaged in Companies Act, 2013.

(f)

Norms for implementation and review of the Outsourcing Policy, Determining the management's responsibility for approving, determining the consideration amount involved and monitoring the outsourcing arrangements, and delegation of authority within the insurance broker;

(g)

The degree of due diligence required for other than-material (non-core) Outsourcing activities.

(h)

At least an annual review of the Outsourcing Policy keeping in mind the changes in the internal and external environment impacting the outsourcing arrangements.

(i)

Annual review of the summary of the outsourced activities of the insurance broker.

(j)

Approval of material outsourcing contracts as per the threshold limits prescribed in the Outsourcing Policy.

(k)

Ensuring that the pricing for related party outsourcing arrangements are consistent with accepted arms' length principles as enshrined in the Companies Act, 2013.

3. Outsourcing Service Providers: An insurance broker can outsource activity to an entity (other than an individual) only where the activity to be outsourced is more than 5% of the total outsourcing expenditure (Material).

4. Due Diligence of Outsourcing Service Providers: 1) An insurance broker shall before outsourcing the activities shall undertake due diligence of outsourcing service providers based on best practices and needs of the broking company such as:

(a)

Does the main objective of the outsource service provider include activities outsourced.

(b)

Existence of the outsourcing service provider as projected.

(c)

Competence and experience to perform the activity proposed to be outsourced to it.

(d)

Assessing the capability of the outsourced Service Provider to employ standards envisaged, while performing outsourced activities.

(e)

Security and internal controls;

(f)

Business continuity management;

(g)

Where considered necessary, insurance brokers shall obtain independent reviews and market feedback on the service provider to supplement its own findings;

(2) Due diligence undertaken during the selection process should be documented and evaluated periodically as part of the monitoring and control process of outsourcing.

5. Outsourcing Agreements: 1) Outsourcing arrangements shall be governed by written agreements that are legally binding for a specified period, subject to periodical renewal, if necessary, that clearly describe all material aspects of the outsourcing arrangement, including the rights and obligations of all parties.

(2) The outsourcing contracts, inter alia, shall have in place certain clauses or conditions listed below, as may be applicable:

(a)

Information and asset ownership rights, information technology, data security and protection of confidential information;

(b)

Guarantee or indemnity from the Outsourcing Service Provider towards his commitment including liability for any failure;

(c)

Contingency planning of the Outsourcing Service Provider to provide business continuity for the outsourced arrangement;

Express clause that the contract shall neither prevent nor impede Insurance broker from meeting its respective regulatory obligations, nor the regulator from exercising its regulatory powers of conducting inspection, investigation, obtaining information from either the Insurance broker or the Outsourcing Service Provider;

(e)

The Insurance broker shall ensure that the Outsourcing service provider shall not sub-contract, whole or substantial portion of any of the Outsourced activity.

The Insurance broker shall factor in the additional risk which flows due to subcontracting at the time of due diligence.

Determination of arm's length price under section 165

9.

[R. 10B of the 1962 Rules]

79. (1) For the purposes of section 165(2) 10, the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction shall be determined by any of the fol-lowing methods provided in this sub-rule, being the most appropriate method, in the manner specified therein.

(a)

comparable uncontrolled price method, by which, —

(i)

the price charged or paid for property transferred or services provided in a comparable uncontrolled transaction, or a number of such transactions, is identified;

(ii)

such price is adjusted to ac-count for differences, if any, between an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transactions or between the enterprises entering into such transactions, which could materially affect the price in the open market; and

(iii)

the adjusted price arrived at under sub-clause (ii) is taken to be an arm's length price in respect of the property transferred or services provided in the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction; or

(b)

resale price method, by which, —

(i)

the price at which property purchased or services obtained by the enterprise from an associated enterprise is resold or are provided to an unrelated enterprise, is identified;

(ii)

such resale price is reduced by the amount of a normal gross profit margin accruing to the enterprise or to an unrelated enterprise from the purchase and resale of the same or similar property or from obtaining and providing the same or similar services, in a comparable uncontrolled transaction, or a number of such transactions;

(iii)

the price so arrived at is further reduced by the expenses incurred by the enterprise directly in connection with the purchase of property or obtaining of services;

(iv)

the price so arrived at is adjusted to take into account the functional and other differences, including differences in accounting practices, if any, between the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transactions, or between the enterprises entering into such transactions, which could materially affect the amount of gross profit margin in the open market; and

(v)

the adjusted price arrived at under sub-clause (iv) is taken to be an arm's length price in respect of the transaction of purchase of property or obtaining of the services by the enterprise from its associated enterprise; or

(c)

cost plus method, by which, —

(i)

the direct and indirect costs of production incurred by the enterprise in respect of property transferred or services provided to an associated enterprise, are determined;

(ii)

the amount of a normal gross profit mark-up on such costs (computed according to the same accounting norms) arising from the transfer or provision of the same or similar property or services by the enterprise, or by an unrelated enterprise, in a comparable uncontrolled transaction, or a number of such transactions, is determined;

(iii)

the normal gross profit mark-up referred to in sub-clause (ii) is adjusted to take into account the functional and other differences, if any, between the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction and the comparable uncontrolled transactions, or between the enterprises entering into such transactions, which could materially affect such profit mark-up in the open market;

(iv)

the costs referred to in sub-clause (i) are increased by the adjusted profit mark­-up arrived at under sub-clause (iii); and

(v)

the sum so arrived at is taken to be an arm's length price in relation to the supply of the property or provision of services by the enterprise; or

(d)

profit split method, which may be applicable mainly, in, —

(i)

an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction involving either the transfer of unique intangibles or unique and valuable contributions by each of the enterprises involved in the transaction; or

(ii)

multiple international trans-actions or specified domestic transactions which are so interrelated that they cannot be evaluated separately for the purpose of determining the arm's length price of any one transaction, under which the following two approaches may be used —

(A)

contribution profit split method, by which, —

(I)

the combined net profit of the associated enterprises arising from the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction in which they are engaged, is determined;

(II)

the relative contribution made by each of the associated enterprises to the earning of such combined net profit, is then evaluated on the basis of the functions performed, assets employed or to be employed and risks assumed by each enterprise and on the basis of reliable external market data, which indicates how such contribution would be evaluated by unrelated enterprises performing comparable functions in similar circumstances;

(III)

the combined net profit is then split amongst the enterprises in proportion to their relative contributions, as evaluated under sub-item (II); and

14. Product/Service Profitability Analysis

14.1 The unit product or service profits are driven by two major components viz. cost per unit and selling price per unit. The cost auditor should analyse if the business belongs to the sellers' market or buyers' market. This would facilitate the assessment of impact of changes in selling prices and changes in costs on the profitability or otherwise of the products or services. While the selling price is a single number, the cost is the sum total of different elements. The cost auditor must ensure that the basis use to allocate indirect costs is consistently adopted by the company.

14.2 In case of services, the unit of measurement is very important and hence carefully selected. Further, due to the diverse nature of services, it is essential to exercise care in analyzing the profitability thereof especially when the services provided are not standard. Many times, there is a combined contract for sale of product along with the service & maintenance contract. In such cases, the cost auditor should bifurcate the sales and costs for each portion and then compute and comment on their respective profitability.

14.3 Care should be taken in splitting the joint costs in case of joint products and by products. The method adopted for separation of costs should be checked to ensure correctness and consistency.

14.4 It would help to separately identify the costs of production, selling & marketing and handling customer services.

14.5 The cost auditor is expected to provide a thorough evaluation to bring out the products and/or services that are contributing more or less to the overall company performance. For convenience purpose, the products and/or services could be classified in groups with similar risk-return profiles. This classification may be different from the 'product groups' in the cost audit report annexures.

14.6 The analysis should separately appraise profitability of newly introduced products or services and also their proportion to the total profits of the organisation. The cost auditor should incorporate the profitability analysis of products discontinued during the period.

14.7 The term "profitability" should be taken with an extended meaning to include, apart from the concept of accounting profit, the ROI analysis as well. It would be useful to analyse profitability of products/services in domestic and export market. Care should be taken to isolate reasons for the changes in the profitability percentages. Similarly, if significant, profitability on sales to the related parties may be separately highlighted.

14.8 The report should specifically highlight the top five and the bottom five products. This will help the company to understand which products or services are contributing to the performance and which are ones that are non-performing. Based on this the suitable corrective actions may be suggested.

The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment. Aggreived the final order, the assessee preferred an appeal before Income Tax Appellate Tribunal on as many as eleven grounds4. However, on two prime arguments cited below, the Assessee specially referred the matter for the consideration of Special Bench5:

Maersk India was a low end back office service provider and should be differentiated from high end research and analytical services like KPO services; and

Abnormally high profit making companies should not be included in the list of comparables.

2. KPO VS. BPO CONTROVERSY – AN ANALYSIS

In both the business formats, it is not a simple case of "K" replacing the "B". BPO usually deals with performing business activities like customer care, finance, HR, voice and data entry functions. The extent of work force required is more process driven and elementary. Generally, the motivation of setting up of BPO operations is substantial cost savings. On the other hand, KPO, being a subset of BPO, involves the outsourcing of core specialized and knowledge based services which may or may not result in cost savings but surely adds value to parent company's endeavours. Services outsourced to KPO are related to research and development, equity and financial analysis, legal services, biotechnology, animation and design and other services to likes of dedicated business solutions. KPO employs qualified professionals having specific industry expertise.

The Hon'ble Special Bench has pronounced that the process followed to identify potential comparables is one of the most critical aspects of the comparability analysis and it should be transparent, systematic and verifiable. Potential comparables in ITeS sector can be identified through applying "broad functionality test" by analyzing the taxpayer's circumstances largely. Further bifurcation of IT enabled services may be done to establish relatively equal degree of comparability. The line of differentiation between KPO and BPO is very thin since KPOs are an upward extension of BPO industry in the value chain. Since KPO is an evolution of BPO, there is a likely-hood where in the process of such evolution, there are entities offering a mix of overlapping services which are difficult to classify as either BPO or KPO, going by their functional profile.

The Special Bench held that IT Enables Services cannot be further bifurcated or classified as BPO and KPO services for comparability purposes in wake of difficulty in classifying services strictly either as low end BPO services or high end KPO services. The Bench advocated a two step process to benchmark transactions in the ITeS sector :-

Identifying potential comparables through conducting a broad functional analysis at ITeS level; and

Comparing the functional profile of tested party with principal functions performed by selected entities, ensuring equal comparability. Such functional filtration process may ensure that the uncontrolled transactions having lesser degree of comparability would get eliminated.

Hence, in essence, the Bench iterated that the selection of final comparables shall depend on facts and circumstances of each case on the basis of functional profile of the tested party.

In light of above analysis, Maersk India is held to be a captive contract service provider mainly rendering back office support services and other incidental services involving some degree of special knowledge and expertise. Hence, Mold-Tek Technologies and eClerx Services were dropped as comparables on the premise that both companies were engaged in providing high-end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise.

3. WHETHER DEFINITIONS IN SAFE HARBOUR RULES CAN BE SANCTIONED IN ALL CASES

One of the contentions put up by the taxpayer for justifying the differentiation between KPO and BPO is the definition of "Information technology enables services" cited in the Final Safe Harbour Rules ("SHR" or "the Rules") released issued by Ministry of Finance on September 18, 2013. The aforesaid definition is an exclusive one that identifies many low-end outsourcing services viz. payroll, revenue accounting, call centre services. "Knowledge process outsourcing services" are separately defined in the aforesaid Rules as outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology requiring application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skill. Hence, the assessee submitted that specific articulation by the CBDT of both BPO and KPO in the SHR demonstrates the differences between the two business layouts.

The Revenue challenged the assessee's reference to the SHR on the ground that the aforesaid rules were released in September 2013 and cannot be applied retrospectively to a case pertaining to AY 2008-09. Besides, the Revenue countered the assessee's reliance on definitions provided in SHR by submitting that the assessee in this case has not exercised the safe harbour option and hence cannot draw an inference from it. However, the Special Bench did not place any strictures on such reliance by non-safe harbour pickers.

3. In the right earnest it would have been proper to remand the case to the AO/TPO to get new set of comparables to arrive at arm's length price. The short point is that before getting on the judgment on suitable comparables it was first necessary to decide the business category to which the assessee and its associated enterprise belonged to and to know this it was necessary to ascertain the relationship between the associated enterprise and the assessee and furthermore, if their business model was such that their activities were dovetailed into each other or were inter-dependent, then the two entities must be taken to have been engaged in one and the same business only. In this case the assessee perhaps succeeded in leading the bench to believe in that the two entities were independent and that the Indian entities' activities were mere support activities, whereas from the reading of the scope of services in the agreement it was apparent that the subsidiary had to work as per instructions of the holding company who acted as an investment advisor and, therefore, in the nature of dependent services. The statement that they were only support services for investment advisory would not make them any less than an investment advisory when these were performed for the holding company as per their instructions. Had the phrase 'as per their instructions' not been there in the agreement it would have made a different situation. In that case their sphere of service might have differed between core service and support service!

With nine rounds of transfer pricing audit completed in January 2014, the challenging days for Indian outsourcing sector does not seem to get over. The total quantum of transfer pricing adjustments made in FY 2012-13 was to the tune of seventy thousand crores1 (for Assessment Year ("AY") 2009-10) up by 54 per cent earlier. Indian outsourcing sector accounts for more than half the total claims in transfer pricing adjustments made during the aforesaid audit cycle from about one-third earlier.

However, as per recently disseminated data, the additions to income of companies undertaking international transaction has dropped by over 14 per cent to sixty thousand crores2 in FY 2014 tax audit cycle (for AY 2010-11). This seems to be a silver lining in an otherwise dismal environment emanating from the North Block.

Outsourcing sector accounts for more than USD 100 billion share in India's economy with big foreign companies like IBM, Capgemini, Microsoft, GE etc. putting forward a big basket of service offerings viz. customer service, risk and fraud management and finance and accounting. In the backdrop of the great demographic dividend, India has been one of the most preferred Knowledge Services Outsourcing ("KSO") destinations holding 70 per-cent share of the global KSO market3. India is poised to emerge as a global hub for KSO by 2015.

Over a period of time, multiplicity of business arrangements have happened in the outsourcing space starting from outsourcing of accounting processes to legal and research process outsourcing. While, Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") service stands for taking up routine operations like data entry, voice calling and accounting services, a shift of functions performed that requires expert analysis and decision making viz. patent application drafting, technical research and advisory activities etc. mark the outset of a new category of Knowledge Process Outsourcing ("KPO") services. This broad bifurcation though coined by the industry itself is important from a transfer pricing stand-point and is analyzed deeply by the Special Bench of Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited discussed in this article.

Being a booming sector, Indian Information Technology ecosystem comprises of many aces to the likes of Infosys, Wipro, Tata Consultancy and other big Indian players. In such backdrop, how adequate would it be to compare margins of smaller IT companies with the abnormal margins of aforesaid gigantic companies having global business outshoots also, is another vexatious TP issue dealt with in detail in the aforesaid judgment.

1. FACTS OF CASE

Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited ("Maersk India") was incorporated in India as a wholly owned subsidiary of Maersk GSC Holdings, part of Maersk Group. Maersk India is in the business of shared services and renders transaction processing support and information technology services. During the year under assessment, Maersk India provided certain IT and IT enabled services to its Associated Enterprises ("AEs") and separately benchmarked the aforesaid transactions under IT and ITeS business segments. Applying Transactional Net Margin Method ("TNMM") with operating profit to total cost ("OP/TC") as Profit level indicator ("PLI"), the assessee selected thirteen comparables and claimed working capital and risk adjustment in its TP report.

In case of ITeS segment, the TPO classified the services provided by Maersk India as KPO services and rejected all but one comparables selected by the assessee and modified the search criteria adopted by assessee. He selected seven comparables including one chosen by the assessee. TPO allowed working capital adjustment but dismissed risk adjustment. In case of IT service segment, TPO computed arm's length margin without allowing working capital adjustment. The AO maintained the TPOs views in the draft assessment order.

Maersk India filed its objections before Dispute Resolution Panel ("DRP") stating that the assessee was a low-end back office service provider being a captive unit working in a zero risk zone and hence should not be categorized as a KPO and high margin comparables selected by the TPO should be dropped. The DRP maintained the high margin comparables selected by TPO on the premise that both high and low margin companies reflect industry profitability and dispensing off super-profit making companies symbolizes addressing only one end of the spectrum and that is not correct. The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment.

The Tribunal held that the financial data of Maple e-solutions was not available for the full financial year but was available only for four months during the financial year 2004-05. It was held that the part period data could not be considered as a comparable to determine the arm's length price.

EMPLOYEES COST 11. In Electronics Data Processing (I) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [IT Appeal No. 420/Hyd/07] the Tribunal held that there was no dispute to the fact that the employees cost to the total turnover of the selected company worked out to be 1.42% as against the industry's average of 30-40% and the assessee's employees cost to turnover percentage was 43%. This fact implied that the selected company had outsourced major portion of its work to third party vendors. Therefore, the company could not be treated as a comparable.

In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that any company with employee cost less than 25% could not be compared with an ITES company – in this case Vishal IT Limited had been adopted by the TPO. This company outsourced its call centre work and, therefore, the employees cost was less than 25% as was the common practice among other ITES. When company had outsourced its ITES, it could not be said that its business results would be comparable to any other ITES provider rendering the services entirely on its own. In such circumstances the net margins of the two comparables could not be on the same basis.

BUSINESS MODEL

12. In Capital IQ Infrastructure Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (International Taxation) [2013] 57 SOT 14/ 32 taxmann.com 21 (Hyd. – Trib.) the Tribunal found that Dispute Resolution Panel, in the proceedings for the assessment year 2008-09 in the assessee's own case, after taking note of the composition of the vendor payments of Coral Hub for the last three years and the fact that it also commenced a new line of business of printing on demand, wherein it printed upon clients request, in view of the major difference in functionality and the business model the Panel was of the view that 'Coral Hub' was not a suitable comparable to the taxpayer and, hence, it needed to be dropped from the final list of comparables.

SUPER PROFIT COMPANIES

13. In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that the super profit margin companies were to be excluded from the list of comparables for the purposes of transfer pricing study – in this case two companies showed profit of more than 100% as compared to other companies taken by the TPO.

EXTRAORDINARY EVENTS

14. In Google India (P.) Ltd. (supra)it was held that in respect of two companies Datamatics Financial Services and Allsec Technologies Limited, the Tribunal found that merely because there were extraordinary events during the financial year without demonstrating as to how these extraordinary events had influenced the profit margin of the companies they could not be excluded from the list of comparables, but the adjustments for such extraordinary events had to be made to the profits of the companies to bring them on par with the assessee before comparing them with the assessee.

ARITHMETIC MEAN

15. First proviso to section 92C(2) provides that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the arithmetical mean of such prices.

In Simphony Marketing Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 55 (Bang. – Trib.)the assessee had selected nine comparables identified by it at arithmetical mean of 14.84% in relation to the disclosed margins of 14.91%, the difference being within the tolerance limit of 5%. The TPO added 18 more comparables to the two accepted by him. The TPO worked out the arithmetical mean at 22.28% after making an adjustment to the benchmark for working capital. If nine comparables which according to the assessee were wrongly included were excluded, it would work out to be an arithmetical mean of 7.97% only as against 14.91% disclosed by the assessee, so that there could have been no addition. The DRP affirmed the addition of TPO. The Tribunal found that out of 20 companies chosen by the TPO as comparables only 11 companies were found to be comparables and their arithmetic mean was only 7.97%. The profit margin cost of the assessee was 14.91% which was made higher than the arithmetic mean of comparable companies chosen by the TPO after the exclusion of some of the comparable companies. The reasons for exclusions of 9 companies were on the following grounds:

During the previous year, there were extraordinary events that took place which warranted exclusion as a comparable;

The comparable company performed knowledge process outsourcing and the assessee was doing business process outsourcing;

The comparable company outsourced most of the work and the assessee was carrying out work by itself;

Tribunals are more inclined (with a few exceptions) to include foreign exchange fluctuation as part of the operating activity. On the other hand, the OECD Guidelines emphasise that while the principle of accounting consistency is essential to be observed, the question of including the foreign exchange gain or loss as part of the cost base depends on whether the same arises from operating or non-operating (i.e. say, trading or investing) activities and the entity that assumes such foreign exchange risk.

The industry dimension A point of consideration, which does not seem to find place in most IT/ITeS rulings (perhaps as the argument is often not adduced in the course of the proceedings) is the treatment adopted by the Revenue authorities, while dealing with taxpayers rendering services to both "service" and "product" companies, spread across various industries. In the course of the economic analysis, no cognizance is given to the end recipient of the services, although there do exist differences in the supply chains of both "service" and "product" companies. Further, even the business and economic circumstances vary for both categories of companies, and the return earned is an immediate indicator of such differences.

In a perfect world, one would want the functional comparability to be viewed in the light of the industry considerations, since the same would help in arriving at a set, which best represents not only the functions undertaken by the taxpayer, but also the return one would expect, while operating in such an industry. However, the lack of financial data for comparable companies operating in a certain domain continues to be a key deterrent in such an analysis. It is for this reason that usually a broader comparability approach is adopted by both taxpayers as well as Revenue authorities, which thus results in arriving at a standard set of comparables companies, without considering either the industry domains in which the taxpayer operates or the business and commercial circumstances of such verticals.

Perhaps, another aspect, which ideally should be considered, prior to determining the arm's length result for the IT/ITeS sector is to additionally analyze whether the services rendered are in the nature of "support services" required for internal consumption and/or subsumed within the larger activities of the Group. In such situations fixing a stand-alone commercial value to such activities is difficult because neither the activity has any use being detached from the final solution, nor the solution itself would be completed without the said activity. Such a scenario will be witnessed when the Indian taxpayer renders services to its Group companies and the same are entirely consumed within the overall primary activity carried on by the Group. A dispassionate value chain analysis should go a long-way in clearing the picture on the true worth of any activity. Having said that, the overall risk-insulated motive of the captive service provider, and thereby its returns being based on risk profiling should be the accepted norm.

To further elaborate, under such a scenario, the service rendered is not a value driver or a source of core competence for the Group. Simply put, the rendition of the service does not augment the revenue potential of the MNC, but may only lead to gains in operating efficiency. Therefore, a market facing activity where the service is ultimately consumed by the end-customer (in whatever form) should invariably lead to the assertion of an arm's length profitability, as opposed to internal consumption of the service for the Group that could form the subject of a cost contribution or a typical safe harbour arrangement.

Mark-ups determined

Tribunals in India have, more often than not, adjudicated on the grievances surrounding comparability analysis specifically on filters applied, quantitative/qualitative analysis of comparables, the true nature of a limited risk service provider and finally on specific issues about comparables as may have been raised by the petitioner. One can safely say that the Tribunals, in their role as an adjudicator, have not commented or expressed an opinion on the level of the mark-up that ought to be applied. They have clearly not taken on the role of a negotiator or a policy maker (like a safe harbour threshold). This continues to be the domain of the Government and the taxman. However, based on certain Tribunal rulings, where principle based approach on comparability has been ascertained, the resultant mark-ups for the IT and ITeS sectors have been hovering in the range of 18-20 per cent and 23-25 per cent as against the 22-25 per cent and 25-30 per cent respectively determined at the TP audit level.

In this background it would be pertinent to mention that retrospective clarification in relation to the tolerance band of 5 per cent not being a standard deduction is rather retrograde and could be viewed as an unjust enrichment to the Indian Revenue authorities. Rather than being forward-looking by considering global practices of applying central tendency, the Government has resorted to empower the Revenue authorities to negotiate with a minor leeway. The fact that the Government has waited for a decade before providing any clarity to both taxpayers as well as the Revenue authorities, and more so after Tribunals adjudicated a standard deduction on the mean, that was the stated intent, is unfortunate and a source of heartburn among the ones who did not get away.

Further, the ALP for the ten year period was computed using arithmetic mean and inter-quartile range and the two results were compared. Whereas the ALP computed from arithmetic mean was 15.31%, the interquartile range gave an ALP of 13.97. This study5 is a conclusive proof of the fact that the ALP computed as per the present Indian framework suffers from several biases and is not a true reflection of the actual 'arm's length price'. As the Indian outsourcing economy continues to boom, it is extremely crucial to adopt a more sophisticated transfer pricing framework to ensure that we align our policies with the best international practices to better resolve our cross border taxation disputes.

As discussed earlier in this article, the Indian IT landscape has multiple players, each of whom undertake different functions and bear different risks. As the nature of functions/operations, business model and performance parameters are different for these entities; they cannot be compared to each other. GICs represent the segment of the IT arena where the risks borne are minimal, functions undertaken are mostly routine like coding, testing etc., and there is no non- routine intangible involved. Hence such a player cannot be compared to an entity that undertakes functions pertaining to the entire value chain of the software development process, starting from conceptua-lization and design to delivery to the final customer.Even if one was to compare, it is necessary to makes adequate adjustments to account for the difference in the risk profile of the same. The transfer pricing officers have alleged that GICs are exposed to the single customer risk as they provide services to their related parties only. Hence the Single customer risks of the GICs can be set off against the market risks borne by the third party comparables. However, the guidelines provide that no two risks can be considered to offset each other and needs to be accounted separately. In this respect, the ITAT has accepted that, typically a GIC is insulated from the market risks faced by the independent comparables and hence adequate adjustments needs to made to account for the same. However there is no clear guidance, in respect to the appropriate method to be followed. In various cases that has been heard by the ITAT, the taxpayer has proposed the use of methods like the CAPM* model, use of Prime Lending rate etc. to do risk adjustments, but the same have been rejected by the ITAT. Further, the ITAT has also observed that while market risk faced by the comparables is an 'existing' risk, the single customer risk borne by GICs, as alleged by the TPOs is only an "anticipated" risk. The challenge for the taxpayer in the coming years is going to be adequately quantifying these risks and accounting for the same.

Taxpayers would often incur certain expenses on behalf of their related parties, purely on account of administrative convenience.Typically, these expenses would be third party costs in the nature of hotel bills, travel expenses, mobile expenses etc. The contentions of the transfer pricing officer has been that such expenses represent payment for services rendered to related parties and has been accordingly adjusted by the officers for the mark-up.

Intra-group services

Payment of management charges or intra group cross charges by Indian subsidiaries to their parent companies has been under the scanner of the tax authorities as an alleged technique of shifting profits outside India. Group entities of MNCs often render shared services to each other. Services are usually of the nature of administrative, human resources, IT, and finance support.This kind of support services within the organization/group encourages specialization by specific groups or units of the MNC. Under such a scenario each unit is not required to develop its own internal team across all the functions, but can tap the expertise of the relevant team from other fellow group entities. This is especially beneficial for smaller subsidiaries or group entities and result in substantial cost savings for them and therefore indirectly benefits them.

However this fact has not been appreciated by the transfer pricing officers, and taxpayers have been asked to provide 'benefit test' and prove that these services are not stewardship and shareholder activities. In most of the cases the transfer pricing officers have held the arm's length price to be nil and have disallowed the entire expense. Even in cases where the services have been beneficial for the taxpayer and have resulted in high margins for the taxpayer, the TPO has made adjustments to the taxpayer.

In this respect, the ITAT has provided relief to taxpayers in form of some landmark judgments where they have analyzed the functions of the taxpayer and have held that the intra-group services satisfy the benefit test and are at arm's length. Further, the ITAT has ruled that it is not the prerogative of the transfer pricing officer to question the business decision of the taxpayer.

For GICs who operate under the cost plus model, such services should not pose any issues, as the costs pertaining to these services would form a part of the cost base for the purpose of mark-up. However there are some GICs who operate on revenue sharing model or hourly rate model and receive such intra-group services from their related party are exposed to this challenge.

35 taxmann.com 584 (Mumbai - Trib.) the ITAT held that in course of transfer pricing proceedings, there can be no question of substituting profit realized by Indian enterprise from its foreign AE with profit realized by foreign AE from ultimate customers for purposes of determining ALP of international transaction of Indian enterprise with its foreign AE. Therefore, an assessee cannot compare profit earned by its foreign AE with outside comparables to prove that price charged by it from transactions with said AE is at ALP However in case of GE Money Financial Services (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 420 (Delhi - Trib.) the ITAT held that foreign AE can be chosen as the tested party if it's the least complex among the transacting parties and comparable data is available.

Companies owing high Intangibles:-

The ITAT Bangalore in case of Momentive Performance Materials (India) (P.) Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 327 (Bangalore Trib.) held that a Company like Infosys holding huge brand value and substantial ownership of intangibles, cannot be compared with a Company having ITES segment with much lesser revenue. The ITAT Delhi also held the same in case of COWI India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 427 (Delhi Trib.).

Companies having extraordinary events:-

ITAT Delhi bench in case of Equant Solutions India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 192 (Delhi Trib.) has held that a Company with extraordinary events like amalgamation, a Company with extraordinary events like corporate restructuring cannot be a good comparable.

Use of Segmental financial data:-

It is settled by the various judicial precedents that where segmental data of a comparable is not available the said Company cannot be accepted as a valid Comparable. In case of Ariba Technologies India (P.) Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 265 (Bangalore Trib.) the assessee was engaged in providing software development services to its AE on a cost plus Basis. The ITAT held that the Company Lucid Software Ltd. cannot be selected as a good comparable on the ground that it employed heavy capital in development of a Product. A Company profitability in the sale of product would be entirely different from the Company, who is involved in service sector and due to non availability of full information about the segmental details as to how much is the sale of product and how much is from the services, this entity cannot be taken into account for comparability

Companies with different Financial Year:-

It has been held in certain cases that a Company having a different financial year cannot be a good comparable. ITAT Bangalore in case of Hewlett- Packard (India) Globalsoft (P.) Ltd. [2015] 63 taxmann.com 136 (Bangalore - Trib.) held that once the annual report of a Company is for a year different from the financial year ending 31st March, then without doubt, it will cease to be good comparable, unless the information received in pursuance to a notice under section 133(6) from such Company, is reconciled with the figures available in such annual report.

Conclusion:-

Transfer pricing is not an exact science and it involves appreciation of various facts as a result of which transfer pricing especially selection of comparables has been a highly litigated area. Whether a Company is a good comparable or not will vary from facts to facts of the case. It is a subjective process and one should make the selection of comparables in light of various judicial pronouncements.

This apart, under the entrepreneurial model for the outbound structures, the Indian entity assumes the role of the Group companies as mentioned aforesaid, carries out the "entrepreneurial activities", could possibly own the intangibles required for the final delivery of the services and will typically be exposed to the business and market risks related to its operations. Given the differences in the functional, asset and risk profiles, even the compensation for the aforesaid models vary based on the functional analysis. While the captive service providers are usually compensated through a fixed rate of return on cost or on a time & material basis, the returns of the entrepreneurs are always market linked. It would be pertinent to mention here that inevitably the compensation is only a derivate of the functions, assets and risks. The stable returns earned by the captive service providers are commensurate with the routine functions and limited risks borne by the captives whereas the returns in the entrepreneur model are also commensurate with the non-routine functions being performed. While fluctuating returns therefore have their highs and lows, the steady returns tend to follow the more consistent middle path, albeit tempered by the lesser risk that they assume in the course of their functions.

From the above discussion, it emerges that a comparison of the functional, asset and risk analysis is basic to any transfer pricing analysis. However, the TP audits and recent Tribunal rulings in India do not seem to be inclined towards appreciating the differences in characterization and risk profiles between a low risk contract service provider and a third-party entrepreneurial companies operating within the same sector.

Furthermore, to account for differences in the functions performed, assets owned and/or deployed and risks assumed, appropriate adjustments such for difference in risk profile, basis of depreciation or working capital position should be carried out between the tested party (i.e. captive service provider) and the uncontrolled third-party entrepreneur companies. Such adjustments help even out any differences between the tested party and comparables companies to arrive at an unbiased "adjusted arm's length price". Such price will better represent the mark-up appropriate for a risk insulated service provider.

Dealing with adjustments in the comparability analysis

The point in relation to the need for a working capital adjustment has been deliberated by various Tribunals, namely Vedaris Technology (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT3, TNT India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4 and Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT5. Therefore the necessity for the same can be considered to be a settled position. In all these instances, the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out working capital adjustment as the same has a material impact on the effective return that the tested party need to earn. Of course, the OECD guidelines endorse the adoption of the working capital adjustment wherever applicable. It is significant to note that working capital adjustment is an effective substitute for any adjustment that may be warranted towards imputed interest consequent to deferred payments arising out of receivables from Group companies.

With regard to the adjustment for equating the basis of capital-asset depreciation, it is observed that in the Indian context, the said adjustment has been more widely accepted and acknowledged for companies in the manufacturing sector as against the services sector. The general belief is that the manufacturing sector requires initial period of high capital investment, whereas the services sector can up its asset base as it renders services. The turnaround time for a services company to become functional is a shorter duration than for a manufacturing plant to start commercial operations. Though the differences in asset bases are varied, it is imperative to adjust the same having regard to the industry/functional activity.

Therefore, such dictums do not rule out the application of the depreciation adjustment in the services sector, since the depreciation adjustment helps even out differences in the depreciation policies adopted by the tested party as against the third-party comparable companies. Having said that, it is imperative to take cognizance of the facts of the case, since application of the depreciation adjustment is case specific and is dependent on the class of assets deployed and the intensity of usage of such assets.

The need for carrying out a risk adjustment is perhaps most critical in the Indian context, considering that a majority of the subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform.

Outliers and the risk dimension

To reiterate, there do exist certain fundamental principles, where the Indian TP legislation deviate from the globally accepted best practices. The adoption of the arithmetical mean as a measure of central tendency in the Indian context as against the inter-quartile range or the median, which are the internationally accepted measures of central tendency, as they tend to eliminate outliers, and are better representatives of the industry averages is one such major exception. This coupled with the use of single year data for the purpose of comparability analysis, daunts taxpayers in the IT/ITeS sector and is the prime reason for the increasing disputes, particularly in this sector. The law, through a proviso, does provide for expanding the base of comparable data, going back up to two further years back from the year of the transaction, thereby allowing for a three-year comparability analysis. Though overseas approaches suggest a 5-year period for any comparability analysis, one may accept a 3-year period specifically for developing countries like India, which has been witnessing contrasting growth year-on-year. Incidentally, the IT/ITeS sectors have been through such tumultuous times over the past decade. However, from the field officers' perspective and indeed the Tribunals, the approach has been to rely on the so-called "contemporaneous data", a phase contained in the legislation but often misused for annual audits. This, along with the concept of mean, has meant that expected mark-up drives comparability selection, rather than the reverse.

The adoption of the arithmetical mean as the arm's length price, hitherto with a limited tolerance band, has its inherent limitations and poses its own set of challenges. Unlike the median and the inter-quartile range, the arithmetical mean tends to be influenced by extreme values and the results are therefore skewed towards either very high/loss making companies. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment.

Introduction

1. The Indian IT/ ITeS industry has witnessed exceptional growth in the last decade and has been instrumental in registering a multi-fold increase in foreign exchange earnings for the country. In addition to fuelling India's economy, this industry is also positively influencing the lives of its people through contributing in employment generation and augmenting standards of living. The industry has helped India transform from a rural and agriculture-based economy to a knowledge based economy.

As per a recent NASSCOM report, the Indian IT-BPO industry's aggregate revenues have crossed the USD 100 billion mark with exports of USD 69 billion in year 2012. Within Software and services exports, IT services accounts for 58 per cent and BPO is nearly 23 per cent, Engineering and R&D ('ER&D') and Software Products account for 19 per cent.

The mitochondria of Indian IT sector can be broadly divided into two segments on the basis of nature of services performed. On one hand, there are Indian IT Companies like Wipro, Infosys, HCL, etc., who have established their footprint on the global scale by establishing offshore software product development centres ('OSPD'). India's OSPD market has experienced double digit growth over the past five years. On the other hand, there are inbound investments by various foreign multi-national IT Companies like Microsoft, IBM, Genpact, Capgemini etc. where predominantly foreign IT majors outsource their research, software development and testing to captive Indian subsidiaries or through Global In-house centres ('GIC').

Various steps involved in software development projects

2. A software development project typically entails various steps starting from conception of the desired software, research and application development, software design, writing and maintaining source code, prototyping, modification, re-engineering, maintenance and other activities.

Ideally, a full-fledged software company should undertake all the phases involved in software development. However, such is not the case always. Mostly, software companies outsource certain parts of their software development functions to their offshore subsidiaries stationed in nations with a rich knowledge base, anticipating cost-effectiveness in operations due to low human resource cost. In such type of arrangements, generally the conceptualization and quality assessment aspects are taken care of by the parent software company only, whereas the captive subsidiaries are only involved in functional research and development activities. Such captive subsidiaries are named as 'contract R&D centres' due to the limited nature of work handled by them. Usually, the major part of risk-taking work in terms of business development, bidding, sales and marketing is done by the parent company in such cases, thereby ensuring consistent work flow to their captive R&D centres. The contract R&D centres in return undertake to complete the work assigned to them as per the quality specifications. This arrangement can be compared to the traditional outsourcing model where the work execution is done by the sub-contracted company (in this case a captive subsidiary) to the satisfaction of the customer (in this case the parent company).

The Transfer Pricing Controversy

3. Transfer Pricing ('TP') is one of the major concerns for IT companies today. There are widespread TP adjustments and additions in many cases. Many issues that are being faced by IT sector today pertain to choice of comparables where divergence of opinion occurs between the taxpayer and the revenue on the inclusion of companies as comparables, matter relating to choice of Most Appropriate Method ('MAM'), issues surrounding the quantitative and qualitative filters, use of multiple year's data, disagreement on crediting the benefit of working capital adjustment, revenue denying the benefit of +/-5 per cent range, etc.

From several TP issues faced by the Indian IT sector today, one major TP issue relates to the margins charged by IT companies. The tax authorities are consistently proposing margin of 20-27 per cent for the IT segment, while the taxpayer attributes a downward trend in the margins, experienced within 12-15 per cent. The comparables selected by the tax authorities are big companies like Wipro, HCL. These are independent business enterprises taking extensive risks and infusing large asset base in their business. The margins computed by the tax authorities swell the moment such comparables are added to the basket of identified comparable companies. On the other hand, in case of captive research centres, major business development functions, risks and assets associated with the software development operations are borne by foreign parent companies, the price paid by them ought to be lower in comparison to cases where both the associated enterprises operate on a principal-to-principal basis.

To address the issues faced by the IT sector companies, a committee chaired by N Rangachary, former Chairman, CBDT was formed last year. The Committee penned out its suggestions in September last year, which were not made public. Out of several suggestions made by the Rangachary Committee, one of the key recommendations has been a 20 per cent safe harbour rate for IT/ ITeS sector. Further, the Committee is understood to be favouring the cost plus method over profit-split method.

The safe harbour rates, as measures of operating profit/total cost, for different categories of services, which are provided under contract service provider model, are as follows : 4. Will safe harbours reduce TP litigation in India?

The authors are of the view that the herald of safe harbour as a tool for reducing TP disputes in India is far flung from reality. Much of the disputes around contract service providers in the fields of IT, ITeS, KPO and R&D, arise due to the uniqueness of the Indian TP regulations in its use of arithmetic mean and a band around the mean, as against the use of median and inter-quartile range adopted by most other TP regimes.

The authors had earlier analysed8 comparable sets widely used for determination of arm's length prices for IT and ITeS companies in the TP assessments for fiscal year (FY) 2006-07, i.e. relevant to the assessment year 2007-08. The IT set comprised of 26 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 1.38% to 60.23%, with an arithmetic mean of 25.04%. Similarly, the ITeS set comprised of 27 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 13.55% to 113.49%, with an arithmetic mean of 30.24%.

Thus, any captive IT or ITeS company with an operating margin of less than 19% and 24% respectively, namely after considering the band of 5% around the arithmetic mean, as prevalent during the material time, would have failed to satisfy the arm's length test for FY 2006-07, as per the country-wide comparable benchmarking sets adopted by the Indian Revenue.

It may be pertinent to highlight that the lower quartiles of the same IT and ITeS sets were at about 14% and 12% respectively. Therefore, the use of inter-quartile range on the same comparables would have enabled captive taxpayers with an operating profitability of 15%, being the intuitive mark-up for most captive IT and ITeS companies, to comply with the arm's length standard. The analysis was re-run on the ITeS comparables used in the TP assessment cycle relating to FY 2007-08, i.e., relevant to the assessment year 2008-09. The lower limit of arm's length price, computed with reference to the 5% tolerable limit around the arithmetic mean, was again observed to be at 19%, while the lower quartile was at 9%.

These analyses vindicate that, but for the ingenuity of the Indian TP regulations, a large fraction of taxpayers falling within the bracket of 15% of operating profitability or even lower, would have remained unscathed, even if one were to otherwise accept the selection of comparables by the Indian Revenue for the IT and ITeS sets, which itself left enough room for debate. Therefore, the introduction of inter-quartile range and median would have better addressed the TP disputes in India and obviated the need for safe harbours, as the pre-dominant objective of introducing safe harbours is to reduce TP litigations in India.

Some may attribute the adoption of arithmetic mean by the Indian Revenue, for the purposes of computing the arm's length price, to the brevity of comparable data available in public databases in the formative years of transfer pricing in India, which inhibited the usage of quartiles. It is observed that ProwessTM, a public database widely used for the purposes of comparable benchmarking analyses in India, reported only 8,067 companies in the year 2002, as compared to 25,949 companies in 2011. Presently another database used for benchmarking analyses, namely Capita line PlusTM, provides data of around 1,000 additional companies over and above the companies provided in ProwessTM. Thus, brevity of data can no longer be the reason or cause for not adopting the more sophisticated approach of the inter-quartile range by the Indian Revenue, as several of the other developing economies, let alone the developed ones, have advocated the usage of inter-quartile range and median for the purposes of computing the arm's length range.

The safe harbour rates proclaimed by India are still not reasonable enough to entice large captive service providers, since opting for safe harbour rates in India might result in such taxpayers facing economic double taxation, as Revenue authorities of the headquarter countries are unlikely to accept the high mark-ups under the unilateral safe harbour rules of India. Furthermore, as the taxpayers adopting safe harbours would be precluded from seeking refuge of MAP, as expressly provided in the safe harbour regulations, the risk of double taxation at headquarter countries is aggravated.

How to benchmark the arm's length price when part of the profits derived by Foreign PE is to be attributed to the Indian PE of the Foreign AE?

7. When a Foreign AE (of an Indian Taxpayer) has a PE in India some challenging issues emerge as is clear from the following:

The PE needs to be treated as a separate hypothetical entity, distinct from its Head Office/Foreign AE (Article 7 of Tax Treaties)

Profits need to be attributed to the PE by assuming that the PE has transacted with its Foreign Head Office at arm's length (Article 7 of the DTAAs)

Profits to PE should be attributed based on arm's length benchmarking under the Transfer Pricing Regulations

Therefore, two separate and distinct bench markings are required: (1) benchmarking to determine the Arm's Length Price (ALP) of transactions between the Indian Taxpayer and its Foreign AE; and (2) benchmarking to determine the profits attributable to the PE, out of total profit derived by the Foreign AE from transactions with the Indian Taxpayer.

In case of Tata Motors European Technical Centre Plc. (supra) the first benchmarking was at issue. The second benchmarking was not in picture because the entire profit from services rendered to Indian AE(TML) was offered to tax in India, apparently by attributing entire profits to the Indian PE. So, there was no question of undertaking any attribution (of profits to PE) exercise.

7.1 What if both the benchmarkings are involved? How to do the benchmarking then?

In such a situation, to attribute arm's length profits to the PE, we will have to carry out two benchmarkings, viz., benchmarking in two stages -

(1)

benchmarking of transaction undertaken by the Indian Taxpayer with its Foreign AE, and

(2)

the benchmarking for attribution of profits from Foreign AE to its Indian PE.

For both stages of benchmarking the mechanism of comparability analysis will be similar – as is laid down in Indian TP Regulations, i.e., selection of Tested Party, selection of Most Appropriate Method, selection of comparables based on Tested Party, Comparability Factors and Reliable Data19.
