Outcome from ITAT

Despite the various measures adopted by the Indian Government, to provide for alternative dispute resolution mechanisms to the taxpayers, an overwhelming number of cases are still landing up before the ITAT. The ITAT too has recognized the requirement of specialized approach to resolve disputes pertaining to transfer pricing and have constituted special benches to address the same across several jurisdictions.

The ITAT has over the past couple of years passed several landmark judgments which has been valuable in respect of providing guidance to taxpayers on how to deal with their transfer pricing issues. The key take aways from these judgments, that are applicable to an IT/BPO company has been with regards to the application of turnover filter, treatment of comparables owning intangibles & brand, threshold limit for related party transactions, functional comparability, market risk etc. However in some cases, like the issue of adjustment for market risk for GICs, the ITAT has principally agreed to the issue and need for risk adjustment, but has not provided any clear direction in respect of the method to be followed.

The ITAT orders have proven to be an invaluable guidance for taxpayers. Although there are several judicial precedents set by the ITAT with respect to the benchmarking/comparability analysis, the Transfer Pricing Officers ("TPO") have not been forthcoming to implement the same in their orders on the reasoning that they have challenged the same before the higher appellate authorities. Hence, even if the taxpayer receives a favourable order from the ITAT for one year, the litigation continues for the subsequent years.

Key Issues/Challenges in the Indian Transfer Pricing Audit process:

Challenges Faced by the Captives/GICs

The Indian IT sector has completed seven rounds of transfer pricing audits and is on the verge of completing the eighth round. Although the TPOs have become more aggressive over the period and are identifying newer transfer pricing issues, the basic issues have remained the same over the years. The Indian Transfer pricing framework principally emphasizes on the 'comparability' analysis for determining the appropriate arm's length price. However, when compared with the international best transfer pricing practices, the Indian framework suffers from certain challenges.

The Indian Rules only allow the use of single year data for the determining the arm's length price of the comparables. Multiple year data, pertaining to not more than two years, can be used only if the taxpayer can prove that the multiple year data has had an impact on the margin earned by it.

Further the Indian regulation provide for the use of 'Arithmetic Mean' instead of the interquartile range to derive the arm's length margin. The arithmetic mean is affected by extreme values or outliers and thus fails as a measure of central tendency. When we adopt arithmetic mean to arrive at the arm's length margin, the presence of even one high margin/loss making comparable can result in a very high/low ALP, thereby distorting the analysis. On the other hand, the interquartile range is a more sophisticated descriptive statistic which eliminates the data points in the bottom and top quarter and is not affected by outliers. This increases the reliability and the robustness of the ALP.

Most GICs are captive delivery centers which receive a steady flow of work from their AEs and hence are shielded from the impacts of business cycle. In return they would typically earn a fixed mark-up every year. In contrast, an independent software developer would experience periodic boom and dip in their business, reflected in the variation in their margin/profitability. Thus to look at the margin of an independent comparable for a single year would not be a true reflection of its general profitability/performance. Use of multiple year data to determine the performance of third party comparables can help in accounting for the impacts of the vagaries of the business cycle and other market and economic factors. However, the same is not allowed as per the Indian Regulations.

The last seven4 years of Transfer Pricing audit experience shows that the TPO has consistently proposed an arm's length price in the range of 20% to 27% for the IT segment. A multiple year margin analysis (from 2001-02 to 2010-11) for all the comparables proposed by the TPO for the past seven years was undertaken. The results showed that the average ALP for the ten year period is similar to the average mark-up enjoyed by most GICs in the IT industry.

Further, the ALP for the ten year period was computed using arithmetic mean and inter-quartile range and the two results were compared. Whereas the ALP computed from arithmetic mean was 15.31%, the interquartile range gave an ALP of 13.97.

To conduct the experiment described in Section 4, we used the previously introduced Indian Tax Authority set of 11 comparable ITES companies.

We compared each test firm to the original arm's-length range established by the 11 companies using the Indian rules. We then calculated (1) whether or not the company is in the range, (2) if the company is below the range, the size of the adjustments to the mean and to the median, and (3) the difference between those adjustments and the "correct" adjustment. For the experiment we assumed that if a company is within the range or above, the Indian Tax Authority would not adjust its tax return.

The Results and Conclusion

The correct aggregate adjustment for the 11 test firms - when we adjust each test firm’s revenue back up to its original amount - would have been Rs. 366 million. This is our benchmark. Two of the test firms, however, were still in or above the arm's-length range. Thus, it is unlikely that their non-arm's-length prices would have garnered attention. The remaining 9 test firms were below the range.

When we adjusted each of these 9 company's NCPM to the set mean, we found that the sum of these adjustments was Rs. 464 million exceeding the correct aggregate adjustment by Rs. 98 million. To put this in perspective, this is an additional tax burden equal to 4.8% of the operating income of the adjusted firms. Since transfer pricing adjustments will only occur with multinational firms it may place them at a substantial disadvantage compared with domestic providers of ITES services.

Alternatively, when we adjusted these same firms to the median of the set, the total adjustment was Rs. 345 million. While much closer to the correct adjustment of Rs. 366, this method of calculation would deprive the Indian Government of Rs. 21 million of tax revenue.

Clearly, due to positive skewness in the dataset, the error resulting from adjustment to the mean is greater than that of adjusting to the median. Yet, as the Indian Tax Authority is committed to adjusting to the mean, we sought to examine a compromise-a third alternative aimed at reducing, to a greater extent, the skewness of the comparable set. As a common way of calculating a meaningful average of a dataset is to remove outliers, we postulated using a "trimmed" mean that might be applied when the comparable set is skewed.

The calculation of a trimmed or truncated mean implies discarding an equal number of the highest and lowest observations. In this case, we trimmed the highest and the lowest observation from the Indian ITES set and recalculated the aggregate adjustment to the mean. As a result, the error in adjustment was only Rs. 14 million, lower than either that of the adjustment to mean or median, noted above. This could be a helpful method of reducing the effect of skewness in data sets, while remaining acceptable to Indian Tax authorities whose law is written in terms of adjusting to the mean.

Our standard for judging the accuracy of a method implicitly took the view of a tax authority seeking to collect an appropriate revenue stream from the multinational firms operating in their jurisdiction collectively. We have not considered the impact on individual firms which were quite varied. Some firms were not adjusted at all as their non-arm's-length pricing was not detected and others were adjusted far more than the known amount of non-arm's-length pricing.

Having established that comparable sets can be skewed and that skewness is directly correlated with an increased difference between the mean and median, it is now time to consider the potential impact on transfer pricing adjustments. The challenge is to determine which method (adjusting to mean or median) might produce a more accurate adjustment.

Our final test endeavors to evaluate the two methods of calculating adjustments (i.e., adjusting to the mean or the median) in an objective and empirical manner. We evaluate this by applying each method to a set of "firms" with known deviations from arm's-length transfer pricing. The method whose adjustment comes closest to that known amount should be the better method.

This methodology presupposes that we know the correct adjustment. In this case we do because we can make manual change to these firms' financial data. We start with the financial data of a firm whose financial results are not affected by related party transactions. We then alter their financial statement to insert a change in the financial statement that reflects the impact of a known amount of non-arm's-length pricing. We now have a financial statement of a new test firm whose results are arm's-length in all ways except for the known change that we have introduced. We do this multiple times to create a whole set of test firms.

To insure comparability between our test firms and the set of comparables, we use the firms in the set of comparables to create the test firms. In this case, we use the set of comparable firms already identified by the India Tax Authority for the ITES industry.

Whether these firms are comparable to any given taxpayer is a separate issue and is dependent on the specific facts and circumstances of each case. We do know, however, that these firms have met the Indian tax authority's standard of being comparable to each other. We are operating on the premise that if Firm A is comparable to some unknown tested party and Firm B is comparable to the same unknown tested party, then Firm A and Firm B should be comparable to each other.

Our experiment is to take each firm in the set of comparables and create a test firm. To create the test firm, we, one at a time, lower each firm's revenue by 15 per cent and hold everything else equal. This test firm is now equivalent to a related party operating in India that has provided all of its services to a foreign related party and that has been undercompensated for these services relative to the arm's-length price. In GE India Technology Centre (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. DIT3 the Bangalore Bench of Tribunal examined issue of selection of comparables in conducting transfer pricing study. The assessee company was carrying on the business of software development and in TP study it adopted comparables which were in the field of development and export of computer software. The assessee contended that even if the assessee is considered as a research and development company, then comparables have to be of the same industry in which the assessee is doing research and development. Since international transactions related to export of customized electronic data, computer software, and any other tangible articles or things as a result of research activity the comparables selected were appropriate in the circumstances of the case. According to the services agreement dated 1-12-2003 the company was to provide research services to the party making such request in different areas of engineering. The TPO observed that the taxpayer was doing the research and development activities and end result is submitted through internet/networking which is reported by the assessee as export of customized electronic data. TPO rejected these comparables on the ground that the company as per its own admission was involved in research and development activity and not in export of computer software. TPO therefore, rejected the assessee's TP study adopting the comparables in the field of computer software holding that they are functionally different. A fresh TP study was made by TPO and three companies were selected out of eight companies engaged in technical consultancy and research and development. The Tribunal held that as far technology related services are concerned TNMM was most appropriate method for computing the arm's length price. However, for purpose of determining arm's length price under TNMM, the FAR analysis as provided in Rule 10B is very essential. So it is essential to consider the correct nature of functions of the assessee to search for the comparables which are engaged in similar functions. It is also essential to take a note of the dissimilarities in the functions of the companies considered for comparison and make suitable adjustments for the same. It further held that TPO had rightly rejected the assessee's TP study as the company was conducting R & D through its multi-disciplinary R&D centre and its activities are for several streams including information technology. On the issue of selection of comparables the Tribunal remanded back the case to Assessing Officer as TPO had not carried out FAR analysis.

Identification of Risk

The CBDT Circular No. 03/2013 also lays emphasis on the identification of risks undertaken by the development centres engaged in contract R& D services. At times taxpayers insist that they are contract R& D service providers with insignificant risks; whereas TPOs treat them full or significant risk bearing entities and therefore, make transfer pricing adjustments. The circular provides various circumstances and conditions on satisfaction of which the development centre in India can be treated as a contract service provider with insignificant risk. It may be worthwhile to mention that there is marked difference between a risk agent and low or insignificant service provider. The nature of risk assumed by the development centre in India would depend upon the role and responsibilities undertaken by the service provider and outcome of the FAR analysis. As held in case of Gap International Sourcing (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4, the FAR analysis provides the broad characterisations of the functions of manufacturer, service provider, and distributor with a further sub-division of low risk service provider, high risk service provider, full-fledged manufacturer, contract manufacturer etc. These characterisations are important to determine the arm's length price of a transaction. But whether the assessee is a risk bearing agent or not is to be considered on the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case. The conditions prescribed in the Board Circular can be a guiding factor but cannot be sufficient to decide the issue.

Location Savings

Location savings is another factor that is considered by transfer pricing authorities during audit. It is considered important when TPO considers TNMM or CUP method as appropriate method by selecting comparable companies engaged in development of intangibles. As per the CBDT Circular No. 02/2013, upward adjustments are required where additional remuneration is not charged for transfer of intangibles due to location savings and location specific advantages of development centres. The Indian approach to adjustments for location savings is also discussed in Chapter 10 of the 'UN Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries5' approved by UN Committee in October 2012. According to Indian tax authorities the expression 'location savings' has wider meaning; it goes beyond the issue of relocating a business from high cost location to a low cost location and relates to any cost advantage. In the Chapter on Indian regulations it is stated that since India provides several location specific advantages to MNE in addition to location savings, the incremental profit from location related advantage can be considered as "location rents".

2.3 Classification issues

A quick perusal of the definitions of these different categories23 indicates that a classification of services on these grounds may be notoriously complicated and require a level of technical expertise in the field of IT that cannot be expected from TPOs. The table below provides an indicative list of possible overlaps: The overlap and the ensuing absurdities may be illustrated by an example. Administering the 'payroll' of a foreign principal is classified explicitly as 'ITES'. However, pension management, employees' health benefits management or retirement benefits management are not strictly 'payroll' and could well be read as 'human resources services'. As a result, companies that manage payroll of current employees satisfy a 20% brightline test; but companies who manage compensation payable to employees after retirement are forced to prove a 25% margin. Similarly, a company that collates data on potential clients of the foreign principal and then 'cold calls' them may be said to be involved in 'data integration', as well as 'business analytics'/'market research'(KPO). On what basis the TPO will distinguish these categories is not clear from the rules.

As the definitions are exhaustive, and not inclusive, some activities that are typically considered as outsourcing processes may fall outside the rules. For example, review of transactional and litigation documents and preparation of due diligence reports are typical KPO activities.24 Yet, these activities are not captured by the term 'legal databases' listed under ITES, or by any of the categories under knowledge process outsourcing.

Further, IT companies often provide ITES and KPO services as a cluster under the same contract. Asking them then to allocate their income to different heads may be impractical.

2.4 Conceptualization and Design

Another aspect of the definition of eligible transactions in the software sector that may run into problems is the fact that the rules exclude research functions that fall within the scope of 'conceptualization' and 'design'.25 In the same breath, they define research services to include seemingly high end activities like the "development of new theorems" or the "development of information technology"26; but also require them to be low end activities that do not involve conceptualisation and design. This definition seems to be poised at a paradox that can be read pedantically to exclude traditional contract research services. For instance, requirement analysis, software testing or minor adaptation to suit local needs are usually outsourced on contract27, but they may easily be bracketed as 'conceptualisation and design'. Requirement analysis which involves enlisting the needs of the client-base from the software, is particularly susceptible as it precedes the code-writing stage. Software testing and subsequent reports that are used to make improvements in the product are also vulnerable to classification as 'conceptualization and design'. Minor adaptation to local needs may easily be bracketed under 'conceptualization and design' if these words are interpreted broadly.

2.5 Insignificant Risk

The rules also prescribe that the eligible assessee rendering ITES, KPO or research services undertake 'Insignificant Risk' to be eligible for safe harbour.28 While the definition per se seems to be consistent with the international understanding that safe harbours be extended to low-end activities, a United Nations appraisal of the practice of TPOs in India indicates that officers require extensive documentation before they accept such a submission.29 Most cases where MNEs have raised arguments as to insignificant risk have been rejected on the grounds of inadequate documentation, and assessees have been classified as firms undertaking substantial risk. There is a danger that TPOs will refuse to recognise that assessees are undertaking insignificant risk under the new rules on the grounds that such a contention was previously rejected before the rules were notified.

Finally, the rules require the Foreign Principal to provide the funds or capital and other economically significant assets including intangibles for research.30 As the criticism of the OECD rules on the same lines indicate31 there is a risk that TPOs will read this pedantically as to exclude transactions where the assessee provides some insignificant intangibles. Industry experts widely hold such a reading to be untenable on the grounds that companies providing contract research services usually have some significant intangibles on their own- such as know-how that they may have developed through experience. Indeed, the problem may be exacerbated by the requirement that capital and funds be provided by the foreign principal. This may lead to the assessee being excluded from the scope of the provisions on slim grounds such as borrowing in its own name from a bank.

The Rationale for the Rate Prescribed:

The operational margin (PBDIT) of 20-30% fixed by the Committee has been widely decried by the Industry as unjustified.32 A number of problems with the Committee's methodology is immediately apparent. The data on which the committee based its decision is not publicly available. Further, the data the committee uses pertain to the A.Y 2008-09.33 Not only is this old, but it also predates the financial crisis and the consequences it had on outsourcing margins. Analysis points to the fact that the operations considered are those bearing negligent risk, and it is implausible that they earn such a broad mark-up. The sector-wise segmentation of the mark-up also seems unjustified on the grounds that the risk profile of the sectors is the same. In addition, what the Rules consider to be activities that are higher on the value chain may also be low-end activities. 34 While the term "Knowledge Process Outsourcing" seems to signify more complex services, experts point out that in reality "human resource" services may mean employee database management; while "engineering and design" may mean converting paper drawings into electronic forms. Thus, a 25% mark-up is not in tune with commercial reality.35 Moreover, the increase in margins from 20 to 22% with the increase in scale may be consistent with the traditional understanding of economies of scale, however, the logic may be misplaced in the low-risk, routine services industry. As the scale increases, the customer may expect a discount for volume which may lower the mark-up. Salaries, which constitute a bulk of the costs of such industries would increase as more people must be recruited to cater to industry demands. As a result, the idea that volume would significantly improve margins may be misguided.

The available data do not corroborate the figure fixed by the Committee. Though studies of the IT/ITES sector in India indicate margins close to or exceeding 20% are frequently reported, importing such data wholesale must be treated with great caution. Such data is based on the performance of the industry leaders like Infosys, Wipro, TCS etc. who often develop their own software products, provide complex services and undertake substantial risk.36 Companies covered by the rules are those that undertake 'insignificant risk', and they cannot be asked to abide by such high benchmarks.

In addition, the Committee accepts that captive centres in developing economies like Philippines or China who offer roughly the same location savings, earn 10%-14% margins.37 No reasons are offered to suggesting that Indian firms enjoy a distinct advantage over these countries, and hence earn higher margins.

More relevant indicators may be found in the ITAT decisions that consider the appropriate profit level indicator of companies with a similar risk profile. Such decisions usually accept margins around 12-15% for software development and ITES Services (as indicated in the table below) and criticise the department's pegging at 20% as unreasonable.

3. Auto-Industry: Unintentional Exclusions

The rules extend a safe harbour to auto component manufacturers and exporters. However, they insist that the assessee export at least 90% of their components to Original Equipment Manufacturers. Original Equipment Manufacturers procure sub-parts from Tier 1 manufacturers and then manufacture more sophisticated components, or assemble various sub-parts. They onsell their wares to automakers, who inturn assemble the final product and sell it to customers.38

The language of the rules complicates the understanding of the scope of the definition. The rules define the eligible international transaction as 'manufacture and export' of auto components. However, they define the 'eligible assessee' as a person, ninety per cent or more of whose turnover is in the nature of sales to an Original Equipment Manufacturer.39

By omitting the qualification that an eligible assessee's turnover must be from sales to an overseas OEM, the rules support the interpretation that an assessee who primarily sells to a domestic OEM, with some negligible sales to a non-resident OEM is covered by the definition. This is because the assessee still satisfies the condition of earning 90% of its turnover from OEMs, and has still engaged in the eligible international transaction of 'manufacture and export' of auto components.

Further OEMs constitute about 30% of the clientele of the auto components industry.40 However, it is unclear how many component industries supply exclusively to OEMs as to meet the stringent threshold of the rules. Around 30% of the clientele of the Auto Component Industry is made up of Tier 1 manufacturers who in turn supply to OEMs, and the rest is divided between Aftermarket sales and Tier II clientele. Excluding firms who supply to such manufacturers is not based on any sound distinction.

A quick perusal of the data indicates that the rate of profitability fixed for auto manufacturers is closer to commercial reality than in the case of the IT sector. An analysis of the Confederation of Indian Industries reports a 10-12% margin for auto-component manufacturers, and includes a number of SMEs in its analysis.41

Thus the aforementioned cases not only rejected the application of the concept of economies of scale to service companies but also struck at the very basis of the turnover filter by breaking the link assumed to be existing between turnovers and margins.

Turnover Filters: The way forward

Does the strong criticism of the turnover filter in the immediately preceding paragraph mean that the turnover filter must be rejected altogether? No - such a measure would be too drastic and uncalled for. Infact, despite the criticism, the turnover filter continues to be applied, though with greater diligence. What is the way forward in establishing an objective, logical and fair use of the turnover filter?

The decision of the High Court of Delhi in Chrys Capital(2015)19 serves in this regard as a guiding light at the end of a tunnel. The High Court observed that "Quantitative and qualitative filters/criteria have been used in different cases to include or exclude comparables. The intuitive logic for excluding big companies from the list of comparables while undertaking the FAR [functions, assets employed and risks undertaken] analysis of a smaller company is attractive, given that such big companies provide services to diverse clientele, perform multifarious functions, often assume risks and employ intangible assets which are specially designed, unlike in the case of smaller companies. The bigger companies have an established reputation in the segment, are well known and employ economies of scale to a telling end. On the other hand, these obvious - and apparent features should not blind the TPO from the obligation to carry out the transfer pricing exercise within the strict mandate of Section 92C and Rules 10A to 10E."

Taking a cue from this decision in Chrys Capital(2015)20, one may proceed with the understanding that determining the arm's length price in India is based on choosing the most appropriate method and conducting a comparability analysis. Where a comparable meets each of the standards enumerated in Rule 10B(2) and the differences between the potential comparable and the taxpayer, if any, can be appropriately eliminated under Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 then the comparable gets a thumbs up in the comparability analysis. Any application of a quantitative filter must not result in the bypassing of this qualitative analysis on the basis of assumed 'the intuitive logic' described in Chrys Capital(2015)21 above. A similar view was also taken in Capgemini (2013)22 and Willis Processing(2013)23.

Thus, taking the liberty of making some suggestions, turnover filters must be applied -

Firstly, by keeping in mind that the purpose to be achieved by the turnover filters as by any quantitative filter is to reduce the effort involved in having to go through a large number of potential comparables during the qualitative analysis, and not as an alternative to conducting a thorough qualitative analysis in accordance with Rules 10B(2) and 10B(3) wherein comparability is tested on a large number of factors and which form the basis of comparability under the Indian transfer pricing regulations.

Secondly, on the basis of the facts of each case; rigid classifications as being cast text stone must be avoided in order to prevent judgments such as the one in McAfee Software(2015)24 (discussed above) where as many as seven companies were excluded as comparables by the ITAT on a very technical application of the turnover filters without any comprehensive comparability analysis.

Thirdly, keeping in mind the grind involved in shifting through the large number of companies with relatively smaller turnovers, a lower turnover filter is desirable. It is also required because smaller turnovers are often suggestive of one of the three situations that the company is in reducing stage, the company is a start-up or the company is winding up. Each of these three situations are avoidable for the purposes of comparability. Thus, a lower turnover filter is a necessity.

4. Intra-group Services

i.

Categorization into Software/BPO/KPO/Contract R&D for Software

Internationally, one of the biggest challenges with adoption of Safe Harbours has been over the interpretation of core and non-core services by taxpayers, leading to several controversies between the taxpayers and the Revenue officials. This may be perceived as a forewarning in the Indian context as the suggested industry sub-classification in the draft rules may be subject to varying interpretation by taxpayers.

For instance, it may be difficult to clearly assign some companies into BPO or KPO as several of the activities defined under these buckets are closely related and often overlapping. Moreover, many companies may offer all or some of these services to their customers, which may make segregation of operating revenue and operating costs for individual service lines a challenge.

Again, some of the services classified under KPO may not necessitate advanced analytical and technical skills, for instance in some cases, Human Resource services may comprise just employee database management; Engineering and design services may include low-end conversion of drawings from 2D to 3D, and Market research services may include only business support and collation of available information from public domain. In this context, the functional, asset and risk profile of such companies would be closer to that of a BPO than a KPO.

A similar dilemma over interpretation of the nature of services is expected to arise between Software and Contract R&D for Software as there is substantial overlap in the activities defined under both the heads. According a separate classification to Contract R&D for Software, distinct from Software Development services is bound to lead to complexities and potential litigation.

The above assumes particular importance in light of the fact that the Safe Harbour proposed for BPO/Software Development is OP/OE equal to or greater than 20% while that for KPO/Contract R&D for Software Development is OP/OE equal to or greater than 30%. The significant variation makes it imperative that the dividing line between the various activities be extremely well defined. On the other hand, it may also be worthwhile to consider whether, given the substantial overlap between the various activities, the line of divide can be completely removed and a uniform profit margin can be prescribed across the board for all underlying service categories.

ii.

High Margins

The most noticeable aspect about the draft Safe Harbours is the high margins notified for the various types of services, particularly for KPO and Contract R&D services of 29-30%. While a certain premium above the arm's length margins was expected by taxpayers in order to factor in the benefits of certainty and compliance relief, the presently notified margins are being perceived to be well beyond any such acceptable premiums.

As per the Rangachary Committee report, these Safe Harbour margins have been determined on the basis of the arm's length margins arrived at by Revenue Officials during the course of Transfer Pricing audits. This may not be a reasonable proposition as a large number of the Transfer Pricing adjustments made by Revenue officials on the basis of such arm's length margins have been overturned by Tax Tribunals/High Court in India on subsequent appeals by the taxpayers. Profit margins are perceived by taxpayers as a decisive factor in opting for the Safe Harbour route. In order for Safe Harbours to evoke the necessary interest from taxpayers and be widely utilized as a dispute avoidance mechanism, it is therefore critical that such high profit margins are re-evaluated and revised appropriately in the final rules.

iii.

Insignificant risk criteria

An important aspect that warrants detailed consideration is the condition of 'insignificant risk' that has been closely integrated with the Safe Harbour for captive service providers. The condition stipulates that the foreign principal should perform economically significant functions, provide necessary capital and funds and own the economically significant assets including intangibles. Further the monitoring and supervision of the taxpayer's activities should vest with the foreign principal. Most importantly, the conduct rather than the contractual terms between the taxpayer and the foreign principal should demonstrate that key business risks are borne by the foreign principal while the Indian captive is insulated from them.

3. Acceptance/rejection of comparables earning abnormally high margins

As per Para 1.47 of the OECD Guidelines, where the application of one or more methods produces a range of figures, a substantial deviation among points in that range may indicate that the data used in establishing some of the points may not be as reliable as the data used to establish the other points in the range or that the deviation may result from features of the comparable data that require adjustments. In such cases, further analysis of those points may be necessary to evaluate their suitability for inclusion in any arm's length range.

Further, Para 3.63 of the OECD Guidelines lay down that, extreme results might consist of losses or unusually high profits. Extreme results can affect the financial indicators that are looked at in the chosen method (e.g. the gross margin when applying a resale price, or a net profit indicator when applying a transactional net margin method). When one or more of the potential comparables have extreme results, further examination would be needed to understand the reasons for such extreme results.

Thus, the OECD Guidelines lay down that in a comparability analysis which throws up more than one comparable, the extreme results or 'outliers' need to be examined in greater detail to understand if there are any abnormal reasons for such extreme results and in such a case they need to excluded. In many foreign jurisdictions where the concept of inter-quartile range is followed, the outliers are automatically rejected. The concept of inter-quartile range also finds support in the UN Practice Manual.

However, under the Indian Income Tax law, the proviso to section 92C(2) provides that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the arithmetic mean of such prices.

The Indian Transfer Pricing administration believes it is possible to use the profit split method to determine arm's length allocation of location savings and rents in cases where comparable uncontrolled transactions are not available.

India being a low cost jurisdiction attracts the attention of a lot of MNE groups who intend to exploit the advantages of location savings and LSAs. As a result it may well be argued that the any tangible benefit accruing to such MNE groups is not exclusive and hence does not provide any durable competitive advantage. 1. Functional comparability

As per Para 1.33 of the OECD Guidelines, application of the arm's length principle is generally based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with conditions in transactions between independent enterprises. For such comparison to be appropriate, the economically relevant characteristics of the situations being compared must be sufficiently comparable. The concept of comparability has been further elucidated by stating that, to be comparable means that none of the differences (if any) between the situations being compared could materially affect the condition being examined in the methodology (e.g. price or margin), or that reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the effect of any such differences.

Para 1.36 lays down the factors that may be considered when determining comparability between controlled and uncontrolled transactions and enterprises. These factors are listed as below:

Characteristics of the property or services transferred,

Functions performed by the parties (taking into account assets used and risks assumed),

Contractual terms,

Economic circumstances of the parties, and

Business strategies pursued by the parties

The above referred principles have also been reiterated in the UN Practice Manual.

The principles of comparability under the Indian Income Tax law also largely mirror the above referred principles laid down in the OECD Guidelines. The same are listed under Rule 10B(2) and Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 ('Rules').

1. TYPICAL BUSINESS MODEL

Typically, Indian outbound IT companies have set up subsidiaries in overseas jurisdictions in order to market their services1. Generally, these companies follow the onsite-offshore model whereby a portion of the project is executed onsite at the client's premises by the subsidiaries and the remainder is offshored to software development centres in India. The typical functions performed by the overseas subsidiaries include the following:

i.

Marketing

ii.

Selling which includes negotiation and concluding of contracts with end customers

iii.

Entering into contracts with end customers for both, onsite and offshore work

iv.

Subcontracting the work to its Indian parent and carrying out onsite activities at client premises

It is relevant to note that the foreign subsidiaries of different Indian multinational groups may perform the above functions at varied levels of intensity i.e. some subsidiaries may perform all the above functions whereas others may perform a more limited function of marketing. Based on the intensity of the functions, the subsidiaries can be characterised either as marketing service providers or as distributors of services which in turn determine the manner of remunerating them. Depending on the intensity of functions, subsidiaries are remunerated as a percentage of the following:

revenue (gross profit), or

net margin of revenues, or

the local costs of subsidiaries (i.e. cost plus mark-up).

The balance revenue earned by overseas subsidiaries from end clients is paid to the Indian parent as remuneration for rendering offshore and related support services.

The Indian parent is significantly involved in driving the entire corporate strategy for the group, developing software products, undertaking R&D, supporting subsidiaries by providing offshore technical expertise and strategic guidance and the service delivery to end clients in relation to the work offshored by the subsidiary. At times, the Indian parent may have to provide a performance guarantee to the end clients of the overseas subsidiaries in order to guarantee the due and timely performance of the obligations agreed. Alternately, a comfort letter is also issued by the Indian parent stating that the overseas subsidiary is part of the same Indian group.

Further, the Indian parent companies also financially assist the subsidiaries by investing in the share capital, providing loans and financial guarantees for working capital or for the purpose of acquisition.

2. CHARACTERISATION OF OVERSEAS SUBSIDIARY AND INTER ALIA SELECTION OF TESTED PARTY AND PLI

Issue

Indian tax authorities, in the case of Indian outbound IT companies, have been typically contending that overseas subsidiaries carry out only marketing functions. Hence, the remuneration policy of percentage of revenue (gross profit) or net margin of revenue is not in line with the functions performed by them and subsidiaries should only be remunerated on a cost plus mark-up and the balance revenues should be passed on to the Indian parent.

Further, citing lack of reliable third-party data in the overseas jurisdiction, tax authorities prefer selecting the Indian parent as the tested party for benchmarking the arm's length margin.

In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the two critical elements of a transfer pricing analysis, viz. the FAR analysis and the economic analysis, cannot be isolated. Characterisation of the entities and inter alia selection of a tested party is the first step in any economic analysis and must find its 'connect' back with the FAR analysis.

While the concept of 'tested party' does not find any mention in Indian regulations, the concept has been laid down in the US regulations, OECD Guidelines as well as the recently released UN TP Manual.

Bottleneck in TP

In a transfer pricing matter more often than not we get to read an observation or a remark by the Courts and Tribunal/DRP that 'we are unable to treat this company fit for comparability analysis for determining the arm's length price for the assessee in the absence of segmental details'. Also benches of the Tribunal in more than one instance have held that 'segmental results does not give a true picture and may not be always be correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses. The Delhi bench of the ITAT in DHL Express (India) (P.) Ltd v. Asstt CIT (2012) 12 ITR (Trib) 658 held that the assessee's objection for rejecting the Transport Corporation of India as comparable is also devoid of any merits, because when pro per comparable companies are available, there is no requirement for making comparison with segmental results which does not give a true picture. Later it also remarked that it is a known fact that segmental results may not be always correct and precise because it is almost impossible to distribute certain common expenses.

However, till date there is no law or section that bars a comparable being chosen on segmental results basis. Transfer pricing is a subjective phenomenon where the assessee has all the right to substantiate its price on whatever material is available with him which may even be in the form of segmental results of an enterprise. Rule 10D proviso says it all on such right given to the assessee. The words 'on the basis of material available with him' in the proviso are sheer pointer to this fact. Hence the view held by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal to hold that segmental results are untrue and unreliable is not in accordance with the law.

Inclusion or exclusion of a comparable make a vital difference in the determination of arms length price because of which a transfer pricing study could actually fail.

It is therefore important that the proviso to rule 10D must also be read as sufficient a provision that enables production of segmental results as a material relevant in the exercise of determination of arm's length price.

It is an irony that on one hand we complain that segmental results are not available and right on the other side we hold stand that the segmental results are not true. These disconnects have to go somehow from the judicial interface.

TP Criteria

In the prime most it is desirable to have the segmental details for revenue/sales of varieties of product and service dealt by an enterprise. At the same time the financials must also provide for segmental details of operating income of respective variety of product and services. These two are essentials for assessing the comparability for carrying out study and determination of arms length price with a testing party. Accounting Standard 17 further states that an enterprise should comply with the requirements of this Standard fully and not selectively. However often we find that there is unallocated sums that are adjusted against the total income for one reason or the other. This kind of reporting goes adverse to the accounting standard and must also be reported as a qualification by the auditor in their report.

Now the proviso to rule 10D of the Income tax Rules, 1962 require upon an assessee to substantiate on the basis of material available with him that the income arising from international transactions entered into by him has been computed in accordance with section 92. One is expected to maintain prescribed documents for this purpose if the value of international transactions exceeds Rs. 1 crore. To substantiate one's price one is required to have matching results of operation of a comparable company. Often there is a difficulty to make such an assessment in the absence of similar comparable hence one employ software with various kind of filters to arrive at one lot of comparables. And out of these some fails for one reason or the other as we go up in the ladder before dispute resolution process, Tribunal and Courts.

If we have segmental accounting in its proper form and substance the entire exercise of transfer pricing could be made more simpler and accurate.

The Information Technology ("IT")/ Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") sector in India has experienced spectacular growth over the past decade and half. The Indian success story in the global outsourcing industry has become a leading example for other developing economies. While this growth model has been discussed from a macro level widely, it is important to study the same from a micro level to understand and evaluate the challenges and advantages faced by the various players who have been a catalyst to this chronicle. This article aims to appraise the Indian IT sector from a transfer pricing perspective.

The Indian IT industry has several players, each of whom faces unique transfer pricing challenges. This article provides an overview of the Indian IT/BPO outsourcing industry, the players and the transfer pricing framework that they operate in.

The Indian IT landscape can be broadly classified based on the nature of players operating in the industry. On one end of the spectrum, there are Indian IT giants like Wipro, Infosys, HCL etc. who represent Indian IT outbound investment in the global IT industry. These are predominantly Indian multinationals that have subsidiaries and branch offices across the globe. On the other end of the spectrum there are Global In-House centers (GIC) or 'captive services providers' who operate as delivery centers for foreign IT Multinationals Corporation ("MNCs") and represent the inbound investment in the Indian IT sector.

The GIC1 segment which till 2003, constituted a very small part of the IT/BPO industry has witnessed spectacular growth over the past few years. Currently the segment contributes to 22% of India's IT-BPO revenue and accounts for almost 21% of the industry's employment. Based on the latest available data, this segment has grown at a CAGR of 22% between 2003 -2010. In the fiscal year 2009-10, the Indian GICs contributed to almost 1% of the national GDP†. Spanning across all the major cities of India the segment provides direct and indirect employment to about 1.8 million people2.

The GIC model has played an important role in the IT/BPO outsourcing industry globally. This model originated in the 80s and 90s, when several big MNCs realized they could substantially lower their operating cost by opening delivery centers in low cost locations like India. The GIC model has been a global success for the IT Industry. Not only has it helped parent MNCs to lower their operational cost, it has boosted the economies of the offshoring locations as well. As per a Nasscom –Everest Report, presently there are about 3000 GICs operating around the globe in various countries.

The Indian IT Industry watch-dog, Nasscom reports that there are presently about 750 IT/BPO MNCs in India and they operate across almost all the verticals like Aerospace & Defence, Automotive, BFSI, Bio-Technology, Chemicals, Computer Hardware, Education, Electronic/Electrical Equipment, Energy, Healthcare, Industrial, Semiconductors, Software/Internet, and Telecommunications, etc. Engineering, Research and Development (ER&D) and Software Product Development companies form the largest segment within the Indian captive industry. This particular segment has especially witnessed a tremendous growth in MNCs opening their ER&D delivery centers in India over the past couple of years. Geography-wise, North America and Europe comprise 90 per cent of this segment in India.

Although India still remains one of the preferred GIC locations in the world, MNCs are increasingly looking towards other low cost destinations like the Philippines, East Asia, Eastern Europe Latin America and even Africa for opening new delivery centers to further their cost arbitrage benefit. Thus, while it is easy to bask in the glory of the success story that India has paved in the realm of the IT Industry, it is crucial to watch out for competition in other emerging IT capabilities in Asia, South America and other parts of the globe. Countries like Philippines, Cost Rica, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Argentina, Sri Lanka etc. have witnessed remarkable growth in IT exports in their economy in the recent past. Being at the nascent stage of the IT Industry, the volume of exports by these economies has been low. But the growth rates experienced by them have been well above the average growth rates of large exporters like the European Union, India and the United States. Between 2005 to 20113 the Philippines IT exports has grown at 69%, Ukraine witnessed a growth of 59% in IT service exports, followed by Argentina and Costa Rica at 37% and 35% respectively.

4. Indian Case Law: What the Tribunals Are Actually Doing

4.1 Dresser-Rand India Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT — The Service-by-Service Test [ITA No. 8753/Mum/2010] The Mumbai ITAT's decision in Dresser-Rand India is methodologically significant for a straightforward reason: the Tribunal refused to accept or reject the management fee in its entirety. Instead, it examined each service category individually against the benefit test. This 'dissection' approach has since become standard methodology in Indian TP litigation.

Dresser-Rand India paid its US parent for a bundled package of services: management oversight, strategic planning, IT infrastructure support, procurement benchmarking, and specialised HR compensation advisory. The Revenue argued that all of this was either shareholder oversight or duplicative of what the Indian management team already did. The taxpayer produced email correspondence with the parent's functional teams, reports received, participation in group management calls, and a cost-plus benchmarking analysis showing a 10% mark-up within the arm's length range.

The outcome was a partial disallowance of approximately 35% of the charge. The Tribunal accepted charges for IT infrastructure support, procurement benchmarking, and specialised HR advisory — where direct delivery evidence existed and where the parent's specific functional competency was demonstrated. It disallowed the general management oversight and strategic planning fees, finding them indistinguishable from shareholder oversight and duplicative of what the Indian management team performed.

The Tribunal drew a useful analytical distinction between what it called 'capability enhancement' services — where the parent provided a specific functional skill not available in India at equivalent cost — and 'capability substitution' services — where the parent was simply providing a more sophisticated version of functions the Indian entity already performed. Only the former survived the benefit test.

The documentation lesson from this case is equally important. The Revenue challenged documents submitted post-assessment as not meeting the contemporaneity standard. The Tribunal accepted contemporaneous records — including informal emails and reports created in the ordinary course — but treated post-audit reconstructions with heightened scepticism. The message: emails and reports generated in the normal course of business operations carry more weight than anything assembled after the inquiry begins.

4.2 Sony India Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT — The Bundled Charge Problem [ITA No. 1026/DEL/2015)

Sony India paid its Japanese parent an integrated charge combining royalties for the Sony brand and technology licences with management service fees covering commercial strategy, supply chain coordination, and marketing support. The aggregate payment was approximately 6.5% of net sales, structured under a single master intercompany agreement.

Sony argued that the integrated structure reflected genuine commercial practice — in the consumer electronics and brand-licensing industry, brand access and management support are commercially inseparable. Bifurcating the arrangement would be economically artificial.

The Delhi ITAT rejected this argument. It held that Indian transfer pricing law requires independent analysis of each element of a controlled transaction. The integrated structure could not immunise the service component from scrutiny. The Tribunal proceeded to evaluate the service component separately and found the documentation insufficient to demonstrate that specific services were delivered and specifically utilised by Sony India — rather than being part of a group-wide programme from which Sony India benefited incidentally.

The practical lesson from Sony India is direct: bundled charges carry higher audit risk than separately identified service charges. Revenue-based allocation formulas for services whose delivery cost does not scale with revenue invite challenge. And an integrated intercompany agreement — however commercially logical — will be pulled apart if it does not allow the transfer pricing officer to isolate and evaluate each element.

5. Key Practical Issues: Where Structures Typically Break Down

5.1 Services Exist on Paper, Not in Reality

The most fundamental failing is also the most common: the intercompany agreement describes services that were never actually performed — or performed so superficially that no sensible officer would accept them as genuine. A management services agreement signed at year-end, charging 2% of revenue for 'strategic advisory and management support', with no supporting records of what was actually delivered, is not a transfer pricing structure. It is a management fee with a transfer pricing label.

The test, at its most basic, is this: can the taxpayer show, with contemporaneous records, that specific services were actually delivered to the Indian entity? Not that the parent company has these functions. Not that the group performed well. But that specific outputs — reports, recommendations, decisions, systems, training — were received and used by the Indian entity.

5.2 Confusing Shareholder Activities with Chargeable Services

This is the most persistent conceptual error in intra-group service structuring. Parents routinely charge for activities that are, in substance, shareholder oversight: board-level monitoring, group-wide risk management reviews, investor relations strategy, consolidated reporting processes. These costs belong to the parent; they cannot be allocated downward.

Our perspective

As a general rule, entrepreneurs should not be considered 'tested parties' and accordingly benchmarked. By virtue of their complex functional and risk profiles, their margins fluctuate heavily with the vagaries of the economy, thus making comparability analysis difficult and unreliable. Further, the financial results of the entrepreneur, being the ultimate fall-out of third-party business, often depend on external economic factors in the market and not on internal pricing policies.

Typically, a 'tested party' would be the

–

Characteristics of the property, goods or services

Functions performed, assets employed and risks assumed

Contractual terms

Market conditions and economic circumstances

Further, an uncontrolled transaction shall be comparable to an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction, if —

none of the differences between the transactions being compared, or between the enterprises entering into such transactions are likely to materially affect the price or cost charged or paid in or the profit arising from such transactions in the open market; or

(ii) reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the material effects of such differences17.

On basis of criteria and conditions laid out above, we may select Indian Comparables when the Indian Taxpayer is chosen as the Tested Party. Conversely, we may select Foreign Comparables when the Foreign AE is chosen as the Tested Party.

So, Foreign Comparables can be considered for benchmarking under the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations when Foreign AE is chosen as the Tested Party, for the reason that reliable data of Indian Comparables is not available.

Next we look at another interesting issue.

6. How to do benchmarking and select comparables when the Foreign AE also has a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India?

6.1 Case of Tata Motors European Technical Centre Plc.'s case (supra)

[Note: The peculiarity of this case is that the Assessee is a Foreign Company, not an Indian Company.]

6.1.1 Facts of the case : The assessee (a Foreign Company), Tata Motor European Technical Centre PLC (TMETC), was incorporated in the United Kingdom (UK). It was a resident of UK and a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Motors Ltd. (TML – an Indian Company). The assessee rendered automotive design and engineering services to Tata Motors Ltd. (TML). For rendering these services the assessee-company sent its employees in India. Those employees were engineers and technical personnel deputed at TML's factory and establishment in India. Thus, the assessee had a Service Permanent Establishment (Service PE) in India.

6.1.2 Assessee's Benchmarking: The assessee benchmarked its service transaction by taking into account the following factors –

The design and engineering services for automotive industries were highly specialized services. Considering the nature of automotive industries in terms of global standards, competition, and growing compliance requirements towards safety and environmental norms, the parallels (or comparables) were not available in India.

The major operation cost incurred by the PE was towards the salary of the employees who had special skills and knowledge. Those employees were paid salary only in the UK.

The PE did not have any independent business in India and it did not enter into any contract with any outside party in India.

Considering these factors the assessee took itself (Foreign AE) as the Tested Party to apply TNMM. Accordingly, comparables located in the UK, rendering similar kind of services, were selected for benchmarking.

6.1.3 Transfer Pricing Officer's view: The Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO), however, observed as under -

Selection of foreign comparables based in the UK was not tenable under the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations.

Because the PE of the assessee was located in India and was carrying on its business within the Indian territory, it had to be treated as a business entity in India, akin to the other corporate entities doing business in India.

Further, assessee's direct and indirect costs were incurred in and in connection with business transactions in India.

In view of the above facts, the TPO held that only Indian comparables had to be selected for benchmarking the assessee's margin.

6.1.4 ITAT's decision in the case :

The decision rendered in the case by the ITAT has been summarized below:

(i)

Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not specify that the comparability analysis of International Transactions has to be strictly with reference to Indian comparables.

(ii)

The Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations, while selecting comparable companies for carrying out the comparability analysis, lay emphasis on FAR analysis and conditions prevailing in the markets in which the parties operate18. If such comparability analysis cannot be done properly by taking Indian comparables - looking to the characteristics and nature of the functions performed and services rendered - then one must consider who should be selected as "Tested Party".

(iii)

Based on selection of the Tested Party, comparables are to be chosen taking into account the economic factors and the functions performed in the conditions prevalent in the location of the tested party.

(iv)

If the tested party itself is foreign based and the services rendered by it are very specific, for which the Indian comparables are not available, or functionally not comparable, then it cannot be held that foreign comparables cannot be selected for benchmarking the Arm's Length Price or margin.

(v)

Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not put any fetters on selection of foreign comparables, if conditions are as such that the Indian comparables do not stand the test of comparability with the tested party.

(vi)

If the tested party has been selected consistent with the functional analysis of the controlled transaction and is the least complex party to the controlled transaction, then even if it is a foreign party, the same should be taken as the basis for carrying out comparability analysis with the uncontrolled transaction by taking into account the business environment in the country where the tested party is being benchmarked.

The Indian IT/ITeS industry is split into four broad segments, viz., Hardware, Software, Services, and Business Process Management ('BPM'). These segments are further sub-divided into the following sub-segments

Figure 1: Segmentation of IT/ITeS market in India

Overview of captives in the Indian IT/ITeS space

Historically the term 'captive' has been used to refer to entities located in low cost geographies, providing 'service delivery operations' to entities within its Group located in different geographies. Thus captives (also referred to as Global In-house Centers ['GICs'] or 'captive IT/ITeS entities') act as an extension of a Multi National Enterprise ('MNE') group, set up to leverage labour arbitrage in certain geographies. Usually only low value adding functions/processes are outsourced to such captives, implying that they act as a cost center for the MNE group which in turn remunerates them on a cost plus mark-up.

Following are the strategic advantages derived by an MNE group in setting up a captive entity:

Labour arbitrage opportunities;

Operational efficiency, where the captives provide cost efficient operations with continuous productivity improvements;

Providing scalability to the MNE Group's business through access to a large talent pool providing high skill capabilities;

Protection of Intellectual Property Rights ('IPRs') of the Group as all the innovations and new product development by the Group need not be shared with third parties.

According to latest estimates of NASSCOM, there are over 825 GICs in India offering IT/ITeS services across Tier I/II/III cities in India. These GICs occupy a very prominent space in the Indian IT/ITeS industry with an employee base of over 530,000 people (comprising 20 per cent of the IT/ITeS employee base in India) and accounting for 17 per cent of the overall IT export revenues in India.2

Application of Transfer Pricing in the Captive IT/ITeS space

Since the MNE Group and the GICs are located in different geographies, the provision of services by the GICs to the MNE Group attracts Transfer Pricing scrutiny under the local tax laws. As referred, the MNE Groups generally outsource low value adding functions to GICs which are performed as per detailed specifications provided by the MNE Group. Since the GICs render services only within the Group and are remunerated on a fixed cost plus mark basis, they don't bear many of the risks associated with entrepreneurial development activity such as market risk, contract risk, financial risk, credit risk etc. Hence the GICs can be categorized as 'low risk contract service providers'.

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ('OECD') has laid down Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations (broadly referred to as 'OECD Guidelines'). The principles outlined under these OECD Guidelines are followed by many countries in drafting their Transfer Pricing laws. While India does not follow the OECD Guidelines, it acts as an observer nation.

As per Para 1.42 of the OECD Guidelines, compensation in a transaction between two enterprises usually reflects the function that each enterprise performs, taking into account the assets used and the risks assumed. Accordingly functional analysis of an international transaction forms the pillar of a Transfer Pricing exercise. Further, as per Para 1.45, material risks assumed by each party to the transaction have to be considered as part of any functional analysis, since the assumption or allocation of risks would influence the conditions of transactions between associated enterprises. Usually in an open market (implying in an arm's length dealing between independent enterprises), the assumption of increased risk would be compensated by an increase in the expected return.

The concept is further explained in Para 1.47 where it is concluded that a contract research provider (akin to a captive IT/ITeS entity) that takes on no meaningful risk would usually expect only a limited return. Accordingly, the relationship between the risk and return profile of associated enterprises in international transactions can be illustrated through Figure 2 below.

Figure 2: Graphical representation of the relationship between the function, asset and risk profile of an entity and its capacity to generate profits

Hence, it can be deduced that low risk entities should have a transfer pricing policy that allows them to generate low but stable benefits. On the other hand, high risk entities will usually have a transfer pricing policy that allows them to generate significant profits or losses. This is consistent with the remuneration model of GICs which are generally remunerated on a cost plus fixed markup for their routine activities. Hence, whether the MNE Group earns supernormal profits or losses, the GIC would always earn a stable but limited return.

Step 7 - Identification of potential comparables (i.e., determining the key characteristics to be met by any uncontrolled transaction in order to be regarded as potentially comparable based on relevant factors identified in Step 3):—There are basically two ways in which the identification of potentially comparable third party transactions can be conducted, i.e., additive approach and deductive approach. It has been held that a blind application of precedent cannot per se be a ground for excluding or including comparables unless factual and functional analysis are carried out—PCIT v. ST Microelectronics (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 262/251 Taxman 484 (Delhi). Any inclusion or exclusion of comparables per se cannot be treated as a question of law unless it is demonstrated to the Court that the ITAT or any other lower authority took into account irrelevant consideration or excluded relevant factors in ALP determination that impact significantly; unless it is demonstrated that there are important functional dissimilarities or vital material facts which go to route of profitability or other material circumstances are involved—PCIT v. Step 8 - Determination of, and making, comparability adjustments (where appropriate):—Where there are differences between the situations being compared that could materially affect the comparison, comparability adjustments must be made, where possible, to improve the reliability of the comparison. Therefore, comparability adjustments should be considered if and only if they are expected to increase the reliability of the results. Relevant considerations include the materiality of the difference for which an adjustment is being considered, the quality of data subject to adjustment, the purpose of the adjustment and the reliability of the approach used to make adjustment. Some examples of comparability adjustments include adjustments for accounting consistency designed to eliminate differences that may arise from different accounting practices between the controlled and uncontrolled transactions, segmentation of financial data to eliminate significant non-comparable transactions, adjustments for differences in capital, functions, assets, risks, capacity utilization1, happening of any abnormal events such as strike.2

However, such adjustments would not be made where the assessee is not able to demonstrate or establish that such an adjustment is relevant and backed up by sufficient evidence—Indian Additives Ltd. v. DCIT [2019] 108 taxmann.com 117/265 Taxman 383 (Mad.).

Step 9—Interpretation and use of data collected, determination of the arm's length remuneration.

10A.18 The concept of re-categorisation of transaction is not identical (or similar) to aggregation or segregation of transactions. Re-categorisation of transaction is a different exercise and would result in re-categorisation of the functions and, therefore, accordingly the comparables. Aggregation or segregation of transactions accepts that the transactions per se do not require re-categorisation of transactions. [2019] 103 taxmann.com 343/262 Taxman 215 (Bom.). 10A.17-8 Quasi-capital loans with normal loans - Usually, loan transactions are benchmarked on the basis of interest rate applicable on said transactions simpliciter which, under the transfer pricing regulations, cannot be compared with a transaction which is something materially different than a loan simpliciter, for example, a non-refundable loan which is to be converted into equity. It is in this context that the loan, which is in the nature of quasi capital, is treated differently than the normal loan transactions. The expression 'quasi capital' is relevant from the point of view of highlighting that a quasi capital loan or advance is not a routine loan transaction simpliciter. The substantive reward for such a loan transaction is not interest but opportunity to own capital. As a corollary to this position, in the cases of quasi capital loans or advances, the comparison of the quasi capital loans is not with the commercial borrowings but with the loans or advances which are given in the same or similar situations. Advances being in the nature of 'quasi capital' cover the situations in which (a) advances were made as capital could not be subscribed to due to regulatory issues and the advancing of loans was only for the period till the same could be converted into equity, and (b) advances were made for subscribing to the capital but the issuance of shares was delayed, even if not inordinately. Clearly, the advances in such circumstances were materially different than the loan transactions simpliciter and that is what was decisive so far as determination of the arm's length price of such transactions was concerned. The reward for time value of money in these cases was opportunity to subscribe to the capital, unlike in a normal loan transaction where reward is interest, which is measured as a percentage of the money advanced. On a conceptual note, several types of debts, particularly long-term unsecured debts, and revenue participation investments could be termed as quasi-capital—Soma Textile & Industries Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 152/154 ITD 745 (Ahmd. - Trib.).

Where assessee received certain amount from its AE on account of reimbursement of expenses in respect of expat tax paid on behalf of employees deputed by parent company, there being no element of service in such reimbursement, it was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM. As observed in the OECD commentaries referred to in the Circular No. 872R, dated 27-9-1999 of the Canada Customs and Revenue Agency, it is important to distinguish between the situation of a taxpayer who renders services for the other members of a group; and a taxpayer who acts solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In the latter situation, the arm's length compensation would be limited to rewarding the agency role. In such a case, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. Whether a taxpayer is providing a service or merely acting as an agent on behalf of the group is a question of fact. In the present case, the details given before DRP clearly showed that what assessee received as reimbursement from AE was nothing but expat tax paid and interest paid on delay in payment of TDS and there could be no element of service in such payment. The taxpayer should be considered as having acted solely as an agent on behalf of the group to acquire services from an arm's length party. In such cases, it would not be appropriate to determine an arm's length charge by referring to a markup on the cost of the services acquired from an arm's length party. It is therefore held that the reimbursement of expenses was to be excluded from revenues and costs for comparability analysis under TNMM and TPO was to be directed to compute ALP after such exclusion—Tesco Hindustan Service Centre (P.) 10A.17-7 Related party transactions - As a rule of prudence, so far as possible a comparable should be considered having no related party transaction. However, it is practically not possible to find out a comparable having no related party transaction. Therefore, a reasonable percentage of the total revenue from the related party transaction can be considered for selecting an uncontrolled comparable. In the normal circumstances, where a good number of comparables are available, then the limit of related party transactions should be 15% of the total revenue and in such case, an entity can be considered as uncontrolled, if related party transactions do not exceed 15% of the total revenue. 15% is an average and should be generally accepted in normal cases as a related party filter.

In cases where comparables are not available in sufficient number, then this threshold limit of related party transaction can be relaxed to 20% of the total revenue. The relaxation upto 20% is purely with a view to make it possible that a larger number of entities are taken as comparable so that the ALP so determined should be based on a broad based and technically represents price in the free market.

In an extreme case where only one or few comparables are available, then an entity having related party transactions not exceeding 25% of the total revenue can be considered so that the ALP should be determined having comparison broad based, though this extreme limit of 25% can be considered only in exceptional cases.
