Thus, if the comparables with 1/6th of the highest margin are acceptable to the assessee then, there is no reason for the assessee to be aggrieved with the comparables of TPO where average margin is within twice the highest margin, case selected by the assessee.

The objection of the assessee will be valid only if there is material to show that high margin in case of high end services is because of nature of activities. But as it has been pointed out earlier, no such material had been produced, therefore, the argument advanced based on low end/high end services in the ITES activities has to be rejected. [Para 20.4]

With broad proposition laid down above, it is necessary to deal with the comparables individually to find out if they are suitable for comparison:

ACCENTIA TECHNOLOGIES LTD.

This comparable has been objected to by the assessee on the ground of functional differences. It has been pointed out that in addition to medical transcription and billing and coding, this company is also involved in software sales.

There is no segment wise result available in case of medical transcription and billing and coding. It is not known by how much the margin is affected by trading in software. Therefore, this company could not be considered as a good comparable. [Para 21.1]

APEX KNOWLEDGE SOLUTIONA LTD.

The assessee has objected to the selection of this comparable on the ground that it is engaged in computer software and database creation services. The annual report of the company for the relevant year has been placed on record which shows that entire revenue has been generated from export of software and related ITES activities. There is no segment wise result available for ITES activity. This company had also been excluded by the Tribunal in case of Willis Processing Services India (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 4544 (MUM) of 2012 dated 13-2-2013]. Therefore, it is opined that this company is not a good comparable and has to be excluded.

APPOLO HEALTH LTD.

This company is also providing IT enabled services. The objection of the assessee is on the ground that the services provided are in the high end segment of ITES, i.e., Medical transcription and Medical BPO. As held earlier, on this ground alone the comparable could not be excluded. However, it has been brought to notice that 81 per cent of the transactions in case of the company are with related parties. With such high RPT, this comparable could not be considered as a good comparable. Therefore, this comparable has to be excluded. [Para 21.3]

ASIT C. MEHTA (NUCLEUS NET SOFT)

The assessee has objected the selection of this comparable on the ground that it is engaged in portfolio management services also, in addition of ITES. The revenue has placed on record the annual report of the company which shows that the assessee is in the field of content development which is an ITES. It is also to be noted that almost entire revenue, i.e., Rs. 6.09 crore is from ITES and only a sum of Rs. 23.26 lakh is from portfolio management service which is insignificant which will not have much impact on the margins. Content development is a high end service but as held earlier on this ground alone it cannot be excluded. As there is no material to show that in case of high end services in ITES industry margins are higher than those in low segment. [Para 21.4]

CALIBER POINT BUSINESS SOLUTIONS LTD.

The assessee has argued that company is not comparable as it is engaged in business process management and other activities. The revenue has placed on record the annual report of the company which shows that segmental accounts are available in case of BPO segment. The Assessing Officer /TPO have taken the entire revenue for the purpose of comparison which will not be appropriate. Therefore, it is directed that the results of only BPO segment have to be considered for the purpose of comparability and subject to the above, the inclusion of this comparable is upheld. Argument based on high segment as held earlier has to be rejected. [Para 21.5]

COSMIC GLOBAL LTD.
IT/ILT: Company which outsources its work is not comparable for ALP determination with a company that does activity inhouse

Comparable E4 Healthcare Business Services (P.) Ltd.

This comparable provides services in the field of healthcare like ambulance, doctor on call, etc., and assessee is rendering services relating to transcription of medical prescription. There is no similarity in the service functionality of both these companies and, therefore, they are functionally dissimilar. As the functionality test is not satisfied between these companies, TPO is directed to exclude this comparable from the list. [Para 9.3]

Comparable ICRO Techno Analysis (P.) Ltd.

This comparable is involved in providing software development and consultancy services, engineering services, Web development and hosting services. Further it is also observed that segmental information in respect of each of these services is not available and, therefore, it is not possible to segregate income earned by this company under each segment. It is also observed that this company holds intangible asset in the form of software whereas in the case of assessee any intangibles that may be developed during the process of rendering services to its AE are owned by AE. Accordingly, this comparable is to be excluded from final list. [Para 9.3]

Comparable Cosmic Global Ltd.

This company has separate segmental information in respect of income earned under 2 different heads. Since services rendered by assessee as well as this comparable under segment medical transcription and consultancy services are similar, there is no infirmity in including this company in the list of comparable. However, TPO is directed to consider revenue earned by this company under the segment medical transcription and consultancy services only for purpose of determining the arm's length price. [Para 9.3]

Comparable Infosys BPO Ltd.

On perusal of financials, it is observed that this company has got huge turnover and goodwill being one of the giants in the software industry. This company has not been considered as comparable for low-end BPO services. Therefore, this company should be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 9.3]

The objections raised by assessee are dealt with in following manner:

Bodhtree Consultancy Ltd.

It is clear from records that this company is having one segment namely software development under which this company is providing software solutions including open and end-to-end web solution, software consultancy, design and development of solution. Further, the company is also providing data cleansing and software development. These services are in the category of software development services and not in ITES. Accordingly, it is held that the software development segment cannot be compared with ITES segment and hence this company cannot be compared with the assessee's ITES segment. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude this company from the list of comparables. [Para 8.3]

e-clerx Services Ltd.

The comparability of this company has been considered by the coordinate bench of this Tribunal in the case of Ariba Technologies of India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2016] 67 taxmann.com 265. In view of the decision of the co-ordinate bench, it is found that this company is engaged in providing data analysis and process solutions and recognized as expert in market financial services, retail and manufacturing. Thus this company was providing complete business solutions which are in different field of services. Therefore, this company cannot be considered as comparable with the low end service provider. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude this company from the list of comparables. [Para 9]

HCL Comnet Systems & Services Ltd. and Information Technologies India Ltd. :

These companies were found to be having more than 15 per cent Related Party Transactions (RPT). Accordingly, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude these companies from the set of comparables. [Para 9.1]

Infosys Ltd.

It is clear from the finding of this Tribunal in the case of Ariba Technologies India (P.) Ltd. (supra), this company is deriving revenue from the software product and has a huge intangible assets apart from the brand value and a leader in the market. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude this company from the list of comparables. [Para 10]

Mold-tek Technology Ltd. (Seg.)

The functional comparability has been considered by this Tribunal in a series of decision including the decision of Special Bench in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 43 taxmann.com 100/147 ITD 83 (Mum.-Trib). The co-ordinate bench of this Tribunal in the case of Ariba Technologies India (P.) Ltd. (supra) has held that this company is engaged in the engineering services being the nature of producing designs, drawings, detailed structure of engineering drawings using 2D and 3D software could not be compared with the assessee and consequently the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude this company from the set of comparables. [Para 12.1]

Accentia Technology Ltd.

The assessee has submitted that there is an extraordinary event of amalgamation during the year under consideration. [Para 13.1]

There is no dispute that amalgamation, merger or acquisition is considered as extraordinary event for the purpose of considering a particular entity as comparable. The co-ordinate bench of this Tribunal in the case of Sony Mobile Communications International AB v. Dy. CIT [2016] 69 taxmann.com 404 (Delhi) held that once acquisition and merger etc. has taken place, it is always likely to affect the profitability of such a company in the year of acquisition etc. There cannot be any standard yardstick to measure the impact of such a factor on the overall profitability of such a company.

Therefore, for limited purpose of considering the said record, this issue is set aside to the record of Assessing Officer/TPO and then decide the issue of comparability of this company in the light of the above observations. [Para 13.3]

Vishal Information Technology Ltd.

The comparability of this company has been examined by this Tribunal in the case of Ariba Technologies India Ltd. (supra), it was found that this company was outsourcing its job and therefore it fails the employee cost filter. Even otherwise when this is getting its work done through outsourcing then the business model of this company is different from the assessee. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude this company from the list of comparables. [Para 14]

Wipro Limited :

IT/ILT: Where assessee, engaged in manufacturing cassia gum powder, rendered marketing support services to its AE, company involved in high end niche market segment of financial contents and company which outsourced its ITES to third party vendors, could not be accepted as valid comparables while determining ALP

Comparable Accentia Technologies Ltd.

This company is functionally dissimilar because Accentia Services and Solutions are focused in two main area: (i) Healthcare Receivables Cycle Management (HRCM) and (ii) Software products for Business Processing Outsourcing (BPO). [Para 15]

It is apparent from the financials of Accentia that it acquired 10 per cent stakes in Trans Services Inc., USA leading to abnormal growth in sale (57 per cent) due to restructuring activities.

The Accentia is not a suitable comparable vis-à-vis the assessee which is a captive service provider for benchmarking the international transactions. Hence, Accentia was excluded from the final set of comparables. [Para 22]

Comparable Cosmic Global Ltd.

The revenue recognition of the Cosmic shows that it has three segments viz., medical transcription Rs. 0.09 crore, translation services Rs. 6.99 crores and Accounts BPO segment Rs. 0.27 crores. However, complete segmental data is not available. Furthermore, Cosmic is having abnormal growth of sales, i.e., 106 per cent as is evident from profit and loss account. [Para 26]

The Cosmic is ordered to be excluded on the ground that this company has outsourced its activities and the outsourcing expenses constitute 57 per cent of the total expenses and that the entire outsourcing is confined to translation charges paid of Rs. 3 crores. So, in view of its outsourced activities and in view of the fact that it is having a different business model and that abnormal growth in sales, i.e., 106 per cent, it is not a suitable comparable vis-à-vis the assessee for benchmarking international transaction qua ITES services, hence ordered to be excluded. [Para 27]

Comparable Eclerx Services Ltd.

When the assessee is a routine ITES, i.e., low end service provider, it cannot be a suitable comparable with Eclerx which is a KPO providing data analytics and data process solutions to global enterprise client and having significant intangibles to the tune of 7.24 per cent. So, high end KPO cannot be compared with low end routine ITES service provider. Eclerx also provides sales and marketing support services to leading global manufacturing, retail, travel and leisure companies through its pricing and profitability service which makes it functionally dissimilar with the assessee. So, in view of the matter, Eclerx is to be excluded from the final set of comparables. [Para 31]

Comparables Axis IT and T Ltd.

Assessee claimed for inclusion of Axis IT & T Ltd. in the list of final comparables. The said company was found to be engaged in the business of providing ITES services as well as software development services and the revenue generated from ITES services was only 53.26 per cent of the total revenue. Since the relevant details of ITES segment were not available, the TPO held that Axis IT & T Ltd. could not be included in the list of final comparables. [Para 8]

Assessee has invited attention to the details furnished to show that the relevant segmental details of Axis IT & T Ltd. are available. In reply to a query raised by the bench in this regard, he, however, accepted that these details are prepared by the assessee on the basis of the final accounts of the said company, viz., Axis IT & T Ltd. A comparative study, however, shows that the details prepared and furnished by the assessee are not tallying with the corresponding figures appearing in the final accounts of Axis IT & T Ltd. As a matter of fact, policy adopted by Axis IT & T Ltd. for segment reporting is given in the relevant schedule forming part of the consolidated financial statement which shows that there are may items of revenue and expenditure, which relate to the group as a whole, are not allocable to segments on a reasonable basis. Keeping in view the same, Axis IT & T cannot be included in the list of final comparables in the absence of reliable segmental details. [Para 9]

2. Genesys International Ltd.

The claim of the assessee for exclusion of Genesys International Corporation Ltd. from the list of final comparable is squarely covered in favour of the assessee by the decision of the co-ordinate bench of the Tribunal, in the case of Parexel International (India) (P.) Ltd., ITA No. 144 (Hyd.) of 2014, dated 30-9-2014 for assessment year 2009-10 holding that they are providing full range of geospatial services to its customers and were to be excluded.

Thus Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude Genesys International Ltd. from the list of comparables. [Para 10]

3. E-Clerx Services Ltd.

The issue involved therein relating to the claim of the assessee for exclusion of e-Clerx Services Ltd. from the list of final comparable is squarely covered in favour of the assessee by the decision of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal, in the case of Parexel International (India) (P.) Ltd.(supra) for assessment year 2009-10 holding that company was involved in diverse nature of services, and there was no segmental data for diversified service portfolio.

4. Cosmic Global Ltd.

The issue involved therein relating to the claim of the assessee for exclusion of Cosmic Global Ltd. from the list of final comparable is squarely covered in favour of the assessee by the decision of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal dated 30-9-2014 in the case of Parexel International (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) the ground that total revenue of the accounts BPO segment of Cosmic Global Ltd. was very low.

In view of said decision, Assessing Officer was directed to exclude said company from comparable list.

Accordingly the Assessing Officer/TPO was directed to recompute the arm's length price by excluding the above three comparables from the final list of comparables and allow appropriate relief to the assessee on this issue. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the assessee has been treated as an ITES back office service provider and even in the case of Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2019] 102 taxmann.com 10 (Hyd. - Trib.), the assessee has been considered as an ITES service provider and the assessment year involved in the appeal in the instant case as well as in the appeal of Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. (supra). It is also observed that the comparables taken by the Transfer Pricing Officer are exactly the same. Therefore, the decision taken in the case of Hyundai Motor India Engg. (P.) Ltd. (supra) would also apply to the assessee. In the said case it was held that the activities of Capgemini Business are much more diversified than the activities of the assessee and unless and until a suitable adjustment can be made, the said company cannot be taken as a comparable. It has been held in a number of cases that where a comparable is into diversified activities, the same can be taken as a comparable provided the segmental results are available. It is observed that the segmental results are not available for ITES services. Therefore, Capgemini Business is to be excluded from the final list of comparables.

As regards Hartron Communications Ltd. is concerned it was observed that before the Transfer Pricing Officer, the assessee had only taken an objection that the said company is functionally dissimilar. Before the Dispute Resolution Panel also, the assessee had also stated that in addition to the BPO, LPO and ITES services, this company is also engaged in providing Intellectual Property services in the nature of patent search, patent protection, and obtaining the trade-mark services, IP Management and, further, in software development services such as Web page Application, Standalone Software Application, Distributed Applications, Desktop/Laptop Applications and Mobile Applications. The assessee had relied upon the Annual Report as well as the website information of the said company to submit as above and pleaded that no segmental information is available. However, the Dispute Resolution Panel has summarily rejected the assessee's contention and has confirmed the assessment order. Since the facts mentioned by the assessee about Hartron Communications need to be verified, it is deemed fit and proper to remit the issue to the file of the Assessing Officer for verification of the assessee's contentions. Thus, it is held that if the company is found to be in diversified activities and no segmental information is available, then this company cannot be taken as a comparable. [Para 10]

Following the same, the Assessing Officer is to be directed to exclude these two companies from the final list of comparables. [Para 11]
Co. outsourcing its activities couldn't be compared with a Co. providing services of its own

Accentia Technologies Ltd., Asit C Mehta Financial Services Ltd., Informed Technologies India Ltd., Spanco Ltd. (seg.) and Vishal Information Technologies Ltd.

Co-ordinate bench of this Tribunal has held in First Advantage Offshore Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [IT (TP) A No. 1086 (Bang.) of 2011, dated 30-4-2013] that employee cost filter is one which had to be applied while selecting comparables in ITES segment. Said decision was also for assessment year 2007-08. Thus, there is doubt that employee cost filter necessarily has to be applied for ITES segment. However, the lower authorities had not applied this filter at all and also not worked out proportion of the employee cost with the total cost and total revenue. As per the assessee, if the employee cost filter of 25 per cent is applied, Accentia Technologies Ltd., Asit C Mehta Financial Services Ltd., Informed Technologies India Ltd., Spanco Ltd. (seg.) and Vishal Information Technologies Ltd., would go out of the list of comparables. This requires a fresh look by the Assessing Officer/TPO. Therefore, the issue of comparability of the above five companies in the ITES segment is set aside and remitted back to the Assessing Officer/TPO for consideration of the employee cost filter after verifying the workout submitted by the assessee in this regard. [Para 42]

Bodhtree Consulting Ltd. (seg.)

As for Bodhtree Consulting Ltd. (seg.), Pune Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Dy. CIT v. Affinity Express India (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 595 (PN) of 2013, dated 29-4-2015] had held that Bodhtree Consulting Ltd. is clearly into software development whereas the assessee company provides ITES. Therefore, Bothtree Consulting Ltd. cannot be considered as a comparable to the assessee. Concerned assessment year being the very same, Bodhtree consulting Ltd. (seg.) has to be excluded from the list of comparables. [Para 43]

Eclerx Services Ltd., Infosys BPO Ltd. and Mold-Tek Technologies Ltd.

The assessee contended that these companies were into knowledge process outsourcing which cannot be compared with assessee who was only providing lower end call centre services. [Para 44]

However, claim of the assessee that technical services rendered by it to the HP group entities were all of lower end has not been successfully demonstrated by it. It is also true that TPO had not gone deeper into this particular claim of the assessee. Therefore, the issue of comparing Eclerx Services Ltd., Infosys BPO Ltd. and Mold-Tek Technologies Ltd. is remitted back to the Assessing Officer/TPO for considering afresh after properly analysing the services rendered by the assessee to its AEs in the ITES segment. [Para 45]

Wipro Ltd. (seg.)

The facts of this company are similar to the facts of Infosys BPO Ltd. Insofar as comparability of Infosys BPO Ltd. is concerned, same had been remitted back to the Assessing Officer/TPO for consideration afresh. Hence, consistency requires that comparability of Wipro Ltd. (seg.) also go back to the Assessing Officer/TPO, for consideration afresh in accordance with law. [Para 46]

Mapel Esolutions Ltd. and Triton Corp. Ltd.

Since the promoters and directors of these companies were involved in frauds, their results were unreliable. However, Maple E Solutions Ltd. formed a part of assessee's own TP study. Therefore while Triton Corp. Ltd. is directed to be excluded from the list of comparables, the question of exclusion of Maple E Solution Ltd. is remitted back to the Assessing Officer/TPO for consideration afresh in accordance with law.[Para 47]

Caliber Point Business Solutions Ltd. HCL Comnet Systems & Services Ltd. (seg.) and R Systems International Ltd. (seg.)
Cos outsourcing BPO work can't be a comparable for an entity undertaking such services in-house

Comparable Clerx Services Ltd.

It can be seen from the Annual Report of the company, that it paid outsourcing charges to the tune of Rs. 8 crore and odd in addition to payment of Salary and wages etc. to its staff, including director's remuneration, to the tune of Rs. 24.54 crore. This divulges that roughly 26 per cent of the activity carried out by this company has been outsourced. As against this, the assessee is doing the entire business at its own without there being any expenditure on outsourcing. This reveals a significant difference in the business model adopted by the assessee and e-Clerx Services Ltd. E-Clerx has also spent more than 26 per cent of the total cost of the employees and job work charges simply on outsourcing, business model of said company being significantly different from that of the assessee, which was not outsourcing any of its work the same renders it non-comparable. Therefore, this company be excluded from the final set of comparables. [Para 6]

There is no elaboration of the nature of services under this segment except the TPO noting that the assessee is 'engaged in KPO activities'. On a pointed query, the assessee contended that the assessee was merely rendering help-desk services under this segment, which is a simplest form of BPO services. There is an apparent conflict between the description of services as stated by the assessee and as recorded in the order of the TPO. [Para 50]

In an attempt to ascertain the correct nature of services, the Master Services Agreement entered into by the assessee with McKinsey is referred to. It is a common Agreement between the assessee and McKinsey for providing both the 'Research and information services' and also 'IT support services'. [Para 51]

It is deducible that the nature of service covered under the 'IT Support services' segment are '(a) Develop, maintain and service the software … and (b) Knowledge management systems and infrastructure issues which would encompass infrastructure support, application support, application operations group and survey development center and such other services as may be requested from time to time'. Thus, it is overt that there is a vast difference about the nature of services as argued by the assessee under this segment as that of 'help desk services', being BPO; and what is coming out from the Master Services Agreement as also inclusive of 'Knowledge management systems and infrastructure issues which would encompass infrastructure support, application support, application operations group and survey development center', which are KPO in nature. [Para 53]

It comes out that employees of assessee consist of 17 IT Analysts, apart from Fast Regional Manager- Asia Pac, 2 Operations Managers, Technology Line Leader, Team Leader, and only 1 Team Assistant. Such a team of experts cannot be recruited only for rendering help-desk services. This prima facie disapproves the assessee's contention of rendering help desk services alone. Unlike the other segment of 'Research and information services' for which the assessee placed on record correspondence of the assessee with the McKinsey companies to divulge the nature of services under all the three sub-groups separately, namely Knowledge on call, Practice research and Analytics, no evidence the assessee has been placed on record to show the nature of services rendered under the segment of 'IT Support services'. [Para 54]

In view of the apparent conflict in what the assessee is stating and what is prima facie coming out from record, without there being any material to show the exact nature of services, the comparability or otherwise of the companies challenged before the Tribunal cannot be decided. Under these circumstances, the impugned order is set aside to this extent and the matter is remitted to the Assessing Officer/TPO for first determining and elaborating the correct nature of services in the order and then deciding the comparability of the companies challenged before the Tribunal. Needless to say, the assessee will be allowed a reasonable opportunity of being heard in this regard. [Para 55]

IT/ILT: Where assessee was rendering software development services to AE, a company earning revenue from three segments namely software services, software products and other services about which segmental information was not available, was not acceptable as comparable

Comparable Mold Tek Technologies Ltd.

The Tribunal in Maersk Global Centres India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 147 ITD 83/43 taxmann.com 100 (Mum. - Trib) while specifically dealing with the comparability of the aforesaid company to a ITES provider, has held that since the company engaged in providing engineering design service which was a high end service in the nature of KPO, it cannot be treated as comparable. In view of the aforesaid decision, this company cannot be treated as comparable to the assessee. [Para 13]

Comparable eClerx Services Ltd.

As per the annual report of this company, it is noted that the company is engaged in offering solutions in the field of data analytics, operations management, audits and re-conciliation, matrics management and reporting services. In fact, the Delhi High Court in Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 377 ITR 533/234 Taxman 573/60 taxmann.com 355, has held that this company being a KPO service provider cannot be considered as a comparable to ITES companies. Therefore, respectfully following said view, eClerx Services Ltd. being functionally different, cannot be treated as comparable to the assessee.

Comparable Vishal Technologies Ltd.

No doubt, assessee in the transfer pricing study has selected this company as a comparable. It is also a fact either before the Transfer Pricing Officer or the DRP, assessee has not raised any specific objection in respect of the aforesaid company. Even then, assessee's objection cannot be overruled for that reason alone. When the Transfer Pricing Officer has rejected the transfer pricing analysis of the assessee the department cannot use it selectively to their advantage. Moreover, it appears from the facts and materials placed on record that this company is different from the assessee considering the fact that it outsources its ITES to third party vendors. In other words, this company does not carry out the ITES activities itself but gets it done through others. This is evident from low employee cost of the company. Compared to the aforesaid practice of this company, the assessee claims to have carried out the ITES activities all by itself, thereby, has incurred a comparatively higher employee cost.

The Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to examine this aspect by verifying the annual report of the company and other relevant documents and if assessee's claim of low employee cost of this company is found to be correct, this company should not be treated as comparable. [Para 61]

Comparable Accentia Technologies Ltd.

Comparability of this company for the very same assessment year came up for consideration before the Tribunal, in Symphony Marketing Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2013] 38 taxmann.com 55 (Bang - Trib), the excluded this company on the reasoning that extraordinary event which took place might have impacted the profitability. In view of the aforesaid, this company cannot be treated as comparable. [Para 64]

Comparable Acropetal Technologies Ltd.

The Tribunal, in Symphony Marketing Solutions India (P.) Ltd. (supra), after perusing the annual report of this company found that major source of income is from providing engineering design service which is not comparable to ITES/BPO functions. The Bench observed that, provision of engineering design service is a high end service amongst the BPO which requires high skill, hence, it can be regarded as KPO service. The Bench, therefore, excluded the company as a comparable to ITES/BPO segment. As these decisions rendered by the Tribunal are for the very same assessment year, respectfully following the same, exclusion of this company from the list of comparable. [Para 67]

Comparable Cosmic Global Ltd.

The Tribunal in the case of ACIT v. Hyundai Motors India Engineering (P.) Ltd. [I.T. Appeal Nos. 1743 & 1917 (Hyd.) of 2014, dated 13-11-2013] has considered the comparability of the company to the assessee and has directed the exclusion of it holding that this company's employee cost is less than 21.30 per cent and most of the cost is with reference to the outsourcing charges or translation charges, and as such this is not a comparable company. [Para 11]

Comparable TCS Serve Ltd.

The Tribunal has held during the relevant financial year, the TCS e-Serve International Ltd. had acquired Captive business processing outsourcing (BPO) arm for an all cash consideration and in return, had acquired the business of an aggregate amount of $2.5 billion over a period of 9.5 years. This definitely is an exceptional circumstance. The Tribunal in a number of decisions held that exceptional circumstance like merger is a reasonable filter to exclude a company from the list of comparables. Therefore, the Assessing Officer/TPO is directed to exclude this company from the final list of comparables. [Para 12.1]

Comparable Accentia Technologies Ltd.

The Tribunal had held that this company operates in a different business strategy of acquiring companies for inorganic growth as its strategy and considering the profit margins of the company and insufficient segmental data, cannot be selected as a comparable. [para 12.2]

Comparable Eclerx Services Ltd.

The Delhi High Court in the case of Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 234 Taxman 573/60 taxmann.com 355 has held that ITeS encompasses a wide spectrum of services that use Information Technology based delivery. Such services could include rendering highly technical services by qualified technical personnel involving advanced skills and knowledge, such as engineering, design and support. While, on the other end of the spectrum, ITeS would also include voice-based call centers that render routine customer support for their clients. Clearly, characteristics of the service rendered would be dissimilar. Further, both service providers cannot be considered to be functionally similar.

The findings of the Tribunal in the above referred case are applicable to the facts of the case and, thus, TPO/Assessing Officer is directed to exclude these companies from the final list of comparables and re-compute the arm's length adjustment accordingly. [Para 12.4]

Comparable Infosys B.P.O. Ltd.

The assessee is a captive unit providing back office support services to its AE alone, which are basically in the nature of processing of insurance claims and the data entry. It can have no valid comparison with Infosys Ltd., as the latter is a full fledged risk taking entrepreneur with diversified business including software product, consulting application, design development, re-engineering and maintenance etc. and which has developed/owns proprietary products. The assessee, being a captive unit, does not own any such proprietary product. Unlike Infosys, the assessee does not have any substantial intangible assets. Similarly, Infosys has spent a lot on Research and development, whereas the assessee has not undertaken any such activity in rendering services to its AE. [Para 5]

Comparable Wipro Ltd. (Seg.)

The facts and circumstances of this company nowhere match with the assessee company. This company is also a giant entity in comparison with the assessee company with marked differences as regards risk profile, nature of services, ownership of IP rights, expenditure on R&D etc. Thus this company, is to be held as incomparable with the assessee. [Para 6]

Comparable HCL Comnet Systems & Services Ltd. (Seg.)

When a company is functionally similar to that of the assessee company, the same cannot be excluded merely because its turnover is at a higher or lower level. Here it is important to mention that section 92C(1) provides for the computation of Arm's Length Prices by one of the methods prescribed therein. First proviso to section 92C(2) clearly provides that when more than one price are determined by the most appropriate method, then the Arm's Length Prices shall be taken to be the arithmetic mean of such prices. It does not talk of excluding the companies with high or low turnover or high or low profit rate.

In view of the fact that the assessee has admitted the functional comparability of the relevant segment of this company and the only difference pointed out is about its higher turnover, this company cannot be excluded from the list of comparable. [Para 7]

Step 6 - Selection of the MAM and depending on the method, determination of the relevant financial indicator.

Step 7 - Identification of potential comparables (i.e., determining the key characteristics to be met by any uncontrolled transaction in order to be regarded as potentially comparable based on relevant factors identified in Step 3):—There are basically two ways in which the identification of potentially comparable third party transactions can be conducted, i.e., additive approach and deductive approach. It has been held that a blind application of precedent cannot per se be a ground for excluding or including comparables unless factual and functional analysis are carried out—PCIT v. ST Microelectronics (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 262/251 Taxman 484 (Delhi). Any inclusion or exclusion of comparables per se cannot be treated as a question of law unless it is demonstrated to the Court that the ITAT or any other lower authority took into account irrelevant consideration or excluded relevant factors in ALP determination that impact significantly; unless it is demonstrated that there are important functional dissimilarities or vital material facts which go to route of profitability or other material circumstances are involved—PCIT v. WSP Consultants India (P.) Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 266/[2018] 253 Taxman 58 (Delhi); PCIT v. Becton Dickinson India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 45/254 Taxman 382 (Delhi).

Step 8 - Determination of, and making, comparability adjustments (where appropriate):—Where there are differences between the situations being compared that could materially affect the comparison, comparability adjustments must be made, where possible, to improve the reliability of the comparison. Therefore, comparability adjustments should be considered if and only if they are expected to increase the reliability of the results. Relevant considerations include the materiality of the difference for which an adjustment is being considered, the quality of data subject to adjustment, the purpose of the adjustment and the reliability of the approach used to make adjustment. Some examples of comparability adjustments include adjustments for accounting consistency designed to eliminate differences that may arise from different accounting practices between the controlled and uncontrolled transactions, segmentation of financial data to eliminate significant non-comparable transactions, adjustments for differences in capital, functions, assets, risks, capacity utilization1, happening of any abnormal events such as strike.2

However, such adjustments would not be made where the assessee is not able to demonstrate or establish that such an adjustment is relevant and backed up by sufficient evidence—Indian Additives Ltd. v. DCIT [2019] 108 taxmann.com 117/265 Taxman 383 (Mad.).

Step 9—Interpretation and use of data collected, determination of the arm's length remuneration.

In practice, the above process is not a linear one. Steps 5 to 7 might need to be carried out repeatedly until a satisfactory conclusion is reached. In cases where it is not possible to find information on comparable transactions (Step 7) and/or to make reasonably appropriate and accurate adjustments (Step 8), taxpayers' might have to select another MAM and repeat the process starting from Step 4.

Software Development Service Segment

The assessee has challenged the decision of the TPO in not aggregating the software services transactions of the assessee for determining the ALP. [Para 19]

The entire purpose behind introducing the TP provisions is to ascertain whether the price charged for an international transaction between two related parties is at arm's length. For achieving this, the controlled transaction has to be compared with one or several uncontrolled transactions carried in the same line of business and with more or less similar facts and circumstances.

It is apparent from the facts and materials on record, that even after merger of Spacelabs with Rapiscan India, maintenance of accounts is entity specific. Though it may be a fact that software development services is a very wide term and takes within its ambit whole software development services, such as medical, security, banking, accountancy, etc., but for comparability analysis, verticals of the software development industry have to be looked into. All types of software development services cannot be clubbed together for comparability analysis, as it will not give an appropriate result. In assessee's case also software development services are for two different services, i.e., security system as well as medical services. It cannot be accepted that operating profit to operating cost of the revenue earned from software development services segment should be considered as a whole for computing the margin of the assessee. Moreover, when assessee has maintained entity specific accounts with segmental details and has also conducted analysis on that basis in its TP study, there is no reason to disturb the order of the TPO and DRP on this issue. [Paras 19, 20]

Regarding inclusion of 'V' in list of comparables Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the predominant view taken by various Benches of the Tribunal including Mumbai, Bangalore and Hyderabad is to exclude the case of 'V' on the reasoning that profit margin in self-provision and outsourcing the services is different. The revenue has focused on the inclusion of this case on the ground that the profit margin in the case of the entities outsourcing services is less than that of the providing in-house services. This contention has the effect of changing the very criterion for selection of comparable cases. Comparability is judged primarily by seeing the functional similarity and then the capital employed and risks undertaken. Higher or lower profit rate is not and can never be a relevant criteria to judge the comparability. In fact, under the TNMM, it is the eventual profit which is sought to be determined at an arm's length by considering all the relevant comparable cases. It is the similarity of the functional profile which needs to be taken into consideration as a first step in the process of selection of comparable cases. If the two companies are functionally different and incapable of comparison, then the similarity of the other factors is of no consequence. [Para 20]

In that view of the matter, a case in which services are outsourced and then provided to its customers cannot be compared with the rendering of in-house services. The pertinent criteria for selection of comparable cases should be similarity in the nature of services and not the higher or lower margin of profit in one case viz-a-viz the other. As there is a vast difference in the cases where the services are outsourced or provided in-house, there cannot be any comparison between such types of cases. The matter is directed to be decided afresh by the Assessing Officer /TPO in consonance with aforesaid observations. [Para 21]

Thirdware Solutions Ltd. Before deciding the comparability or otherwise of these five companies, it is sine qua non to ascertain the nature of services rendered by the assessee under this segment. This segment has two classifications, namely, Software development services and Maintenance support services. Software development services refers to the development of modules by the assessee and also parts of modules for software being used by its overseas group entities. Maintenance support services refer to the services including bug fixing, carrying out maintenance and support services of software used by its overseas group entities.

The assessee entered into a services agreement under which, it became responsible for providing software development and maintenance support services to its overseas group entities. For this purpose, the assessee got compensation on the basis of cost plus mark-up. Revenue from software development services accounts for approximately 20 per cent of total revenue under the software development and maintenance support services earned by the assessee and the remaining 80 per cent is towards software maintenance support services. [Para 11]

With the above understanding of the nature of services carried out by the assessee in segment of 'Provision of software development and maintenance support segment', it is necessary to examine if the five companies contested by the assessee are, in fact, comparable.[Para 12]

Avani Cimcon Ltd.

It was noted from rewards that the Mumbai Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Net Hawk Networks India Pvt. Ltd. v. ITO (ITA No.7633/N/2012). Vide its order dated 6-11-2013, has noticed Avani Cimcon Ltd., to be a Product based company and not providing software development services. No contrary material has been placed on record by the revenue to show the functional profile of this company matching with the assessee. When contrasted with the assessee company, which was engaged in providing software development and maintenance services to its group concerns, one fails to see as to how a software product company like Avani Cimcon having intellectual property rights over some of the products developed by it, can be compared with the assessee on an entity level. Therefore, it is necessary to order for the elimination of this company from the list of comparables. [Para 14]

KALS Information Systems Ltd. (Seg.)

It was noted that this company consisted of STPI unit engaged in development of software and software products. The paper book contains segmental information of this company which has been divided into two parts, namely, 'Application software segment' and 'Training segment'. It is the 'Application software segment' of this company, which has been adopted by the TPO. The development of software and all software products have been clubbed under the 'Application software' segment. Since the figures of this company taken by the TPO for making comparison with the assessee include the effect of software products as well, apart from software development services, the same cannot be considered as comparable for the same reasons as assigned above for eliminating Avani Cimcon Ltd. A product company cannot be compared with a company engaged in providing software development services because of difference in the inherent characteristics of both. Therefore, this company has to be excluded from the set of comparables. [Para 16]

Infosys Technologies Ltd.

The assessee is only a captive unit rendering services to its AE alone without acquiring any intellectual property rights in the work done by it in the development of software. The Delhi High Court in CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 taxmann.com 289 considered the giantness of Infosys Ltd., in terms of risk profile, nature of services, number of employees, ownership of branded products and brand related profits, etc. in comparison with such factors prevailing in the case of Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra) being, a captive unit providing software development services without having any IP rights in the work done by it.

After making comparison of various factors as enumerated above, the Delhi High Court held Infosys Ltd. to be incomparable with Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra). The facts of the instant case are more or less similar inasmuch as the extant assessee is also a captive service provider with a limited number of employees at its disposal and also not owning any branded products with no expenditure on R&D etc. When one considers all the above factors in a holistic manner, there remains absolutely no doubt that Infosys Technologies Ltd. is incomparable to the assessee company. Thus following the judgment of the jurisdictional High Court in Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. (supra), it is held that Infosys Technologies Ltd., cannot be held as comparable with the assessee company. This company is, therefore, directed to be excluded from the list of comparables. 2. KPO VS. BPO CONTROVERSY – AN ANALYSIS

In both the business formats, it is not a simple case of "K" replacing the "B". BPO usually deals with performing business activities like customer care, finance, HR, voice and data entry functions. The extent of work force required is more process driven and elementary. Generally, the motivation of setting up of BPO operations is substantial cost savings. On the other hand, KPO, being a subset of BPO, involves the outsourcing of core specialized and knowledge based services which may or may not result in cost savings but surely adds value to parent company's endeavours. Services outsourced to KPO are related to research and development, equity and financial analysis, legal services, biotechnology, animation and design and other services to likes of dedicated business solutions. KPO employs qualified professionals having specific industry expertise.

The Hon'ble Special Bench has pronounced that the process followed to identify potential comparables is one of the most critical aspects of the comparability analysis and it should be transparent, systematic and verifiable. Potential comparables in ITeS sector can be identified through applying "broad functionality test" by analyzing the taxpayer's circumstances largely. Further bifurcation of IT enabled services may be done to establish relatively equal degree of comparability. The line of differentiation between KPO and BPO is very thin since KPOs are an upward extension of BPO industry in the value chain. Since KPO is an evolution of BPO, there is a likely-hood where in the process of such evolution, there are entities offering a mix of overlapping services which are difficult to classify as either BPO or KPO, going by their functional profile.

The Special Bench held that IT Enables Services cannot be further bifurcated or classified as BPO and KPO services for comparability purposes in wake of difficulty in classifying services strictly either as low end BPO services or high end KPO services. The Bench advocated a two step process to benchmark transactions in the ITeS sector :-

Identifying potential comparables through conducting a broad functional analysis at ITeS level; and

Comparing the functional profile of tested party with principal functions performed by selected entities, ensuring equal comparability. Such functional filtration process may ensure that the uncontrolled transactions having lesser degree of comparability would get eliminated.

Hence, in essence, the Bench iterated that the selection of final comparables shall depend on facts and circumstances of each case on the basis of functional profile of the tested party.

In light of above analysis, Maersk India is held to be a captive contract service provider mainly rendering back office support services and other incidental services involving some degree of special knowledge and expertise. Hence, Mold-Tek Technologies and eClerx Services were dropped as comparables on the premise that both companies were engaged in providing high-end services involving specialized knowledge and domain expertise.

3. WHETHER DEFINITIONS IN SAFE HARBOUR RULES CAN BE SANCTIONED IN ALL CASES

One of the contentions put up by the taxpayer for justifying the differentiation between KPO and BPO is the definition of "Information technology enables services" cited in the Final Safe Harbour Rules ("SHR" or "the Rules") released issued by Ministry of Finance on September 18, 2013. The aforesaid definition is an exclusive one that identifies many low-end outsourcing services viz. payroll, revenue accounting, call centre services. "Knowledge process outsourcing services" are separately defined in the aforesaid Rules as outsourcing services provided mainly with the assistance or use of information technology requiring application of knowledge and advanced analytical and technical skill. Hence, the assessee submitted that specific articulation by the CBDT of both BPO and KPO in the SHR demonstrates the differences between the two business layouts.

The Revenue challenged the assessee's reference to the SHR on the ground that the aforesaid rules were released in September 2013 and cannot be applied retrospectively to a case pertaining to AY 2008-09. Besides, the Revenue countered the assessee's reliance on definitions provided in SHR by submitting that the assessee in this case has not exercised the safe harbour option and hence cannot draw an inference from it. However, the Special Bench did not place any strictures on such reliance by non-safe harbour pickers.

With nine rounds of transfer pricing audit completed in January 2014, the challenging days for Indian outsourcing sector does not seem to get over. The total quantum of transfer pricing adjustments made in FY 2012-13 was to the tune of seventy thousand crores1 (for Assessment Year ("AY") 2009-10) up by 54 per cent earlier. Indian outsourcing sector accounts for more than half the total claims in transfer pricing adjustments made during the aforesaid audit cycle from about one-third earlier.

However, as per recently disseminated data, the additions to income of companies undertaking international transaction has dropped by over 14 per cent to sixty thousand crores2 in FY 2014 tax audit cycle (for AY 2010-11). This seems to be a silver lining in an otherwise dismal environment emanating from the North Block.

Outsourcing sector accounts for more than USD 100 billion share in India's economy with big foreign companies like IBM, Capgemini, Microsoft, GE etc. putting forward a big basket of service offerings viz. customer service, risk and fraud management and finance and accounting. In the backdrop of the great demographic dividend, India has been one of the most preferred Knowledge Services Outsourcing ("KSO") destinations holding 70 per-cent share of the global KSO market3. India is poised to emerge as a global hub for KSO by 2015.

Over a period of time, multiplicity of business arrangements have happened in the outsourcing space starting from outsourcing of accounting processes to legal and research process outsourcing. While, Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") service stands for taking up routine operations like data entry, voice calling and accounting services, a shift of functions performed that requires expert analysis and decision making viz. patent application drafting, technical research and advisory activities etc. mark the outset of a new category of Knowledge Process Outsourcing ("KPO") services. This broad bifurcation though coined by the industry itself is important from a transfer pricing stand-point and is analyzed deeply by the Special Bench of Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited discussed in this article.

The industry dimension A point of consideration, which does not seem to find place in most IT/ITeS rulings (perhaps as the argument is often not adduced in the course of the proceedings) is the treatment adopted by the Revenue authorities, while dealing with taxpayers rendering services to both "service" and "product" companies, spread across various industries. In the course of the economic analysis, no cognizance is given to the end recipient of the services, although there do exist differences in the supply chains of both "service" and "product" companies. Further, even the business and economic circumstances vary for both categories of companies, and the return earned is an immediate indicator of such differences.

In a perfect world, one would want the functional comparability to be viewed in the light of the industry considerations, since the same would help in arriving at a set, which best represents not only the functions undertaken by the taxpayer, but also the return one would expect, while operating in such an industry. However, the lack of financial data for comparable companies operating in a certain domain continues to be a key deterrent in such an analysis. It is for this reason that usually a broader comparability approach is adopted by both taxpayers as well as Revenue authorities, which thus results in arriving at a standard set of comparables companies, without considering either the industry domains in which the taxpayer operates or the business and commercial circumstances of such verticals.

Perhaps, another aspect, which ideally should be considered, prior to determining the arm's length result for the IT/ITeS sector is to additionally analyze whether the services rendered are in the nature of "support services" required for internal consumption and/or subsumed within the larger activities of the Group. In such situations fixing a stand-alone commercial value to such activities is difficult because neither the activity has any use being detached from the final solution, nor the solution itself would be completed without the said activity. Such a scenario will be witnessed when the Indian taxpayer renders services to its Group companies and the same are entirely consumed within the overall primary activity carried on by the Group. A dispassionate value chain analysis should go a long-way in clearing the picture on the true worth of any activity. Having said that, the overall risk-insulated motive of the captive service provider, and thereby its returns being based on risk profiling should be the accepted norm.

To further elaborate, under such a scenario, the service rendered is not a value driver or a source of core competence for the Group. Simply put, the rendition of the service does not augment the revenue potential of the MNC, but may only lead to gains in operating efficiency. Therefore, a market facing activity where the service is ultimately consumed by the end-customer (in whatever form) should invariably lead to the assertion of an arm's length profitability, as opposed to internal consumption of the service for the Group that could form the subject of a cost contribution or a typical safe harbour arrangement.

Mark-ups determined

Tribunals in India have, more often than not, adjudicated on the grievances surrounding comparability analysis specifically on filters applied, quantitative/qualitative analysis of comparables, the true nature of a limited risk service provider and finally on specific issues about comparables as may have been raised by the petitioner. One can safely say that the Tribunals, in their role as an adjudicator, have not commented or expressed an opinion on the level of the mark-up that ought to be applied. They have clearly not taken on the role of a negotiator or a policy maker (like a safe harbour threshold). This continues to be the domain of the Government and the taxman. However, based on certain Tribunal rulings, where principle based approach on comparability has been ascertained, the resultant mark-ups for the IT and ITeS sectors have been hovering in the range of 18-20 per cent and 23-25 per cent as against the 22-25 per cent and 25-30 per cent respectively determined at the TP audit level.

In this background it would be pertinent to mention that retrospective clarification in relation to the tolerance band of 5 per cent not being a standard deduction is rather retrograde and could be viewed as an unjust enrichment to the Indian Revenue authorities. Rather than being forward-looking by considering global practices of applying central tendency, the Government has resorted to empower the Revenue authorities to negotiate with a minor leeway. The fact that the Government has waited for a decade before providing any clarity to both taxpayers as well as the Revenue authorities, and more so after Tribunals adjudicated a standard deduction on the mean, that was the stated intent, is unfortunate and a source of heartburn among the ones who did not get away.

The Assessee was a 100 per cent subsidiary of 'D', Liechtenstein, engaged in business of rendering inbound, outbound and domestic travel services to India, Nepal and Bangladesh.

During relevant year, assessee entered into international transactions relating to outbound and inbound travel related services with its AE.

The assessee applied the resale price method ("RPM") as most appropriate method. In response to the query raised by the TPO it was explained that the assessee had earned a gross profit margin of 9.58 per cent and in the unrelated segment it had earned a gross profit margin of 9.18 per cent in respect of the outbound travel related services.

Since the gross profit margin at 9.58 per cent was higher than the gross profit margin of unrelated party at 9.18 per cent, the international transactions were claimed to be at arm's length price.

Similarly in respect of the travel related services in the inbound segment, the assessee applied Cost Plus Method with gross profit to cost (GP/Total cost) and PLI.

Since the assessee was engaged in the sale of similar services to unrelated parties it was submitted that the gross margin earned in the case of the international transaction was 4.76 per cent and that in unrelated segment was 6.25 per cent.

According to assessee, since the profit margin was within the range of +/- five per cent in terms of proviso to section 92C(2), the international transaction was at arm's length price.

The TPO opined that the segmental information has been created to arbitrarily allocate the cost and thereby reduce the losses. He was also of the view that the segmental accounts were drawn 'without any explained or disclosed allocation key' and therefore could not be relied upon to determine the segmental results.

Consequently, the TPO disregarding the segmental accounts and rejecting the transaction wise benchmarking done by the assessee in the transfer pricing documentation applied TNMM considering OP/sales as PLI at entity level and comparing such margin earned by the assessee using external comparables.

On basis of TNMM, certain addition was made to assessee's ALP.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the applicability of TNMM. He, however, was of view that in the absence of any concrete evidence to show that the books of account or the segmental accounts were manipulated, there was no ground to reject the segmental accounts prepared by the assessee.

This study5 is a conclusive proof of the fact that the ALP computed as per the present Indian framework suffers from several biases and is not a true reflection of the actual 'arm's length price'. As the Indian outsourcing economy continues to boom, it is extremely crucial to adopt a more sophisticated transfer pricing framework to ensure that we align our policies with the best international practices to better resolve our cross border taxation disputes.

As discussed earlier in this article, the Indian IT landscape has multiple players, each of whom undertake different functions and bear different risks. As the nature of functions/operations, business model and performance parameters are different for these entities; they cannot be compared to each other. GICs represent the segment of the IT arena where the risks borne are minimal, functions undertaken are mostly routine like coding, testing etc., and there is no non- routine intangible involved. Hence such a player cannot be compared to an entity that undertakes functions pertaining to the entire value chain of the software development process, starting from conceptua-lization and design to delivery to the final customer.Even if one was to compare, it is necessary to makes adequate adjustments to account for the difference in the risk profile of the same. The transfer pricing officers have alleged that GICs are exposed to the single customer risk as they provide services to their related parties only. Hence the Single customer risks of the GICs can be set off against the market risks borne by the third party comparables. However, the guidelines provide that no two risks can be considered to offset each other and needs to be accounted separately. In this respect, the ITAT has accepted that, typically a GIC is insulated from the market risks faced by the independent comparables and hence adequate adjustments needs to made to account for the same. However there is no clear guidance, in respect to the appropriate method to be followed. In various cases that has been heard by the ITAT, the taxpayer has proposed the use of methods like the CAPM* model, use of Prime Lending rate etc. to do risk adjustments, but the same have been rejected by the ITAT. Further, the ITAT has also observed that while market risk faced by the comparables is an 'existing' risk, the single customer risk borne by GICs, as alleged by the TPOs is only an "anticipated" risk. The challenge for the taxpayer in the coming years is going to be adequately quantifying these risks and accounting for the same.

Taxpayers would often incur certain expenses on behalf of their related parties, purely on account of administrative convenience.Typically, these expenses would be third party costs in the nature of hotel bills, travel expenses, mobile expenses etc. The contentions of the transfer pricing officer has been that such expenses represent payment for services rendered to related parties and has been accordingly adjusted by the officers for the mark-up.

Intra-group services

Payment of management charges or intra group cross charges by Indian subsidiaries to their parent companies has been under the scanner of the tax authorities as an alleged technique of shifting profits outside India. Group entities of MNCs often render shared services to each other. Services are usually of the nature of administrative, human resources, IT, and finance support.This kind of support services within the organization/group encourages specialization by specific groups or units of the MNC. Under such a scenario each unit is not required to develop its own internal team across all the functions, but can tap the expertise of the relevant team from other fellow group entities. This is especially beneficial for smaller subsidiaries or group entities and result in substantial cost savings for them and therefore indirectly benefits them.

However this fact has not been appreciated by the transfer pricing officers, and taxpayers have been asked to provide 'benefit test' and prove that these services are not stewardship and shareholder activities. In most of the cases the transfer pricing officers have held the arm's length price to be nil and have disallowed the entire expense. Even in cases where the services have been beneficial for the taxpayer and have resulted in high margins for the taxpayer, the TPO has made adjustments to the taxpayer.

In this respect, the ITAT has provided relief to taxpayers in form of some landmark judgments where they have analyzed the functions of the taxpayer and have held that the intra-group services satisfy the benefit test and are at arm's length. Further, the ITAT has ruled that it is not the prerogative of the transfer pricing officer to question the business decision of the taxpayer.

For GICs who operate under the cost plus model, such services should not pose any issues, as the costs pertaining to these services would form a part of the cost base for the purpose of mark-up. However there are some GICs who operate on revenue sharing model or hourly rate model and receive such intra-group services from their related party are exposed to this challenge.

On the revenue's appeal before the Tribunal:

We have carefully considered submissions of Ld. Representatives of parties and the orders of authorities below. We observe that assessee in the assessment year under consideration is engaged in the business of providing IT enabled services and IT services. The assessee has adopted for both services in determining ALP TNMM method. The assessee while making TP study for determining ALP has 14 companies as comparable in respect of IT Enabled services segment and 22 companies comparable in respect of IT services segment and arrived at arithmetic means at 9.59 per cent and 10.24 per cent respectively as against 19.73 per cent of assessee's operating margin for IT enabled services and 23 per cent for IT services. However, TPO while making its TP study aggregated both segments. TPO considered functionality of 14 comparable companies furnished by assessee in respect of its IT enabled services and out of it he found 8 companies as comparable and rejected the balance 6 companies as not comparable. Since TPO found that 8 comparable companies provided in TPO report of assessee were inadequate in number, he took 25 set of comparable companies for IT enabled services . It is relevant to state that out of 25 set of those companies, 3 companies are common with assessee's own set of comparables. Assessee disputed 21 companies out of 25 comparable companies considered by department and filed objections before TPO as well as before DRP. TPO considered ALP of assessee's international transaction with associated enterprises by adopting arithmetic mean of 27.84 per cent and suggested upward adjustment of Rs. 9,29,93,816, after rejecting the objections of assessee. DRP in its order passed under section 144C(5) confirmed adjustment suggested by TPO with the direction to AO to give working capital adjustment by following decision of DRP in assessee's own case for assessment year 2006-07. As mentioned herein above, AO made assessment under section 143(3), read with section 144C but did not comply with direction of DRP to give working capital adjustment and stated that relevant details of comparables to give working capital adjustment is required and it also requires an exhaustive exercise before giving working capital adjustment.

During the course of hearing, the assessee disputed functionality, assets and risk of 7 companies as not comparable out of 30 comparable cases considered by TPO to arrive at arithmetic means of 27.84 per cent with the assessee company. The assessee submitted that actual margin of all 30 comparable companies considered by TPO is 26.5 per cent as per their annual reports. The Revenue did not dispute said contention of assessee and submitted that this could be verified by AO while giving effect to order of ITAT.

The assessee-company was engaged in activities like EPC lump sum turnkey contracts, engineering design services, supervision services, translation services and feasibility studies. During the year in question, it rendered services to 'T' group concerns through its personnel either from India or by deputation at the 'T' office or at the construction site. The assessee had a fully owned subsidiary called ICB. This company received revenues from its AE, JTS to the tune of Rs. 26.26 crore, which constituted 59 per cent of its total revenues. The assessee computed Arm's Length Price by using Transactional Net Margin Method using Profit Level Indicator as Operating profit to Cost. In its transfer pricing study, the assessee chose twelve cases as comparable giving average margin of operating profit to cost at 15.37 per cent. The assessee declared that its margin from international transactions with AEs at 75.48 per cent on cost was better than the average profit margin on similar base of twelve comparable cases shown by it. The Assessing Officer made a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA(1). The TPO took a view that, (i) twelve cases considered by the assessee as comparable were functionally different on end level and, hence, should be excluded for benchmarking. (ii ) ICB was an internally comparable case which had earned 66.77 per cent profit margin over total cost. It was only this cost which should be considered for determining ALP in assessee's case. (iii ) The assessee's contention that ICB had related party transactions of Rs. 29.53 crore including Rs. 26.26 crore as receipts from JTS and, hence, the same be excluded as controlled transactions, was not acceptable. The TPO thus adopted net profit margin over cost at 66.77 per cent for determining ALP in respect of the payments received by the assessee from its AEs and resultantly proposed adjustment of Rs. 7.13 crore (after rectification). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that (a) the TPO was wrong in rejecting all the twelve comparable cases cited by the assessee on entity level. Ten cases out of such twelve were functionally comparable on segment level. (b) ICB was functionally different inasmuch as it entered into the project business executing various electrical and instrumentation projects while the assessee's international transactions were in relation to service segment. (c) Transactions of ICB with JTS constituted related party transactions and, hence, the case of ICB should be excluded from the comparable cases. (d) On the basis of remaining ten comparable cases, the assessee's transactions with its AEs and its margin on cost at 75.48 per cent or even 44.21 per cent, was at arm's length and hence no addition was warranted. The Accountant Member in his opinion held that JTS was AE of ICB and, hence, the transactions between them constituted (d) controlled transactions. In that view of the matter, he ruled out the case ICB for determining the ALP in respect of the assessee's international transactions. It was further held that the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in accepting ten out of twelve cases considered by the assessee in its transfer pricing study as comparable because the assessee had given segmental data whereas the TPO rejected these cases due to non-comparability at the entity level. He, therefore, declined to interfere with the view of the Commissioner (Appeals) in this regard, thereby dismissing the appeal of the Revenue. On the other hand, the Judicial Member did not agree with the reasons as well as finding of the Accountant Member on the issue of internal comparable. The sum and substance of his finding was that when a transaction with AE was found and accepted at ALP, then such comparable transaction could also be considered for determining ALP in respect of other cases having transactions with its AEs. By applying this logic to the present situation, he opined that since the transactions between ICB and JTS were found to be at ALP, there was no reason to ignore such internally comparable transaction for determining ALP in respect of the assessee's international transactions. He held that the contrary view of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue, as upheld by the Accountant Member, was not sustainable. In view of difference of opinion between the two Members of the Tribunal, the matter was referred to the Third Member.

HELD (AS PER THIRD MEMBER)

Issue of jurisdiction of Third Member

35 taxmann.com 584 (Mumbai - Trib.) the ITAT held that in course of transfer pricing proceedings, there can be no question of substituting profit realized by Indian enterprise from its foreign AE with profit realized by foreign AE from ultimate customers for purposes of determining ALP of international transaction of Indian enterprise with its foreign AE. Therefore, an assessee cannot compare profit earned by its foreign AE with outside comparables to prove that price charged by it from transactions with said AE is at ALP However in case of GE Money Financial Services (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 420 (Delhi - Trib.) the ITAT held that foreign AE can be chosen as the tested party if it's the least complex among the transacting parties and comparable data is available.

Companies owing high Intangibles:-

The ITAT Bangalore in case of Momentive Performance Materials (India) (P.) Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 327 (Bangalore Trib.) held that a Company like Infosys holding huge brand value and substantial ownership of intangibles, cannot be compared with a Company having ITES segment with much lesser revenue. The ITAT Delhi also held the same in case of COWI India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 427 (Delhi Trib.).

Companies having extraordinary events:-

ITAT Delhi bench in case of Equant Solutions India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 192 (Delhi Trib.) has held that a Company with extraordinary events like amalgamation, a Company with extraordinary events like corporate restructuring cannot be a good comparable.

Use of Segmental financial data:-

It is settled by the various judicial precedents that where segmental data of a comparable is not available the said Company cannot be accepted as a valid Comparable. In case of Ariba Technologies India (P.) Ltd [2016] 67 taxmann.com 265 (Bangalore Trib.) the assessee was engaged in providing software development services to its AE on a cost plus Basis. The ITAT held that the Company Lucid Software Ltd. cannot be selected as a good comparable on the ground that it employed heavy capital in development of a Product. A Company profitability in the sale of product would be entirely different from the Company, who is involved in service sector and due to non availability of full information about the segmental details as to how much is the sale of product and how much is from the services, this entity cannot be taken into account for comparability

Companies with different Financial Year:-

It has been held in certain cases that a Company having a different financial year cannot be a good comparable. ITAT Bangalore in case of Hewlett- Packard (India) Globalsoft (P.) Ltd. [2015] 63 taxmann.com 136 (Bangalore - Trib.) held that once the annual report of a Company is for a year different from the financial year ending 31st March, then without doubt, it will cease to be good comparable, unless the information received in pursuance to a notice under section 133(6) from such Company, is reconciled with the figures available in such annual report.

Conclusion:-

Transfer pricing is not an exact science and it involves appreciation of various facts as a result of which transfer pricing especially selection of comparables has been a highly litigated area. Whether a Company is a good comparable or not will vary from facts to facts of the case. It is a subjective process and one should make the selection of comparables in light of various judicial pronouncements.
