This study5 is a conclusive proof of the fact that the ALP computed as per the present Indian framework suffers from several biases and is not a true reflection of the actual 'arm's length price'. As the Indian outsourcing economy continues to boom, it is extremely crucial to adopt a more sophisticated transfer pricing framework to ensure that we align our policies with the best international practices to better resolve our cross border taxation disputes.

As discussed earlier in this article, the Indian IT landscape has multiple players, each of whom undertake different functions and bear different risks. As the nature of functions/operations, business model and performance parameters are different for these entities; they cannot be compared to each other. GICs represent the segment of the IT arena where the risks borne are minimal, functions undertaken are mostly routine like coding, testing etc., and there is no non- routine intangible involved. Hence such a player cannot be compared to an entity that undertakes functions pertaining to the entire value chain of the software development process, starting from conceptua-lization and design to delivery to the final customer.Even if one was to compare, it is necessary to makes adequate adjustments to account for the difference in the risk profile of the same. The transfer pricing officers have alleged that GICs are exposed to the single customer risk as they provide services to their related parties only. Hence the Single customer risks of the GICs can be set off against the market risks borne by the third party comparables. However, the guidelines provide that no two risks can be considered to offset each other and needs to be accounted separately. In this respect, the ITAT has accepted that, typically a GIC is insulated from the market risks faced by the independent comparables and hence adequate adjustments needs to made to account for the same. However there is no clear guidance, in respect to the appropriate method to be followed. In various cases that has been heard by the ITAT, the taxpayer has proposed the use of methods like the CAPM* model, use of Prime Lending rate etc. to do risk adjustments, but the same have been rejected by the ITAT. Further, the ITAT has also observed that while market risk faced by the comparables is an 'existing' risk, the single customer risk borne by GICs, as alleged by the TPOs is only an "anticipated" risk. The challenge for the taxpayer in the coming years is going to be adequately quantifying these risks and accounting for the same.

Taxpayers would often incur certain expenses on behalf of their related parties, purely on account of administrative convenience.Typically, these expenses would be third party costs in the nature of hotel bills, travel expenses, mobile expenses etc. The contentions of the transfer pricing officer has been that such expenses represent payment for services rendered to related parties and has been accordingly adjusted by the officers for the mark-up.

Intra-group services

Payment of management charges or intra group cross charges by Indian subsidiaries to their parent companies has been under the scanner of the tax authorities as an alleged technique of shifting profits outside India. Group entities of MNCs often render shared services to each other. Services are usually of the nature of administrative, human resources, IT, and finance support.This kind of support services within the organization/group encourages specialization by specific groups or units of the MNC. Under such a scenario each unit is not required to develop its own internal team across all the functions, but can tap the expertise of the relevant team from other fellow group entities. This is especially beneficial for smaller subsidiaries or group entities and result in substantial cost savings for them and therefore indirectly benefits them.

However this fact has not been appreciated by the transfer pricing officers, and taxpayers have been asked to provide 'benefit test' and prove that these services are not stewardship and shareholder activities. In most of the cases the transfer pricing officers have held the arm's length price to be nil and have disallowed the entire expense. Even in cases where the services have been beneficial for the taxpayer and have resulted in high margins for the taxpayer, the TPO has made adjustments to the taxpayer.

In this respect, the ITAT has provided relief to taxpayers in form of some landmark judgments where they have analyzed the functions of the taxpayer and have held that the intra-group services satisfy the benefit test and are at arm's length. Further, the ITAT has ruled that it is not the prerogative of the transfer pricing officer to question the business decision of the taxpayer.

For GICs who operate under the cost plus model, such services should not pose any issues, as the costs pertaining to these services would form a part of the cost base for the purpose of mark-up. However there are some GICs who operate on revenue sharing model or hourly rate model and receive such intra-group services from their related party are exposed to this challenge.

'Comparable uncontrolled transaction', meaning of

10A.5 As per OECD TP Guidelines, a 'comparable uncontrolled transaction' is a transaction between two independent parties that is comparable to the controlled transaction under examination. It can be either a comparable transaction between one party to the controlled transaction and an independent party (known as 'internal comparable') or between two independent parties, neither of which is a party to the controlled transaction (known as 'external comparable'). Internal comparables would provide more reliable and accurate data than external comparables. This is because external comparables are difficult to obtain, incomplete and difficult to interpret. Hence, internal comparables are to be preferred over external comparables.

In California Software Co. Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 213/139 ITD 652 (Chennai - Trib.), it was held that in an environment where sufficient number of external comparables were available, it is imperative to examine those external comparables also alongwith internal comparables so as to come to a balanced finding on matters relating to deciding of ALP and consequential adjustment called for, if any. Internal comparables are also influenced by various factors, which may distort the acceptability norm, if not examined with the touchstone of unbiased conclusion generated out of a study of external comparables.

In Diageo India (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2013] 34 taxmann.com 284/59 SOT 150 (Mum. - Trib.), it was held that where there is similarity in nature of transactions and functions between controlled transactions with related party and uncontrolled transactions with unrelated party, internal comparability should be preferred, as it would result into more appropriate arm's length price requiring least amount of adjustments.

"Uncontrolled transaction" has also been defined in Rule 10A(ab), for the purposes of Rules 10AB to 10E, which means a transaction between enterprises other than AEs, whether resident or non-resident. Therefore, uncontrolled transactions may be between residents or non-residents; this is immaterial. However, they should not be between two AEs; but between 2 independent enterprises. For example, A and B are associated enterprises. C and D are independent parties (non-associated). Transaction between C and D is uncontrolled transaction as both A and B are concerned. Transaction between A and C/A and D are uncontrolled transactions as far as B is concerned. Transaction between B and C/B and D are uncontrolled transactions as far as A is concerned.

Once it is not in dispute that 'uncontrolled transaction' is a statutorily defined term, there is no room for discarding or questioning this definition on the basis of superior logic in an alternative definition. Such heroics are not called for in the process of judicial interpretation. Whether the transactions are with associated enterprises resident in India or with associated enterprises resident outside India, the prices at which such transactions are entered into with such enterprises cannot be taken as 'comparable uncontrolled price' for the purpose of determining the arm's length price. It is, therefore, the prices on which the assessee has sold the same products to resident associated enterprises cannot be taken as benchmark for ascertaining the arm's length price of its similar sale transaction with the non-resident enterprise. Once necessary inputs for ascertaining the ALP under CUP are not available, there cannot be any occasion to apply the same—Gemstone Glass (P.) Ltd. v. Joint CIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 1/[2016] 156 ITD 176 (Ahmd. - Trib.).

The very word 'comparable' means that the group of entities should be in a homogeneous group. They should not be wildly dissimilar or unlike or poles apart. Hence, for TP analysis, comparables should be selected who provide services of the same character performing similar functions and having similar levels of assets and risks.

Thus, locating proper comparables, i.e., comparable uncontrolled transactions is at the root of ALP mechanism.

The authoritative statement of arm's length principle is found in Article 9(1) of the OECD Model Tax Convention. It provides that "where conditions are made or imposed between the 2 AEs in their commercial or financial relations which differ from those which would be made between independent enterprises, then any profits which would, but for those conditions, have accrued to one of the enterprises, but, by reason of those conditions, have not so accrued, may be included in the profits of that enterprise and taxed accordingly".

By seeking to adjust profits by reference to the conditions which would have obtained between independent enterprises in comparable uncontrolled transactions, the arm's length principle follows the approach of treating the members of an MNE group as operating as separate entities rather than as inseparable parts of a single unified business due to which attention is focussed on the nature of the transactions between those members and on whether the conditions thereof differ from the conditions that would be obtained in comparable uncontrolled transactions. Such an analysis of controlled and uncontrolled transactions (referred to as "comparability analysis") is at the heart of the application of the arm's length principle.

Article 9(1) is the foundation for comparability analysis because it introduces the need for a comparison between conditions (including prices) made or imposed between AEs and those which would be made between independent enterprises in order to determine whether there is a need for re-writing the accounts for the purpose of calculating tax liabilities of AEs and a determination of the profits which would have accrued at arm's length in order to determine the quantum of any re-writing of accounts.

There are several reasons why OECD member countries and other jurisdictions have adopted the arm's length principle such as:—

(i)

It provides broad parity of tax treatment for members of MNE group and independent enterprises.

(ii)

It puts AEs and independent enterprises on a more equal footing for tax purposes since it avoids the creation of tax advantages or disadvantages that would otherwise distort the relative competitive positions of either type of entity.

(iii)

Its objective is to find a reasonable estimate of an arm's length outcome based on reliable information.

(iv)

It also promotes the growth of international trade and investment by removing tax considerations from economic decisions.

On the other hand, some hardships faced in adoption of arm's length principle are:—

(i)

There are some significant cases wherein this principle is difficult and complicated to apply such as MNE dealing in the integrated production of highly specialised goods, in unique intangibles, and/or in the provision of specialised services.

(ii)

This principle is viewed by some as inherently flawed merely because the separate entity approach may not always account for the economies of scale and interrelation of diverse activities created by integrated businesses.

(iii)

Another practical difficulty is that AEs may engage in transactions that independent enterprises would not undertake.

(iv)

In certain cases, the principle may result in an administrative burden for both the taxpayer and the tax administrations of evaluating significant numbers (including obtaining adequate information) and types of cross-border transactions. Since the principle requires taxpayers and tax administrations to evaluate uncontrolled transactions and the business activities of the independent enterprises, it can demand a substantial amount of data. However, the information or data which is accessible may be incomplete and difficult to comprehend, or in some cases, it may be impossible to obtain information due to geographical constraints or even due to confidentiality concerns of the independent enterprises.

The arm's length principle is sound in theory since it provides the closest approximation of the workings of an open market in cases where property such as goods, other types of tangible or intangible assets, is transferred or services are rendered between AEs. While it may not always be straightforward to apply in practice, it does generally produce appropriate levels of income between members of MNE groups, acceptable to tax administration. However, a move away from this principle would abandon the sound theoretical basis and threaten the international consensus thereby substantially increasing the risk of double taxation.

[2019] 103 taxmann.com 343/262 Taxman 215 (Bom.). 10A.17-8 Quasi-capital loans with normal loans - Usually, loan transactions are benchmarked on the basis of interest rate applicable on said transactions simpliciter which, under the transfer pricing regulations, cannot be compared with a transaction which is something materially different than a loan simpliciter, for example, a non-refundable loan which is to be converted into equity. It is in this context that the loan, which is in the nature of quasi capital, is treated differently than the normal loan transactions. The expression 'quasi capital' is relevant from the point of view of highlighting that a quasi capital loan or advance is not a routine loan transaction simpliciter. The substantive reward for such a loan transaction is not interest but opportunity to own capital. As a corollary to this position, in the cases of quasi capital loans or advances, the comparison of the quasi capital loans is not with the commercial borrowings but with the loans or advances which are given in the same or similar situations. Advances being in the nature of 'quasi capital' cover the situations in which (a) advances were made as capital could not be subscribed to due to regulatory issues and the advancing of loans was only for the period till the same could be converted into equity, and (b) advances were made for subscribing to the capital but the issuance of shares was delayed, even if not inordinately. Clearly, the advances in such circumstances were materially different than the loan transactions simpliciter and that is what was decisive so far as determination of the arm's length price of such transactions was concerned. The reward for time value of money in these cases was opportunity to subscribe to the capital, unlike in a normal loan transaction where reward is interest, which is measured as a percentage of the money advanced. On a conceptual note, several types of debts, particularly long-term unsecured debts, and revenue participation investments could be termed as quasi-capital—Soma Textile & Industries Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2015] 59 taxmann.com 152/154 ITD 745 (Ahmd. - Trib.).

10A.17-9 Guarantee commission - In the matter of guarantee commission, the adjustment made by the TPO were based on instances restricted to the commercial banks providing guarantees and did not contemplate the issue of a corporate guarantee. No doubt these are contracts of guarantee, however, when they are commercial banks that issue bank guarantees which are treated as the blood of commerce being easily encashable in the event of default, and if the bank guarantee had to be obtained from commercial banks, the higher commission could have been justified. In the present case, it is assessee-company that is issuing corporate guarantee to the effect that if the subsidiary AE does not repay loan availed of it from ICICI, then in such event, the assessee would make good the amount and repay the loan. The considerations which applied for issuance of a corporate guarantee are distinct and separate from that of bank guarantee and, accordingly, commission charged cannot be called in question, in the manner TPO has done. Thus, such comparison is not as between like transactions but the comparisons are between guarantees issued by the commercial banks as against a corporate guarantee issued by holding company for the benefit of its AE, a subsidiary company—CIT v. This method should not be used unless the net profit indicators are determined from uncontrolled transactions of the same taxpayer in comparable circumstances, or where the comparable uncontrolled transactions are those of an independent enterprise, the differences between the AEs and independent enterprises that have a material effect on the net profit indicator being used are adequately taken into account. Thus, where differences in the characteristics of the enterprises being compared have a material effect on the net profit indicators being used, it would not be appropriate to apply the TNMM without making adjustments for such differences.

The TNMM has seen a transition from a disfavoured comparable method to possibly the most appropriate TP method due to ease and flexibility of applying the compatibility criteria and enhanced availability of comparables. Net profit record/data is assessable and within reach. It is readily and easily available, entity-wise in the form of audited accounts. This method is a preferred TP arm's length principle for its proficiency, convenience and reliability. Ideally, in this method, preference should be given to internal or in-house comparables. In absence of internal comparables, the taxpayer can and would need to rely upon external comparables. For several reasons, database providers, it is apparent, have the requisite information and data of external comparables to enable comparability analysis of the controlled and uncontrolled transactions with necessary adjustment to obtain reliable results under TNMM. This method also works to the benefit and advantage of the tax authorities in view of convenience and easier availability of data not only from third party providers, but on their own level, i.e., assessment records of other parties.

Even while applying the TNMM, comparables cannot be picked on the basis of broad classification under various heads and that the actual functional profile of the comparable must be similar, if not same, to that of the taxpayer-assessee. In comparability analysis, the business environment, demand and supply of the services, assets employed and, competence to provide different services are factors which would have a material bearing on the profitability of the entities and, therefore, regard must be had to such factors. In the application of this method, broad similarity in the domain of services is not enough and the overall FAR analysis of the comparable sought to be used must be similar with the taxpayer-assessee—PCIT v. Open Solutions Software Services (P.) Ltd. [2020] 116 taxmann.com 708 (Delhi).

TNMM method is more tolerant to variation in comparability and is more suitable when there is no high degree of comparability between the transactions. Basis of selection of a comparable depends upon quantum of adjustment that it would permit rather than other factors—Asstt. CIT v. Schlafhorst Marketing Co. Ltd. [2011] 13 taxmann.com 104/47 SOT 120 (URO) (Mum. - Trib.).

TNMM has almost become the 'default' method for taxpayers in recent years. The key advantage of the TNMM is that there is often available data in the public domain about the net profits that comparable independent businesses earn from their trading activities in comparable markets with other third parties. As such, the TNMM often proves easier to apply than, say, the Cost Plus or RPM methods, and TNMM is less sensitive to minor differences in the products being sold—Gemstone Glass (P.) Ltd. v. JCIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 1/[2016] 156 ITD 176 (Ahd. - Trib.).

Overview of captives in the Indian IT/ITeS space

Historically the term 'captive' has been used to refer to entities located in low cost geographies, providing 'service delivery operations' to entities within its Group located in different geographies. Thus captives (also referred to as Global In-house Centers ['GICs'] or 'captive IT/ITeS entities') act as an extension of a Multi National Enterprise ('MNE') group, set up to leverage labour arbitrage in certain geographies. Usually only low value adding functions/processes are outsourced to such captives, implying that they act as a cost center for the MNE group which in turn remunerates them on a cost plus mark-up.

Following are the strategic advantages derived by an MNE group in setting up a captive entity:

Labour arbitrage opportunities;

Operational efficiency, where the captives provide cost efficient operations with continuous productivity improvements;

Providing scalability to the MNE Group's business through access to a large talent pool providing high skill capabilities;

Protection of Intellectual Property Rights ('IPRs') of the Group as all the innovations and new product development by the Group need not be shared with third parties.

According to latest estimates of NASSCOM, there are over 825 GICs in India offering IT/ITeS services across Tier I/II/III cities in India. These GICs occupy a very prominent space in the Indian IT/ITeS industry with an employee base of over 530,000 people (comprising 20 per cent of the IT/ITeS employee base in India) and accounting for 17 per cent of the overall IT export revenues in India.2

Application of Transfer Pricing in the Captive IT/ITeS space

Since the MNE Group and the GICs are located in different geographies, the provision of services by the GICs to the MNE Group attracts Transfer Pricing scrutiny under the local tax laws. As referred, the MNE Groups generally outsource low value adding functions to GICs which are performed as per detailed specifications provided by the MNE Group. Since the GICs render services only within the Group and are remunerated on a fixed cost plus mark basis, they don't bear many of the risks associated with entrepreneurial development activity such as market risk, contract risk, financial risk, credit risk etc. Hence the GICs can be categorized as 'low risk contract service providers'.

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development ('OECD') has laid down Transfer Pricing Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises and Tax Administrations (broadly referred to as 'OECD Guidelines'). The principles outlined under these OECD Guidelines are followed by many countries in drafting their Transfer Pricing laws. While India does not follow the OECD Guidelines, it acts as an observer nation.

As per Para 1.42 of the OECD Guidelines, compensation in a transaction between two enterprises usually reflects the function that each enterprise performs, taking into account the assets used and the risks assumed. Accordingly functional analysis of an international transaction forms the pillar of a Transfer Pricing exercise. Further, as per Para 1.45, material risks assumed by each party to the transaction have to be considered as part of any functional analysis, since the assumption or allocation of risks would influence the conditions of transactions between associated enterprises. Usually in an open market (implying in an arm's length dealing between independent enterprises), the assumption of increased risk would be compensated by an increase in the expected return.

The concept is further explained in Para 1.47 where it is concluded that a contract research provider (akin to a captive IT/ITeS entity) that takes on no meaningful risk would usually expect only a limited return. Accordingly, the relationship between the risk and return profile of associated enterprises in international transactions can be illustrated through Figure 2 below.

Figure 2: Graphical representation of the relationship between the function, asset and risk profile of an entity and its capacity to generate profits

Hence, it can be deduced that low risk entities should have a transfer pricing policy that allows them to generate low but stable benefits. On the other hand, high risk entities will usually have a transfer pricing policy that allows them to generate significant profits or losses. This is consistent with the remuneration model of GICs which are generally remunerated on a cost plus fixed markup for their routine activities. Hence, whether the MNE Group earns supernormal profits or losses, the GIC would always earn a stable but limited return.

With nine rounds of transfer pricing audit completed in January 2014, the challenging days for Indian outsourcing sector does not seem to get over. The total quantum of transfer pricing adjustments made in FY 2012-13 was to the tune of seventy thousand crores1 (for Assessment Year ("AY") 2009-10) up by 54 per cent earlier. Indian outsourcing sector accounts for more than half the total claims in transfer pricing adjustments made during the aforesaid audit cycle from about one-third earlier.

However, as per recently disseminated data, the additions to income of companies undertaking international transaction has dropped by over 14 per cent to sixty thousand crores2 in FY 2014 tax audit cycle (for AY 2010-11). This seems to be a silver lining in an otherwise dismal environment emanating from the North Block.

Outsourcing sector accounts for more than USD 100 billion share in India's economy with big foreign companies like IBM, Capgemini, Microsoft, GE etc. putting forward a big basket of service offerings viz. customer service, risk and fraud management and finance and accounting. In the backdrop of the great demographic dividend, India has been one of the most preferred Knowledge Services Outsourcing ("KSO") destinations holding 70 per-cent share of the global KSO market3. India is poised to emerge as a global hub for KSO by 2015.

Over a period of time, multiplicity of business arrangements have happened in the outsourcing space starting from outsourcing of accounting processes to legal and research process outsourcing. While, Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") service stands for taking up routine operations like data entry, voice calling and accounting services, a shift of functions performed that requires expert analysis and decision making viz. patent application drafting, technical research and advisory activities etc. mark the outset of a new category of Knowledge Process Outsourcing ("KPO") services. This broad bifurcation though coined by the industry itself is important from a transfer pricing stand-point and is analyzed deeply by the Special Bench of Mumbai Tribunal in the case of Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited discussed in this article.

Being a booming sector, Indian Information Technology ecosystem comprises of many aces to the likes of Infosys, Wipro, Tata Consultancy and other big Indian players. In such backdrop, how adequate would it be to compare margins of smaller IT companies with the abnormal margins of aforesaid gigantic companies having global business outshoots also, is another vexatious TP issue dealt with in detail in the aforesaid judgment.

1. FACTS OF CASE

Maersk Global Centres (India) Private Limited ("Maersk India") was incorporated in India as a wholly owned subsidiary of Maersk GSC Holdings, part of Maersk Group. Maersk India is in the business of shared services and renders transaction processing support and information technology services. During the year under assessment, Maersk India provided certain IT and IT enabled services to its Associated Enterprises ("AEs") and separately benchmarked the aforesaid transactions under IT and ITeS business segments. Applying Transactional Net Margin Method ("TNMM") with operating profit to total cost ("OP/TC") as Profit level indicator ("PLI"), the assessee selected thirteen comparables and claimed working capital and risk adjustment in its TP report.

In case of ITeS segment, the TPO classified the services provided by Maersk India as KPO services and rejected all but one comparables selected by the assessee and modified the search criteria adopted by assessee. He selected seven comparables including one chosen by the assessee. TPO allowed working capital adjustment but dismissed risk adjustment. In case of IT service segment, TPO computed arm's length margin without allowing working capital adjustment. The AO maintained the TPOs views in the draft assessment order.

Maersk India filed its objections before Dispute Resolution Panel ("DRP") stating that the assessee was a low-end back office service provider being a captive unit working in a zero risk zone and hence should not be categorized as a KPO and high margin comparables selected by the TPO should be dropped. The DRP maintained the high margin comparables selected by TPO on the premise that both high and low margin companies reflect industry profitability and dispensing off super-profit making companies symbolizes addressing only one end of the spectrum and that is not correct. The DRP further disapproved the segmental bifurcation of services by the assessee as IT and ITeS. DRP directed the TPO to benchmark the international transactions with ten final comparables comprising of five comparables selected by the assessee and TPO each. The Panel did not allow relief on risk adjustment.

This case was earlier included by the assessee in the list of comparables in the transfer pricing study by considering multiple-year data. [Para 12.1] The legal objection taken by the revenue that the assessee should be prohibited from taking a stand contrary to the one which was taken at the stage of the TP study or during the course of proceedings before the authorities below cannot be accepted. It goes without saying that the object of assessment is to determine the income in respect of which the assessee is rightly chargeable to tax. As the income not originally offered for taxation, if otherwise chargeable, is required to be included in the total income, in the same breath, any income wrongly included in the total income, which is not otherwise chargeable, should be excluded. There can be no estoppel against the provisions of the Act. Extending this proposition further to the context of the transfer pricing, if the assessee fails to report an otherwise comparable case, then the TPO is obliged to include it in the list of comparables, and in the same manner, if the assessee wrongly reported an incomparable case as comparable in its TP study and then later on claims that it should be excluded then, there should be nothing to forbid the assessee from claiming so, provided the TPO is satisfied that the case so originally reported as comparable is, in fact, not comparable. "Eli Lilly and Company Vs. Commissioner – 84 TC 996 (1985)" , the Tax Court rejected the CUP method because the adjustment could not be made on account of differences arising due to credit terms, supply of raw material, packaging, product quality and patent. If there are many adjustments to be made to the uncontrolled sales in comparison with the controlled sales, then the CUP method cannot be termed reliable and reasonable to be an arms length price for transfer pricing evaluation. U.S. Regulation 1.482-3(b)(5) provides that when the CUP method is to be applied on the basis of the public data, it should be a widely and routinely used data. The data should have been used for setting up prices for controlled transactions in the same way, as it is being used for uncontrolled transactions.

In the case of "Intervet India Private Ltd., Vs. ACIT , Mumbai – (2010) TII – 12- ITAT-MUM-TP", the following facts have been brought out clearly for the use of a CUP method :

A reasonably accurate adjustment has to be made for

The elimination of material factors such as the price , the cost or profit arising from a transaction with an associated enterprise Vs. unrelated party

Volume Off-take discounts, credit period and forex risks has to be adjusted for

Economic and market conditions in which the Associated Enterprise functions Vs. unrelated party – sale to a wholesale agent Vs. the final user has to be considered and adjusted for

In VVF Limited Vs. DCIT – (ITANo.673 –MUM – 08), it was held by the ITAT that the transaction of lending money by the assessee by way of interest free foreign currency loan to its foreign subsidiaries, should be compared with a company lending in foreign currency to unrelated party. It was observed that the ICICI Bank had advanced foreign currency loan to the assessee at LIBOR plus 3%. This can be taken as an "internal CUP" as the credit rating of subsidiary merges with the credit rating of the Parent. The comparison of interest should not be benchmarked with the Cash Credit @14% given to the Assessee.

In another case, DCIT Vs. M/s 3 Global Services Private Limited (ITA No.1812/MUM/2009), Mumbai the ITAT held that per hour billing rate published by the NASSCOM for a specific business segment as an "external CUP" in determining the arms’ length price.

The Assessee operates in the voice-based customer care sub-segment of IT-enabled services industry. The assessee rendered services to its associated enterprise and the selected CUP method as the Most Appropriate Method to justify the arm’s length price of its international transactions. The assessee applied the CUP method , relying on the hourly rate of the "customer care" published by the NASSCOM and a report prepared by the Batliwala & Karani Securities (India) Pvt. Ltd.,- an equity research company.

The Transfer Pricing Officer rejected the CUP method selected by the Assessee and chose Transaction Net Margin Method (TNMM) as the Most Appropriate Method selecting five companies operating in various segments – such as KPO, Content Development, Data Conversion, Software and the like, These segments are totally different from the Voice Based Customer Support Services performed by the Assessee. On appeal, the CIT ( Appeals) agreed to Assessee’s contention and rejected the TNMM method proposed by the TPO stating that the comparables selected do not belong to the Voice Based BPO services.

The Revenue went on appeal to the ITAT. The ITAT categorically stated that per hour rate of a specific sub-segment of the ITES industry can be considered as the CUP provided the assessee applying such rate belongs to such sub-segment. Further, companies operating in different segment of the industry cannot be selected as comparable for applying the TNMM.

Let us take an example, of an Indian company exporting a particular component to its Associated Enterprise for which there is no comparable transaction available and no other company in the industry does sell those components.

In order to justify the arms length pricing of such a specific transaction, the Indian company can submit the Cost Sheet certified by a Cost Accountant and justify the Export Price. It can defend the profit margins earned on sale of component to its AE with that of its profit margins earned on sale of the total unit. This can be termed as an "internal CUP".

In the case of National Semiconductor Corp Vs. Commissioner (67 TCM (CCH)2849 (1994)(US Tax Court), it was held that It is equally important to determine the adjustments to account for the differences in price of controlled and uncontrolled transactions. This case lays down the conditions that should exist to apply the CUP method.

The Uncontrolled price is comparable to the controlled price if the physical property and circumstances involved in the uncontrolled transactions are identical or nearly identical to the controlled transactions that any differences have no effect on price or such differences can be reflected by a reasonable number of adjustments to the price of the uncontrolled transactions

Adjustments can be made only where such differences have a definite and reasonably ascertainable effect on the price

Under the CUP method, the comparables should be drawn from the transactions that are comparable from the economic and business perspective

The assessee-company was engaged in activities like EPC lump sum turnkey contracts, engineering design services, supervision services, translation services and feasibility studies. During the year in question, it rendered services to 'T' group concerns through its personnel either from India or by deputation at the 'T' office or at the construction site. The assessee had a fully owned subsidiary called ICB. This company received revenues from its AE, JTS to the tune of Rs. 26.26 crore, which constituted 59 per cent of its total revenues. The assessee computed Arm's Length Price by using Transactional Net Margin Method using Profit Level Indicator as Operating profit to Cost. In its transfer pricing study, the assessee chose twelve cases as comparable giving average margin of operating profit to cost at 15.37 per cent. The assessee declared that its margin from international transactions with AEs at 75.48 per cent on cost was better than the average profit margin on similar base of twelve comparable cases shown by it. The Assessing Officer made a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA(1). The TPO took a view that, (i) twelve cases considered by the assessee as comparable were functionally different on end level and, hence, should be excluded for benchmarking. (ii ) ICB was an internally comparable case which had earned 66.77 per cent profit margin over total cost. It was only this cost which should be considered for determining ALP in assessee's case. (iii ) The assessee's contention that ICB had related party transactions of Rs. 29.53 crore including Rs. 26.26 crore as receipts from JTS and, hence, the same be excluded as controlled transactions, was not acceptable. The TPO thus adopted net profit margin over cost at 66.77 per cent for determining ALP in respect of the payments received by the assessee from its AEs and resultantly proposed adjustment of Rs. 7.13 crore (after rectification). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that (a) the TPO was wrong in rejecting all the twelve comparable cases cited by the assessee on entity level. Ten cases out of such twelve were functionally comparable on segment level. (b) ICB was functionally different inasmuch as it entered into the project business executing various electrical and instrumentation projects while the assessee's international transactions were in relation to service segment. (c) Transactions of ICB with JTS constituted related party transactions and, hence, the case of ICB should be excluded from the comparable cases. (d) On the basis of remaining ten comparable cases, the assessee's transactions with its AEs and its margin on cost at 75.48 per cent or even 44.21 per cent, was at arm's length and hence no addition was warranted. The Accountant Member in his opinion held that JTS was AE of ICB and, hence, the transactions between them constituted (d) controlled transactions. In that view of the matter, he ruled out the case ICB for determining the ALP in respect of the assessee's international transactions. It was further held that the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in accepting ten out of twelve cases considered by the assessee in its transfer pricing study as comparable because the assessee had given segmental data whereas the TPO rejected these cases due to non-comparability at the entity level. He, therefore, declined to interfere with the view of the Commissioner (Appeals) in this regard, thereby dismissing the appeal of the Revenue. On the other hand, the Judicial Member did not agree with the reasons as well as finding of the Accountant Member on the issue of internal comparable. The sum and substance of his finding was that when a transaction with AE was found and accepted at ALP, then such comparable transaction could also be considered for determining ALP in respect of other cases having transactions with its AEs. By applying this logic to the present situation, he opined that since the transactions between ICB and JTS were found to be at ALP, there was no reason to ignore such internally comparable transaction for determining ALP in respect of the assessee's international transactions. He held that the contrary view of the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue, as upheld by the Accountant Member, was not sustainable. In view of difference of opinion between the two Members of the Tribunal, the matter was referred to the Third Member.

Introduction

1. The Indian IT/ ITeS industry has witnessed exceptional growth in the last decade and has been instrumental in registering a multi-fold increase in foreign exchange earnings for the country. In addition to fuelling India's economy, this industry is also positively influencing the lives of its people through contributing in employment generation and augmenting standards of living. The industry has helped India transform from a rural and agriculture-based economy to a knowledge based economy.

As per a recent NASSCOM report, the Indian IT-BPO industry's aggregate revenues have crossed the USD 100 billion mark with exports of USD 69 billion in year 2012. Within Software and services exports, IT services accounts for 58 per cent and BPO is nearly 23 per cent, Engineering and R&D ('ER&D') and Software Products account for 19 per cent.

The mitochondria of Indian IT sector can be broadly divided into two segments on the basis of nature of services performed. On one hand, there are Indian IT Companies like Wipro, Infosys, HCL, etc., who have established their footprint on the global scale by establishing offshore software product development centres ('OSPD'). India's OSPD market has experienced double digit growth over the past five years. On the other hand, there are inbound investments by various foreign multi-national IT Companies like Microsoft, IBM, Genpact, Capgemini etc. where predominantly foreign IT majors outsource their research, software development and testing to captive Indian subsidiaries or through Global In-house centres ('GIC').

Various steps involved in software development projects

2. A software development project typically entails various steps starting from conception of the desired software, research and application development, software design, writing and maintaining source code, prototyping, modification, re-engineering, maintenance and other activities.

Ideally, a full-fledged software company should undertake all the phases involved in software development. However, such is not the case always. Mostly, software companies outsource certain parts of their software development functions to their offshore subsidiaries stationed in nations with a rich knowledge base, anticipating cost-effectiveness in operations due to low human resource cost. In such type of arrangements, generally the conceptualization and quality assessment aspects are taken care of by the parent software company only, whereas the captive subsidiaries are only involved in functional research and development activities. Such captive subsidiaries are named as 'contract R&D centres' due to the limited nature of work handled by them. Usually, the major part of risk-taking work in terms of business development, bidding, sales and marketing is done by the parent company in such cases, thereby ensuring consistent work flow to their captive R&D centres. The contract R&D centres in return undertake to complete the work assigned to them as per the quality specifications. This arrangement can be compared to the traditional outsourcing model where the work execution is done by the sub-contracted company (in this case a captive subsidiary) to the satisfaction of the customer (in this case the parent company).

The Transfer Pricing Controversy

3. Transfer Pricing ('TP') is one of the major concerns for IT companies today. There are widespread TP adjustments and additions in many cases. Many issues that are being faced by IT sector today pertain to choice of comparables where divergence of opinion occurs between the taxpayer and the revenue on the inclusion of companies as comparables, matter relating to choice of Most Appropriate Method ('MAM'), issues surrounding the quantitative and qualitative filters, use of multiple year's data, disagreement on crediting the benefit of working capital adjustment, revenue denying the benefit of +/-5 per cent range, etc.

From several TP issues faced by the Indian IT sector today, one major TP issue relates to the margins charged by IT companies. The tax authorities are consistently proposing margin of 20-27 per cent for the IT segment, while the taxpayer attributes a downward trend in the margins, experienced within 12-15 per cent. The comparables selected by the tax authorities are big companies like Wipro, HCL. These are independent business enterprises taking extensive risks and infusing large asset base in their business. The margins computed by the tax authorities swell the moment such comparables are added to the basket of identified comparable companies. On the other hand, in case of captive research centres, major business development functions, risks and assets associated with the software development operations are borne by foreign parent companies, the price paid by them ought to be lower in comparison to cases where both the associated enterprises operate on a principal-to-principal basis.

To address the issues faced by the IT sector companies, a committee chaired by N Rangachary, former Chairman, CBDT was formed last year. The Committee penned out its suggestions in September last year, which were not made public. Out of several suggestions made by the Rangachary Committee, one of the key recommendations has been a 20 per cent safe harbour rate for IT/ ITeS sector. Further, the Committee is understood to be favouring the cost plus method over profit-split method.

Bad debts, not a relevant fact in determining ALP - Merely because assessee has paid royalty even in respect of the products sold by it to the clients, who had not paid for the same, it would make no difference to the determination of the ALP of the transaction since s. 92C provides the basis for determining the ALP and does not either expressly or impliedly consider failure of the assessee's customers to pay for the products sold to them to be a relevant factor in determining the ALP [CIT v. COMPARABILITY

Benchmarking when can be reliable - In order for the benchmarking studies to be reliable for the purposes of determining the ALP, it would be essential that the entities selected as comparables are functionally similar and are subject to the similar business environment and risks as the tested party. In order to impute an ALP to a controlled transaction, it would be essential to ensure that the instances of uncontrolled entities/transactions selected as comparables are similar in all material aspects that have any bearing on the value or the profitability, as the case may be, of the transaction. Any factor, which has an influence on the PLI, would be material and it would be necessary to ensure that the comparables are also equally subjected to the influence of such factors as the tested party. This would, obviously, include business environment, nature and functions performed by the tested party and the comparable entities, value addition in respect of products and services provided by parties, business model, and the assets and resources employed. It cannot be disputed that the functions performed by an entity would have a material bearing on the value and profitability of the entity. It is, therefore, obvious that the comparables selected and the tested party must be functionally similar for ascertaining a reliable ALP [Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 355/234 Taxman 573 (Delhi), SLP granted inCIT v. Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 287/[2017] 244 Taxman 153 (SC)].

Comparison allowed with foreign parties also - The assertion that comparison can be made by choosing comparable of domestic cases not using any foreign brand is contrary to the provisions and amounts to rewriting of law. The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Also see, Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), followed inPCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

Data for comparison - While determining comparability of transactions, multiple year data can only be included in manner provided in above Rule 10B(4) and, thus, it is not open to assessee to rely upon PY's data as a general rule [Chryscapital Investment Advisors (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417/232 Taxman 20 (Delhi)].

To conduct the experiment described in Section 4, we used the previously introduced Indian Tax Authority set of 11 comparable ITES companies.

We compared each test firm to the original arm's-length range established by the 11 companies using the Indian rules. We then calculated (1) whether or not the company is in the range, (2) if the company is below the range, the size of the adjustments to the mean and to the median, and (3) the difference between those adjustments and the "correct" adjustment. For the experiment we assumed that if a company is within the range or above, the Indian Tax Authority would not adjust its tax return.

The Results and Conclusion

The correct aggregate adjustment for the 11 test firms - when we adjust each test firm’s revenue back up to its original amount - would have been Rs. 366 million. This is our benchmark. Two of the test firms, however, were still in or above the arm's-length range. Thus, it is unlikely that their non-arm's-length prices would have garnered attention. The remaining 9 test firms were below the range.

When we adjusted each of these 9 company's NCPM to the set mean, we found that the sum of these adjustments was Rs. 464 million exceeding the correct aggregate adjustment by Rs. 98 million. To put this in perspective, this is an additional tax burden equal to 4.8% of the operating income of the adjusted firms. Since transfer pricing adjustments will only occur with multinational firms it may place them at a substantial disadvantage compared with domestic providers of ITES services.

Alternatively, when we adjusted these same firms to the median of the set, the total adjustment was Rs. 345 million. While much closer to the correct adjustment of Rs. 366, this method of calculation would deprive the Indian Government of Rs. 21 million of tax revenue.

Clearly, due to positive skewness in the dataset, the error resulting from adjustment to the mean is greater than that of adjusting to the median. Yet, as the Indian Tax Authority is committed to adjusting to the mean, we sought to examine a compromise-a third alternative aimed at reducing, to a greater extent, the skewness of the comparable set. As a common way of calculating a meaningful average of a dataset is to remove outliers, we postulated using a "trimmed" mean that might be applied when the comparable set is skewed.

The calculation of a trimmed or truncated mean implies discarding an equal number of the highest and lowest observations. In this case, we trimmed the highest and the lowest observation from the Indian ITES set and recalculated the aggregate adjustment to the mean. As a result, the error in adjustment was only Rs. 14 million, lower than either that of the adjustment to mean or median, noted above. This could be a helpful method of reducing the effect of skewness in data sets, while remaining acceptable to Indian Tax authorities whose law is written in terms of adjusting to the mean.

Our standard for judging the accuracy of a method implicitly took the view of a tax authority seeking to collect an appropriate revenue stream from the multinational firms operating in their jurisdiction collectively. We have not considered the impact on individual firms which were quite varied. Some firms were not adjusted at all as their non-arm's-length pricing was not detected and others were adjusted far more than the known amount of non-arm's-length pricing.

Another contention of the Indian revenue authorities in relation to captive development centers in India is that the cost savings associated with operating in a low cost jurisdiction like India (commonly referred to as 'location savings') should be considered while carrying out comparability analysis. This is also emphasized in the United Nations Practice Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries (also referred to as the 'UN Practice Manual'). Further, the Location Specific Advantages ('LSAs') derived by MNEs in addition to the location savings are further identified in the UN Practice Manual as below:

Highly specialized skilled manpower and knowledge

Access and proximity to growing local/regional market

Large customer base with increased spending capacity

Superior information network

Superior distribution network

Incentives

Market premium

The Indian Transfer Pricing administration believes it is possible to use the profit split method to determine arm's length allocation of location savings and rents in cases where comparable uncontrolled transactions are not available.

India being a low cost jurisdiction attracts the attention of a lot of MNE groups who intend to exploit the advantages of location savings and LSAs. As a result it may well be argued that the any tangible benefit accruing to such MNE groups is not exclusive and hence does not provide any durable competitive advantage. Accordingly, it becomes very difficult to quantify and allocate any location specific benefits between AEs.

In fact the profit split method is also advocated by the Indian revenue authorities in case of development centers engaged in significant R&D activities. In this regard, it is pertinent to note the CBDT had issued Circular 2/2013 dated 26 March 2013 promoting the use of profit split method for benchmarking of R&D activities by development centers in India. The said circular was subsequently withdrawn upon representations from the industry about possible misinterpretation of the said circular. However, the CBDT issued Circular 6/2013 dated 29 June 2013 providing guidelines to identify R&D service providers with insignificant risk. Although the circular aims to provide clarity in analyzing the functions of captive development centers in India and thereby the selection of the most appropriate method for benchmarking, it may well be argued that the same is still amenable to misinterpretation giving rise to transfer pricing disputes.

Transfer Pricing litigation in the captive IT/ITeS space

Following are the broad areas of litigation that have emerged over the years consequent to the aggressive approach adopted by the revenue:

1. Functional comparability

As per Para 1.33 of the OECD Guidelines, application of the arm's length principle is generally based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with conditions in transactions between independent enterprises. For such comparison to be appropriate, the economically relevant characteristics of the situations being compared must be sufficiently comparable. The concept of comparability has been further elucidated by stating that, to be comparable means that none of the differences (if any) between the situations being compared could materially affect the condition being examined in the methodology (e.g. price or margin), or that reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the effect of any such differences.

Para 1.36 lays down the factors that may be considered when determining comparability between controlled and uncontrolled transactions and enterprises. These factors are listed as below:

Characteristics of the property or services transferred,

Functions performed by the parties (taking into account assets used and risks assumed),

Contractual terms,

Economic circumstances of the parties, and

Business strategies pursued by the parties

The above referred principles have also been reiterated in the UN Practice Manual.

The principles of comparability under the Indian Income Tax law also largely mirror the above referred principles laid down in the OECD Guidelines. The same are listed under Rule 10B(2) and Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 ('Rules').

The principles of comparability enshrined in the OECD Guidelines as well as the Indian Income Tax law, were relied upon by the Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. Agnity India Technologies (P.) Ltd. [2013] 219 Taxman 26/36 taxmann.com 289, wherein the Hon'ble High Court upheld the ruling of the Delhi Tribunal in deeming Infosys Limited as functionally not comparable to a captive service provider like Agnity India Technologies (P.) Further, an uncontrolled transaction shall be comparable to an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction, if —

(i)

none of the differences between the transactions being compared, or between the enterprises entering into such transactions are likely to materially affect the price or cost charged or paid in or the profit arising from such transactions in the open market; or

(ii) reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the material effects of such differences17.

On basis of criteria and conditions laid out above, we may select Indian Comparables when the Indian Taxpayer is chosen as the Tested Party. Conversely, we may select Foreign Comparables when the Foreign AE is chosen as the Tested Party.

So, Foreign Comparables can be considered for benchmarking under the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations when Foreign AE is chosen as the Tested Party, for the reason that reliable data of Indian Comparables is not available.

Next we look at another interesting issue.

6. How to do benchmarking and select comparables when the Foreign AE also has a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India?

6.1 Case of Tata Motors European Technical Centre Plc.'s case (supra)

[Note: The peculiarity of this case is that the Assessee is a Foreign Company, not an Indian Company.]

6.1.1 Facts of the case : The assessee (a Foreign Company), Tata Motor European Technical Centre PLC (TMETC), was incorporated in the United Kingdom (UK). It was a resident of UK and a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Motors Ltd. (TML – an Indian Company). The assessee rendered automotive design and engineering services to Tata Motors Ltd. (TML). For rendering these services the assessee-company sent its employees in India. Those employees were engineers and technical personnel deputed at TML's factory and establishment in India. Thus, the assessee had a Service Permanent Establishment (Service PE) in India.

6.1.2 Assessee's Benchmarking: The assessee benchmarked its service transaction by taking into account the following factors –

The design and engineering services for automotive industries were highly specialized services. Considering the nature of automotive industries in terms of global standards, competition, and growing compliance requirements towards safety and environmental norms, the parallels (or comparables) were not available in India.

The major operation cost incurred by the PE was towards the salary of the employees who had special skills and knowledge. Those employees were paid salary only in the UK.

The PE did not have any independent business in India and it did not enter into any contract with any outside party in India.

Considering these factors the assessee took itself (Foreign AE) as the Tested Party to apply TNMM. Accordingly, comparables located in the UK, rendering similar kind of services, were selected for benchmarking.

6.1.3 Transfer Pricing Officer's view: The Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO), however, observed as under -

Selection of foreign comparables based in the UK was not tenable under the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations.

Because the PE of the assessee was located in India and was carrying on its business within the Indian territory, it had to be treated as a business entity in India, akin to the other corporate entities doing business in India.

Further, assessee's direct and indirect costs were incurred in and in connection with business transactions in India.

In view of the above facts, the TPO held that only Indian comparables had to be selected for benchmarking the assessee's margin.

6.1.4 ITAT's decision in the case :

The decision rendered in the case by the ITAT has been summarized below:

(i)

Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not specify that the comparability analysis of International Transactions has to be strictly with reference to Indian comparables.

(ii)

The Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations, while selecting comparable companies for carrying out the comparability analysis, lay emphasis on FAR analysis and conditions prevailing in the markets in which the parties operate18. If such comparability analysis cannot be done properly by taking Indian comparables - looking to the characteristics and nature of the functions performed and services rendered - then one must consider who should be selected as "Tested Party".

(iii)

Based on selection of the Tested Party, comparables are to be chosen taking into account the economic factors and the functions performed in the conditions prevalent in the location of the tested party.

(iv)

If the tested party itself is foreign based and the services rendered by it are very specific, for which the Indian comparables are not available, or functionally not comparable, then it cannot be held that foreign comparables cannot be selected for benchmarking the Arm's Length Price or margin.

(v)

Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not put any fetters on selection of foreign comparables, if conditions are as such that the Indian comparables do not stand the test of comparability with the tested party.

(vi)

If the tested party has been selected consistent with the functional analysis of the controlled transaction and is the least complex party to the controlled transaction, then even if it is a foreign party, the same should be taken as the basis for carrying out comparability analysis with the uncontrolled transaction by taking into account the business environment in the country where the tested party is being benchmarked.

Data for comparison - While determining comparability of transactions, multiple year data can only be included in manner provided in above Rule 10B(4) and, thus, it is not open to assessee to rely upon PY's data as a general rule [Chryscapital Investment Advisors (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417/232 Taxman 20 (Delhi)]. If, from the available data of a comparable company, results for the FY can reasonably be extrapolated, then such a company cannot be excluded from comparable list on ground of having different accounting year [CIT v. Visual Graphics Computing Services India (P.) Ltd. [2020] 120 taxmann.com 123/274 Taxman 481 (Mad.)].

Published data available from stock or commodity exchanges could also form basis of prices in both uncontrolled and controlled transactions [CIT v. Cargill Food India Ltd. [2017] 88 taxmann.com 470 (Delhi)].

Risk adjustment - Risk adjustment could be given only on a company-to-company basis considering the level of risk involved between assessee and the comparable [CIT v. Visual Graphics Computing Services India (P.) Ltd. [2020] 120 taxmann.com 123/274 Taxman 481 (Mad.)].

Loss making (or abnormally high profit making) companies - In Rule 10B(2), the benchmarks for comparison as specified being preceded by the word 'namely' is exhaustive. Therefore, it is not permissible to include new reference point while making comparison. The aforesaid Rule does not require exclusion of a company from comparability analysis only because it had suffered a loss in a particular year. However, it must be clarified that in the facts of a particular case, a loss could be a symptom to enquire/examine whether it is on account of any of the reference point referred to in Rule 10B(2) would get attracted [CIT v. Welspun Zucchi Textiles Ltd. [2017] 77 taxmann.com 137/245 Taxman 132 (Bom.); Joy Alukkas India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 49 taxmann.com 437/[2015] 228 Taxman 35 (Mag.) (Ker.), SLP granted inAsstt. CIT v. Joy Alukkas India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 181 (SC)].

Company incurring persistent losses coupled with declining turnover indicates its abnormal functional circumstances could not be accepted as comparable [Steria India Ltd. v. DCIT [2018] 92 taxmann.com 120/255 Taxman 110 (Delhi)]. However, loss-making companies should not be excluded where there was no dispute as regards functional profile of assessee being similar to said company [PCIT v. Nokia Siemens Network India (P.) Ltd. [2019] 111 taxmann.com 445 (Delhi)].

Merely because an entity makes high or extremely high profits (or losses) does not, ipso facto, lead to its exclusion from the list of comparables for the purposes of determination of ALP. In such circumstances, an enquiry under Rule 10B(3) ought to be carried out to determine as to whether the material differences between the assessee and the said entity can be eliminated. Unless such differences cannot be eliminated, the entity should be included as a comparable [Chryscapital Investment Advisors (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 417/232 Taxman 20 (Del.)]. However, company having abnormally high profit margin (say, 57%) for subject AY as compared to in preceding FY (say, 15%) would not be a normal business condition and, hence, incomparable [PCIT v. Barclays Technology Centre India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 95 taxmann.com 170 (Bom.)].

The assessee had done the Segmental Reporting in accordance with Accounting Standard (AS) 17 issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) and had reflected the same in its annual report. The segmental data given by the assessee with regard to profitability out of rendering of services to related party and unrelated party has been rejected by the TPO on the ground that the assessee had allocated more cost to unrelated party segment. The reporting mandated as per AS-17 issued by ICAI is totally for a different purpose and cannot be used at any stretch of imagination by the TPO to determine the segmental profitability of AE and Non-AE transactions. In fact the segment reporting done in AS-17 issued by ICAI does not bifurcate between AE and Non-AE transactions. It is done in the instant case only based on various business segments of the assessee and whereas the TP assessment is based on margins derived on AE and Non-AE transactions.

It is not in dispute that the assessee had furnished the segmental workings of profitability of transactions with AE and Non-AE duly certified by a chartered accountant. This had been summarily rejected by the TPO on the ground that it is not forming part of audited financial statements of the assessee company. In this regard, the TPO had not understood the fact that the audited financial statements are prepared in the format and as per the requirements of the Companies Act, 1956 and has nothing to do with the requirements of transfer pricing assessments and documentation thereon.

Hence, the action of the TPO in placing reliance on AS-17 Segment Reporting in the instant case for comparison of the margins of AE and Non-AE transactions is not tenable in law and is highly unwarranted. The TPO had considered the PLI by working out the OP/Turnover instead of working out the same on total costs. The assessee had derived PLI of 27.50 per cent margin in respect of transactions rendered to its AEs (for both SD and BPO together) which is above the 20 per cent safe harbour rules specified by the CBDT. Conclusion

3. In the right earnest it would have been proper to remand the case to the AO/TPO to get new set of comparables to arrive at arm's length price. The short point is that before getting on the judgment on suitable comparables it was first necessary to decide the business category to which the assessee and its associated enterprise belonged to and to know this it was necessary to ascertain the relationship between the associated enterprise and the assessee and furthermore, if their business model was such that their activities were dovetailed into each other or were inter-dependent, then the two entities must be taken to have been engaged in one and the same business only. In this case the assessee perhaps succeeded in leading the bench to believe in that the two entities were independent and that the Indian entities' activities were mere support activities, whereas from the reading of the scope of services in the agreement it was apparent that the subsidiary had to work as per instructions of the holding company who acted as an investment advisor and, therefore, in the nature of dependent services. The statement that they were only support services for investment advisory would not make them any less than an investment advisory when these were performed for the holding company as per their instructions. Had the phrase 'as per their instructions' not been there in the agreement it would have made a different situation. In that case their sphere of service might have differed between core service and support service!

Taxman 113 (Delhi), it has been observed that the assertion that comparison can be made by choosing comparable of domestic cases not using any foreign brand is contrary to the provisions and amounts to rewriting of law. The two independent enterprises must be two unrelated parties having no connection. It does not matter whether the comparables are domestic enterprises or not. However, and it is manifest that the comparable should have similar rights, if any, as the tested party in the brand name, trademark, etc.. As a general rule, the tested party is the one to which a TP method can be applied in the most reliable manner and for which the most reliable comparables can be found, i.e., it will most often be one that has the less complex functional analysis. When applying RPM, CPM or TNMM, it is necessary to choose the party to the transaction for which a financial indicator is tested. In Virtusa Consulting Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2021] 124 taxmann.com 309/282 Taxman 95 (Mad.), it has been held that normally, the tested party should be the least complex party to the controlled transaction and there is no bar for selection of tested party either local or foreign party and neither the 1961 Act nor the TP Guidelines provides so and the selection of the tested party is to further the object of the comparability analysis by making it less complex and requiring fewer adjustment. Thus, where the assessee-company was a more complex entity when compared to its foreign AE, said foreign AE could also be selected as a tested party. Also see, PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.).

The tested party normally should be the party in respect of which reliable data for comparison is easily and readily available and fewest adjustments in computations are needed. It may be local or foreign entity, i.e., one party to the transaction. Generally, least of the complex controlled taxpayer should be taken as a tested party. But where comparable or almost comparable, controlled and uncontrolled transactions or entities are available, it may not be right to eliminate them from consideration because they look to be complex. If the taxpayer wishes to take foreign AE as a tested party, then it must ensure that it is such an entity for which the relevant data for comparison is available in public domain or is furnished to the tax administration. The taxpayer is not then entitled to take a stand that such data cannot be called for or insisted upon from the taxpayer—Ranbaxy Laboratories Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2008] 110 ITD 428/167 Taxman 30 (Delhi-Trib).

A functional analysis of the tested party or the independent enterprise, as the case may be, is required to determine whether the transactions are comparable and the adjustments are required to be made to obtain reliable results. The tested party would have to consider other factors, like cost of assets of comparable companies, etc., while applying the return on assets measure. Ordinarily, the tested party has to be the party providing services because it is on the basis of rate of return on sales or cost or operating assets that transactional margin is computed. These parameters are generally available in the case of a party providing services—Aztec Software & Technology Services Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2007] 107 ITD 141/162 Taxman 119/15 SOT 49 (Bang. - Trib.) (SB).

10A.5-2 Number of comparables required - Under the Transfer Pricing Regulations, the number of comparables may be one or more than one; but there is no upper limit prescribed u/s 92C. Therefore, the size of number of comparables has not been prescribed under the provisions of TP Regulations provided under the Income-tax Act. There cannot be a fixed criteria or parameter for number of comparables, which can be universally applied to each and every case for determination of the ALP. It is an accepted rule of sampling that larger size of sample would better and adequate represent the lot or population to which the sample belongs. Therefore, to get an adequate result and better representation, the size of sample must be large enough. The same rule is applicable in the case of number of comparables selected for representing the true and correct ALP in relation to the international transaction. The endeavour should be made to bring more and more comparables so that a proper and realistic price can be determined which represents the price prevailing in the open market. Where the number of comparables available is large, then it is always better to consider as many as possible number of comparables which can give an adequate and proper representation of the price prevailing in open market in the said industry, business, trade etc., to which the comparables and international transactions belong.

Having established that comparable sets can be skewed and that skewness is directly correlated with an increased difference between the mean and median, it is now time to consider the potential impact on transfer pricing adjustments. The challenge is to determine which method (adjusting to mean or median) might produce a more accurate adjustment.

Our final test endeavors to evaluate the two methods of calculating adjustments (i.e., adjusting to the mean or the median) in an objective and empirical manner. We evaluate this by applying each method to a set of "firms" with known deviations from arm's-length transfer pricing. The method whose adjustment comes closest to that known amount should be the better method.

This methodology presupposes that we know the correct adjustment. In this case we do because we can make manual change to these firms' financial data. We start with the financial data of a firm whose financial results are not affected by related party transactions. We then alter their financial statement to insert a change in the financial statement that reflects the impact of a known amount of non-arm's-length pricing. We now have a financial statement of a new test firm whose results are arm's-length in all ways except for the known change that we have introduced. We do this multiple times to create a whole set of test firms.

To insure comparability between our test firms and the set of comparables, we use the firms in the set of comparables to create the test firms. In this case, we use the set of comparable firms already identified by the India Tax Authority for the ITES industry.

Whether these firms are comparable to any given taxpayer is a separate issue and is dependent on the specific facts and circumstances of each case. We do know, however, that these firms have met the Indian tax authority's standard of being comparable to each other. We are operating on the premise that if Firm A is comparable to some unknown tested party and Firm B is comparable to the same unknown tested party, then Firm A and Firm B should be comparable to each other.

Our experiment is to take each firm in the set of comparables and create a test firm. To create the test firm, we, one at a time, lower each firm's revenue by 15 per cent and hold everything else equal. This test firm is now equivalent to a related party operating in India that has provided all of its services to a foreign related party and that has been undercompensated for these services relative to the arm's-length price.
