TRANSACTION

Aggregation allowed - The use of the term 'transaction' with the vowel 'an' instead of the term 'transactions' should not be given undue notability and prominence thereby meaning a single independent transaction and not a group or bundle of transactions. The use of expression 'class of transaction', 'functions performed by the parties' in section 92C(1) illustrates to the contrary, that the word 'transaction' can never include and would exclude bundle or group of connected transactions. Similarly, the meaning of the term 'transaction' in section 92F(v) as well as Rule 10A(d) does not bar or prohibit clubbing of closely connected or intertwined or continuous transactions. Thus, it would be inappropriate to proceed with the arm's length computation methods with a pre-conceived suppositions on singularity as a statutory mandate. Clubbing of closely linked, which would include continuous transactions, may be permissible and not ostracized [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Also see, CIT v. ESPN Software India Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 323/[2018] 252 Taxman 171 (Delhi).

Adjustment on individual transaction basis - Where segmental results are available, adjustment can only be made on the basis of individual transaction and not on aggregation basis [PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.)].

Re-categorisation of transaction - The concept of re-categorisation of transaction is not identical (or similar) to aggregation or segregation of transactions. Re-categorisation of transaction is a different exercise and would result in re-categorisation of the functions and, therefore, accordingly the comparables. A simple example of re-categorisation would be cases of 'thin capitalisation'. Aggregation or segregation of transactions accepts that the transactions per se do not require re-categorisation of transactions. However, in a given case when there is re-categorisation of transaction, as a consequence, segregation or aggregation may be required. However, the two aspects/principles prevail and operate in their own field [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Del.)].

METHODS TO COMPUTE ARM'S LENGTH PRICE (ALP)

Adoption of different method by authorities - ALP is to be computed in accordance with the provisions of s. 92C(1) by adopting one of laid down methods at the discretion of competent authority; and mere fact that assessee has chosen one of said methods does not take away discretion of competent authority to select any other method which may be considered to be more appropriate for purpose of determining true income [Coca Cola India Inc. v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 177 Taxman 103 (P&H)].

Use of more than one method - If it is established that the sale of various goods and/or the provision of services formed one composite indivisible transaction, then more than one method of TP shall not be used for computing ALP [Knorr-Bremse India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 63 taxmann.com 186/[2016] 236 Taxman 318 (P&H)].

If the assessee had applied more than one of the permissible methods for determining ALP, then qua each of such transactions, the TPO is required to give reasons as to why one of such methods is being preferred over the others by a reasoned order [Honda Motorcycle & Scooters India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2016] 76 taxmann.com 75 (P&H)].

Comparable uncontrolled price method (CUPM) - CUP method followed by a logistic service provider was appropriate particularly when price determination for all business associates, whether associated enterprises or independent enterprises, was on same terms and as per same business model and profit sharing ratio of transaction between assessee and AEs was not different from that with a third party, viz., 50:50 in this field of business activity [PCIT v. Toll Global Forwarding India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 66 taxmann.com 53/237 Taxman 326 (Delhi)].

AO was not justified in rejecting CUP method adopted by the assessee on the ground that the price charged or paid was on the basis of a broker quote and it did not reflect in the price of the actual transaction [CIT v. Cargill Food India Ltd. [2017] 88 taxmann.com 470 (Delhi)].

This method is unlikely to be reliable if each party to a transaction makes unique and valuable contributions. There are cases where a party to a transaction makes contributions that are not unique (say, use of non-unique intangibles such as non-unique business processes or non-unique market knowledge). In such cases, it may be possible to meet the comparability requirements to apply a traditional transaction method or TNMM because the comparables would also be expected to use a comparable mix of non-unique contributions. However, the lack of unique and valuable contributions involved in a particular transaction does not automatically imply that this method is the most appropriate method (MAM).

Since an appropriate level of segmentation of taxpayer's financial data is needed when determining or testing the net profit it earns from a controlled transaction, therefore, it would be unjustified to apply TNMM on a company-wide basis if the company engages in a variety of different controlled transactions that cannot be appropriately compared on an aggregate basis with those of an independent enterprise.

CIT [2016] 71 taxmann.com 290/242 Taxman 260 (Delhi), it has been observed that Rule 10B(1)(e) does not permit use of Berry ratio is unsustainable since it has been clear from the plain language that the net profit margin could be computed having regard to "any other relevant base". Berry ratio is a ratio of operating profits to operating expenses. In cases where operating expenses is considered as a relevant base, there would be no difficulty in using Berry ratio as the PLI. This Berry ratio was used by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in the USA in the case of E. I. Du Pont DE Nemouts & Co. v. United, (1979) States 608 F. 2d 445 to sustain their stand that substantial part of the profits of a subsidiary in Switzerland were rightly allocated to Du Pont. Charles H. Berry, an economist (since deceased) provided necessary evidence in support of IRS's stand by using the ratio of operating profits to selling, general and administration expenses to show that more than fair share of profits had been transferred to Du Pont's Swiss subsidiary. This ratio came to be known by the name of the economist who had used it in the aforementioned case. The aforesaid case concerned the allocation of profits between Du Pont De Nemours, an American company engaged in manufacture of chemicals, and its wholly owned subsidiary established in Switzerland (Du Pont International SA, referred to as 'DISA'). Berry ratio was used in the above context to show that the average ratio in the case of 21 distributors was 129.3% and in the case of DISA, it was 281.5% for the year 1959 and 397.1% in the year 1960. It is relevant to note that in that case also the Commissioner of Revenue did not reallocate the profits between DISA and Du Pont on the basis of Berry ratio but on the basis of applying the resale price method. Berry ratio was only introduced as an expert evidence by IRS to defend the challenge to such reallocation. In other words, the said ratio was only used to show that DISA had made extraordinarily high profits and IRS had rightly exercised its jurisdiction to reallocate such profits of DISA to Du Pont. The Du Pont's challenge to the said ratio as being inappropriate measure was rejected by the Court in the following words:—Whatever the general limits of any particular gauge of industry profitability, plaintiff cannot escape the basic thrust of defendant's proof. Defendant has shown that DISA made extraordinarily high profits which the Commissioner reallocated to an economically reasonable level.

3. Acceptance/rejection of comparables earning abnormally high margins

As per Para 1.47 of the OECD Guidelines, where the application of one or more methods produces a range of figures, a substantial deviation among points in that range may indicate that the data used in establishing some of the points may not be as reliable as the data used to establish the other points in the range or that the deviation may result from features of the comparable data that require adjustments. In such cases, further analysis of those points may be necessary to evaluate their suitability for inclusion in any arm's length range.

Further, Para 3.63 of the OECD Guidelines lay down that, extreme results might consist of losses or unusually high profits. Extreme results can affect the financial indicators that are looked at in the chosen method (e.g. the gross margin when applying a resale price, or a net profit indicator when applying a transactional net margin method). When one or more of the potential comparables have extreme results, further examination would be needed to understand the reasons for such extreme results.

Thus, the OECD Guidelines lay down that in a comparability analysis which throws up more than one comparable, the extreme results or 'outliers' need to be examined in greater detail to understand if there are any abnormal reasons for such extreme results and in such a case they need to excluded. In many foreign jurisdictions where the concept of inter-quartile range is followed, the outliers are automatically rejected. The concept of inter-quartile range also finds support in the UN Practice Manual.

However, under the Indian Income Tax law, the proviso to section 92C(2) provides that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the arithmetic mean of such prices.

Under the head 'Managements Discussion and Analysis' of this company, it has been stated that this company provides services to both horizontal and vertical focus areas. The Horizontal focus areas are Sourcing and Procurement (S & P), Customer Services (CS), Finance and Accounting (F & A), Legal Process Outsourcing (LPO), Sales and Fulfilment (S & F), Analytics (AT), Business Platform (BP), Business Transformation Services (BTS), Human Resources Outsourcing (HRO) and Technology Solution Optimization (TSO). The Vertical focus areas of services are Financial Services & Insurance (FSI) Manufacturing (MFG), Energy, Utilities Communication & Services (ECS) and Retail, Consumer Packaged Foods, Logistics & Life Services (RCL). From the above, it is clear that 'Infosys' offers a gamut of different and diversified services which cannot be compared with routine back office services provided by the assessee. In fact, it is mentioned in the annual report that the company 'Infosys' provides business process management services which are different from routine back office services. It is also to be seen that this company enjoys significant brand value and owns intangible assets which clearly establish that Infosys is different from the assessee in the case on hand. [Para 7.4.1]

This company has consistently been rejected as a comparable to companies rendering routine back office services in various judicial pronouncements of the Tribunal; including the two decisions cited by the assessee. In the case of CGI Informaiton Systems & Management Consultants (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2018] 94 taxmann.com 97 (Bangalore - Trib) for the Assessment Year 2012-13, cited by the assessee, this company 'Infosys' has been excluded from the list of comparables for the reason that it has brand value which had an impact on its pricing and margins. As the facts of the year under consideration are similar, the decision rendered in the earlier year would apply to the year under consideration as well. In this factual view of the matter, it is to be held that Infosys BPO, stands on a totally different footing from a company engaged in rendering routine back office ITES; being both functionally different and having brand value and, therefore, is to be excluded from the final set of comparables. [Para 7.4.2]

Comparable Company Microland:

It is to be seen that the services rendered by company 'Microland' under Infrastructure Management services are Server Management, Database Management, storage management, Archival Management, Network Management, etc., which has been classified as different from the back office processing services rendered by companies like the assessee in the case on hand. In view of this, there is no basis for the TPO to contend that the aforesaid services rendered by 'Microland' are ITES, when the company itself has classified these services as different from ITES and characterized the same as a different business segment. In these factual circumstances, contention of the assessee that the Infrastructure Management services segment of 'Microland' is different and distinct with ITES as has been classified by the company in its annual report for the year under consideration is to be accepted. It is also to be observed that the TPO himself has reached the same conclusion in the subsequent assessment year 2015-16; that the Infrastructure segment services segment is not comparable to ITES. [Para 8.4.3]

The annual report of 'Microland' for the year under consideration, the segmental details of the two business segments are provided from which it is seen that out of the total revenue of Rs. 34.471 lakhs, the revenue from ITES segment is Rs. 1959 lakhs; which is 5.68 per cent of the total revenue. As, it is already been concluded that the infrastructure services segment is a different business segment not comparable to ITES rendered; this company, 'Microland' fails the filter adopted by the TPO that companies whose service income is less than 75 per cent of total operating revenue are to be excluded. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, as discussed above, and in view of the above factual findings, company Microland is to be excluded from the final set of comparables in the case on hand. [Para 8.4.4]

In GE India Technology Centre (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. DIT3 the Bangalore Bench of Tribunal examined issue of selection of comparables in conducting transfer pricing study. The assessee company was carrying on the business of software development and in TP study it adopted comparables which were in the field of development and export of computer software. The assessee contended that even if the assessee is considered as a research and development company, then comparables have to be of the same industry in which the assessee is doing research and development. Since international transactions related to export of customized electronic data, computer software, and any other tangible articles or things as a result of research activity the comparables selected were appropriate in the circumstances of the case. According to the services agreement dated 1-12-2003 the company was to provide research services to the party making such request in different areas of engineering. The TPO observed that the taxpayer was doing the research and development activities and end result is submitted through internet/networking which is reported by the assessee as export of customized electronic data. TPO rejected these comparables on the ground that the company as per its own admission was involved in research and development activity and not in export of computer software. TPO therefore, rejected the assessee's TP study adopting the comparables in the field of computer software holding that they are functionally different. A fresh TP study was made by TPO and three companies were selected out of eight companies engaged in technical consultancy and research and development. The Tribunal held that as far technology related services are concerned TNMM was most appropriate method for computing the arm's length price. However, for purpose of determining arm's length price under TNMM, the FAR analysis as provided in Rule 10B is very essential. So it is essential to consider the correct nature of functions of the assessee to search for the comparables which are engaged in similar functions. It is also essential to take a note of the dissimilarities in the functions of the companies considered for comparison and make suitable adjustments for the same. It further held that TPO had rightly rejected the assessee's TP study as the company was conducting R & D through its multi-disciplinary R&D centre and its activities are for several streams including information technology. On the issue of selection of comparables the Tribunal remanded back the case to Assessing Officer as TPO had not carried out FAR analysis.

Identification of Risk

The CBDT Circular No. 03/2013 also lays emphasis on the identification of risks undertaken by the development centres engaged in contract R& D services. At times taxpayers insist that they are contract R& D service providers with insignificant risks; whereas TPOs treat them full or significant risk bearing entities and therefore, make transfer pricing adjustments. The circular provides various circumstances and conditions on satisfaction of which the development centre in India can be treated as a contract service provider with insignificant risk. It may be worthwhile to mention that there is marked difference between a risk agent and low or insignificant service provider. The nature of risk assumed by the development centre in India would depend upon the role and responsibilities undertaken by the service provider and outcome of the FAR analysis. As held in case of Gap International Sourcing (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4, the FAR analysis provides the broad characterisations of the functions of manufacturer, service provider, and distributor with a further sub-division of low risk service provider, high risk service provider, full-fledged manufacturer, contract manufacturer etc. These characterisations are important to determine the arm's length price of a transaction. But whether the assessee is a risk bearing agent or not is to be considered on the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case. The conditions prescribed in the Board Circular can be a guiding factor but cannot be sufficient to decide the issue.

Location Savings

Location savings is another factor that is considered by transfer pricing authorities during audit. It is considered important when TPO considers TNMM or CUP method as appropriate method by selecting comparable companies engaged in development of intangibles. As per the CBDT Circular No. 02/2013, upward adjustments are required where additional remuneration is not charged for transfer of intangibles due to location savings and location specific advantages of development centres. The Indian approach to adjustments for location savings is also discussed in Chapter 10 of the 'UN Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries5' approved by UN Committee in October 2012. According to Indian tax authorities the expression 'location savings' has wider meaning; it goes beyond the issue of relocating a business from high cost location to a low cost location and relates to any cost advantage. In the Chapter on Indian regulations it is stated that since India provides several location specific advantages to MNE in addition to location savings, the incremental profit from location related advantage can be considered as "location rents".

4. Intra-group Services

i.

Categorization into Software/BPO/KPO/Contract R&D for Software

Internationally, one of the biggest challenges with adoption of Safe Harbours has been over the interpretation of core and non-core services by taxpayers, leading to several controversies between the taxpayers and the Revenue officials. This may be perceived as a forewarning in the Indian context as the suggested industry sub-classification in the draft rules may be subject to varying interpretation by taxpayers.

For instance, it may be difficult to clearly assign some companies into BPO or KPO as several of the activities defined under these buckets are closely related and often overlapping. Moreover, many companies may offer all or some of these services to their customers, which may make segregation of operating revenue and operating costs for individual service lines a challenge.

Again, some of the services classified under KPO may not necessitate advanced analytical and technical skills, for instance in some cases, Human Resource services may comprise just employee database management; Engineering and design services may include low-end conversion of drawings from 2D to 3D, and Market research services may include only business support and collation of available information from public domain. In this context, the functional, asset and risk profile of such companies would be closer to that of a BPO than a KPO.

A similar dilemma over interpretation of the nature of services is expected to arise between Software and Contract R&D for Software as there is substantial overlap in the activities defined under both the heads. According a separate classification to Contract R&D for Software, distinct from Software Development services is bound to lead to complexities and potential litigation.

The above assumes particular importance in light of the fact that the Safe Harbour proposed for BPO/Software Development is OP/OE equal to or greater than 20% while that for KPO/Contract R&D for Software Development is OP/OE equal to or greater than 30%. The significant variation makes it imperative that the dividing line between the various activities be extremely well defined. On the other hand, it may also be worthwhile to consider whether, given the substantial overlap between the various activities, the line of divide can be completely removed and a uniform profit margin can be prescribed across the board for all underlying service categories.

ii.

High Margins

The most noticeable aspect about the draft Safe Harbours is the high margins notified for the various types of services, particularly for KPO and Contract R&D services of 29-30%. While a certain premium above the arm's length margins was expected by taxpayers in order to factor in the benefits of certainty and compliance relief, the presently notified margins are being perceived to be well beyond any such acceptable premiums.

As per the Rangachary Committee report, these Safe Harbour margins have been determined on the basis of the arm's length margins arrived at by Revenue Officials during the course of Transfer Pricing audits. This may not be a reasonable proposition as a large number of the Transfer Pricing adjustments made by Revenue officials on the basis of such arm's length margins have been overturned by Tax Tribunals/High Court in India on subsequent appeals by the taxpayers. Profit margins are perceived by taxpayers as a decisive factor in opting for the Safe Harbour route. In order for Safe Harbours to evoke the necessary interest from taxpayers and be widely utilized as a dispute avoidance mechanism, it is therefore critical that such high profit margins are re-evaluated and revised appropriately in the final rules.

iii.

Insignificant risk criteria

An important aspect that warrants detailed consideration is the condition of 'insignificant risk' that has been closely integrated with the Safe Harbour for captive service providers. The condition stipulates that the foreign principal should perform economically significant functions, provide necessary capital and funds and own the economically significant assets including intangibles. Further the monitoring and supervision of the taxpayer's activities should vest with the foreign principal. Most importantly, the conduct rather than the contractual terms between the taxpayer and the foreign principal should demonstrate that key business risks are borne by the foreign principal while the Indian captive is insulated from them.

COST PLUS METHOD - SOME FOREIGN PRECEDENTS

7. CPM, one should imagine, should be easier to apply, but it does not appear to be so, as is evident from some precedents from abroad.

It was pointed out in Seagate Technology Inc. & Consolidated Subsidiaries v. Commissioner [1994] 102 TC No. 9, that in adoption of cost plus method, the determination of cost could present problems. The issue in this case related to the difference in understanding, whether the manufacture of hard disk drives for personal computers was undertaken on a consignment basis or otherwise or whether material cost was to be included as cost in the facts of the case. The Court agreed with the administration on the point that the assessee could not prove that the mark-up was appropriate. But at the same time, revenue also did not apply the cost plus method in the proper manner. It found that cost of raw material should have been included and adequate weight should have been given for risk element. It had made its own decision to accept the cost of subsidiary relating to materials, labour and overheads with a mark of 20 per cent over such cost.

The adequacy of mark-up, where cost plus method was adopted became a matter of controversy in Altama Delta Corp. v. Commissioner [1995] 104 TC No. 22. The Court held that neither resale price method nor CUP method was suitable in respect of a company manufacturing combat boots with shoe uppers purchased from a subsidiary in Puerto Rico at a price agreed on cost sharing method, a method accepted under U.S. law, which was understood by the Tax Court as adoption of cost plus method utilising gross profit margin, which was preferable to operating profits. But then, the comparative case chosen was not of a manufacturer of a component of combat boot, but another fashion footwear industry. The Court finally decided a mark-up of gross profit at the average of two past years, in view of the fact that the assessee was working under a Government contract and the manufacturer of uppers was taking no risk.

In National Semiconductor Corp. & Consolidated Subsidiaries TC Memo 1994-195 (1994), the assessee was a supplier of requirements for semi-conductor industries involving electronic products, with most of its sales to unrelated parties. But manufacture was done by its Asean subsidiaries located in different countries, while the U.S. holding company was making loss. Even so, the price charged by subsidiaries was sought to be proved as correct with reference to the arm’s length price on cost plus method. The necessary cost data and support for the profit adopted as arm’s length profit were lacking, and, thus, cost plus method was found unacceptable. None of the other methods prescribed in the transfer pricing regulations was capable of being adopted in the facts of assessee’s case. At the same time, it was felt that the assessee could not have incurred losses, if the price had been at arm’s length, therefore, the Tax Court employed modifications to the methodology proposed by either parties and their experts, so as to correct their errors.

Transactional net margin method (TNMM) - In case the tested party is engaged in single line of business, there is no bar or prohibition from applying the TNMM on entity-level basis. The focus of this method is on net profit amount in proportion to the appropriate base or the PLI. In fact, when transactions are inter-connected, combined consideration may be the most reliable means of determining the arm's length price. There are often situations where closely linked and connected transactions cannot be evaluated adequately on separate basis. Segmentation may be mandated when controlled bundled transactions cannot be adequately compared on an aggregate basis. Thus, the taxpayer can aggregate the controlled transactions if the transactions meet the specified common portfolio or package parameters. For complex entities or where one of the entities is not plain vanilla distributor, it should be applied when necessary and applicable comparables on functional analysis, with or without adjustments are available. Otherwise, the TNMM should not be adopted or applied on account of being an inappropriate method. TNMM would not be the most appropriate method when there are considerable value additions by the subsidiary AEs. It would also not be appropriate and proper to apply the TNMM in case the Indian assessed is engaged in manufacturing activities and distribution and marketing of imported and manufactured products, as interconnected transactions [Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi)].

TNMM is appropriate method for determining ALP in case of Service PE as TNMM apportions total operating profits arising from transaction on basis of sales, cost of assets, etc. [DIT v. Morgan Stanley & Co. [2007] 162 Taxman 165 (SC)].

Where a company's financial results indicated widely fluctuating and erratic results, it would be unsafe to assess arm's length price based on TNMM taking into account results of said company [PCIT v. Allscripts (India) (P.) Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 305/241 Taxman 545 (Guj.)].

Where assessee had undertaken international transactions of import and export of raw materials and components and import of semi-finished goods, finished goods and advertising material, said transaction should be benchmarked by applying TNMM instead of CUPM or RPM [Rayban Sun Optics India Ltd. v. However, the silver lining on the cloud is that after 14 years since inception of transfer pricing legislation, the Hon'ble Finance Minister in his Budget Speech while presenting the Finance (No.2) Act, 2014 in the Lok Sabha announced the introduction of range concept and multiple year data in comparability analysis. The Hon'ble Finance Minister announced:

The introduction of range concept for determination of arm's length price; and

Use of multiple year data replacing the existing practice of using single year data for comparability analysis.

The Finance (No.2) Act, 2014 inserted a third proviso to section 92C(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, with effect from 1 April 2014, providing that where more than one price is determined by the most appropriate method, the arm's length price in relation to an international transaction or specified domestic transaction shall be computed in such manner as may be prescribed and accordingly the first and the second proviso shall not apply. It is significant to note that the first and second provisos to the section 92C(2) have effectively been deleted with effect from 1 April 2014. It was the first proviso to section 92C(2) that provided for arithmetic mean to be taken as the arm's length price where more than one price is determined as the arm's length price. Hence even though the rules in relation to the third proviso to section 92C(2) are yet to be notified, the deletion of the first and second proviso makes it imperative that sooner rather than later these rules will be introduced and objectively applied by the revenue.

It will be pertinent to read the fine print once the rules are notified, to understand the implementation of these concepts. Both these concepts, if implemented in letter and spirit, will go a long way in aligning India's transfer pricing laws with accepted international practices.

4. Other issues involved in transfer pricing litigation

a.

Export Earnings filter – While carrying out benchmarking of captive service providers (both IT & ITeS), one of the arguments has been that since the captive entities are exporting 100% of their services, similar comparables should be adopted which are substantially engaged in export of services. The argument of the revenue has been that earnings in foreign exchange cannot be compared to earnings in local currency and hence companies engaged in providing services domestically cannot be adopted as comparables. This view has consistently been upheld by the Tribunals and companies failing the export earnings filter have been rejected.

b.

Onsite revenue filter – There is generally a difference in the business models of companies engaged in providing services remotely at onsite locations and the offshore service providers like captive IT/ITeS entities. The markets and other economic conditions are different in onsite operations when compared to offshore operations. Accordingly margins earned by companies predominantly engaged in providing onsite services are not comparable to companies engaged in providing services offshore. The argument has been upheld by the Tribunals time and again and predominant onsite service providing companies have been excluded as comparables.

10A.9-3 Applications/Usage of CPM - This method is probably most useful where semi-finished goods are sold between associated parties, where associated parties have concluded joint facility agreements or long-term buy and supply arrangements, or where the controlled transaction is the provision of services. The ITAT relied upon the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines, the UN Manual on Transfer Pricing and US TP Regulations to hold that the Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not reject the concept of foreign comparables, if the Tested Party is Foreign AE.

Coming to the specific concerns raised by the TPO the ITAT held as under:

There could be no dispute in this case that the Tested Party was Tata Motor European Technical Centre PLC (TMETC), the assessee (a UK Company), whose operating profit was to be benchmarked. For such benchmarking the reliable data of comparables was available in the country (UK) where the assessee was located. So, the data of those UK comparables had to be taken into account for carrying out the comparability analysis to benchmark the Arm's Length Price.

The assessee (TMETC), for rendering services in India, was incurring all its costs like direct costs, employee costs, legal and professional fees, rent and other operating expenses in the UK. Those costs had to be taken into consideration for determining the profit margin.

Because all the main costs attributable to the PE were based on cost incurred in the UK, it could be very well said that PE was influenced by the economic and financial conditions of the UK, as against the Indian economic factors. The Indian economic factors were not at all influencing the cost or margin of the assessee.

The PE in India was a service PE, having no establishment in India, incurring no costs in India, and deploying no fixed assets in India. Therefore, it could not be held that the Service PE was an independent Indian enterprise. Nothing had been brought on record that assessee's Profit Margin was influenced by the economic factors in India.

Hence, it could not be held that Indian comparables could be used to benchmark the service transaction between TMETC and Tata Motors Ltd.

For this reason, the finding of the TPO as well as DRP that PE was an Indian enterprise, working in India, and that its margin was to be benchmarked with Indian comparables, was not accepted.

How to benchmark the arm's length price when part of the profits derived by Foreign PE is to be attributed to the Indian PE of the Foreign AE?

7. When a Foreign AE (of an Indian Taxpayer) has a PE in India some challenging issues emerge as is clear from the following:

The PE needs to be treated as a separate hypothetical entity, distinct from its Head Office/Foreign AE (Article 7 of Tax Treaties)

Profits need to be attributed to the PE by assuming that the PE has transacted with its Foreign Head Office at arm's length (Article 7 of the DTAAs)

Profits to PE should be attributed based on arm's length benchmarking under the Transfer Pricing Regulations

Therefore, two separate and distinct bench markings are required: (1) benchmarking to determine the Arm's Length Price (ALP) of transactions between the Indian Taxpayer and its Foreign AE; and (2) benchmarking to determine the profits attributable to the PE, out of total profit derived by the Foreign AE from transactions with the Indian Taxpayer.

In case of Tata Motors European Technical Centre Plc. (supra) the first benchmarking was at issue. The second benchmarking was not in picture because the entire profit from services rendered to Indian AE(TML) was offered to tax in India, apparently by attributing entire profits to the Indian PE. So, there was no question of undertaking any attribution (of profits to PE) exercise.

7.1 What if both the benchmarkings are involved? How to do the benchmarking then?

In such a situation, to attribute arm's length profits to the PE, we will have to carry out two benchmarkings, viz., benchmarking in two stages -

(1)

benchmarking of transaction undertaken by the Indian Taxpayer with its Foreign AE, and

(2)

the benchmarking for attribution of profits from Foreign AE to its Indian PE.

For both stages of benchmarking the mechanism of comparability analysis will be similar – as is laid down in Indian TP Regulations, i.e., selection of Tested Party, selection of Most Appropriate Method, selection of comparables based on Tested Party, Comparability Factors and Reliable Data19.

The Information Technology ("IT")/ Business Process Outsourcing ("BPO") sector in India has experienced spectacular growth over the past decade and half. The Indian success story in the global outsourcing industry has become a leading example for other developing economies. While this growth model has been discussed from a macro level widely, it is important to study the same from a micro level to understand and evaluate the challenges and advantages faced by the various players who have been a catalyst to this chronicle. This article aims to appraise the Indian IT sector from a transfer pricing perspective.

The Indian IT industry has several players, each of whom faces unique transfer pricing challenges. This article provides an overview of the Indian IT/BPO outsourcing industry, the players and the transfer pricing framework that they operate in.

The Indian IT landscape can be broadly classified based on the nature of players operating in the industry. On one end of the spectrum, there are Indian IT giants like Wipro, Infosys, HCL etc. who represent Indian IT outbound investment in the global IT industry. These are predominantly Indian multinationals that have subsidiaries and branch offices across the globe. On the other end of the spectrum there are Global In-House centers (GIC) or 'captive services providers' who operate as delivery centers for foreign IT Multinationals Corporation ("MNCs") and represent the inbound investment in the Indian IT sector.

The GIC1 segment which till 2003, constituted a very small part of the IT/BPO industry has witnessed spectacular growth over the past few years. Currently the segment contributes to 22% of India's IT-BPO revenue and accounts for almost 21% of the industry's employment. Based on the latest available data, this segment has grown at a CAGR of 22% between 2003 -2010. In the fiscal year 2009-10, the Indian GICs contributed to almost 1% of the national GDP†. Spanning across all the major cities of India the segment provides direct and indirect employment to about 1.8 million people2.

The GIC model has played an important role in the IT/BPO outsourcing industry globally. This model originated in the 80s and 90s, when several big MNCs realized they could substantially lower their operating cost by opening delivery centers in low cost locations like India. The GIC model has been a global success for the IT Industry. Not only has it helped parent MNCs to lower their operational cost, it has boosted the economies of the offshoring locations as well. As per a Nasscom –Everest Report, presently there are about 3000 GICs operating around the globe in various countries.

The Indian IT Industry watch-dog, Nasscom reports that there are presently about 750 IT/BPO MNCs in India and they operate across almost all the verticals like Aerospace & Defence, Automotive, BFSI, Bio-Technology, Chemicals, Computer Hardware, Education, Electronic/Electrical Equipment, Energy, Healthcare, Industrial, Semiconductors, Software/Internet, and Telecommunications, etc. Engineering, Research and Development (ER&D) and Software Product Development companies form the largest segment within the Indian captive industry. This particular segment has especially witnessed a tremendous growth in MNCs opening their ER&D delivery centers in India over the past couple of years. Geography-wise, North America and Europe comprise 90 per cent of this segment in India.

Although India still remains one of the preferred GIC locations in the world, MNCs are increasingly looking towards other low cost destinations like the Philippines, East Asia, Eastern Europe Latin America and even Africa for opening new delivery centers to further their cost arbitrage benefit. Thus, while it is easy to bask in the glory of the success story that India has paved in the realm of the IT Industry, it is crucial to watch out for competition in other emerging IT capabilities in Asia, South America and other parts of the globe. Countries like Philippines, Cost Rica, Russian Federation, Ukraine, Argentina, Sri Lanka etc. have witnessed remarkable growth in IT exports in their economy in the recent past. Being at the nascent stage of the IT Industry, the volume of exports by these economies has been low. But the growth rates experienced by them have been well above the average growth rates of large exporters like the European Union, India and the United States. Between 2005 to 20113 the Philippines IT exports has grown at 69%, Ukraine witnessed a growth of 59% in IT service exports, followed by Argentina and Costa Rica at 37% and 35% respectively.

The net profit indicator of the taxpayer from the controlled transaction may be established in any of the following manner:—

(a)

Internal comparable - By referring to the net profit indicator that the same taxpayer earns in comparable uncontrolled transactions; or

(b)

External comparable - By referring to the net profit indicator earned by an independent enterprise in comparable uncontrolled transactions.

Where assessee had undertaken transactions with both AEs and non-AEs, and it had not only maintained segmental details of such transactions, but had also undertaken comparative analysis in its TP study, internal TNMM had to be adopted as most appropriate method for determining ALP—NTT Data Global Delivery Services Ltd. v. 10A.11-2 Considerations in determining net profit indicator - As a matter of principle, only those items that directly or indirectly relate to the controlled transaction at hand and are of an operating nature should be taken into account in determining the net profit indicator. Similarly, when analysing the transactions between the independent enterprises to the extent they are needed, profits attributable to transactions that are not similar to the controlled transactions under examination should be excluded from the comparison. Finally, when the net profit indicators of an independent enterprise are used, the profits attributable to the transactions of the independent enterprise must not be distorted by controlled transactions of that enterprise.

Summarised process when comparability analysis is performed

10A.16 Below is a description of a typical process that can be followed when performing a comparability analysis. This process is considered an accepted good practice but it is not a compulsory one, and any other search process leading to the identification of reliable comparables may be acceptable as reliability of the outcome is more important than process:—

Step 1 - Determination of years to be covered:—In practice, examining multiple year data is often useful in a comparability analysis but it is not a systematic requirement. It should be used where they add value to the TP analysis. Multiple year data can improve the understanding of long-term arrangements and also be useful in providing information about the relevant business and product life cycles of the comparables. Hence, it would not be appropriate to set prescriptive guideline as to the number of years to be covered by multiple year analysis. Nevertheless, the use of multiple year data does not necessarily imply the use of multiple year averages.

However, it is generally useful to examine data from both the year under consideration and prior years since the use of past year's data will show whether a taxpayer's reported loss on a transaction is part of a history of losses on similar transactions, the result of particular economic conditions in a prior year that increased costs in the subsequent year, or a reflection of the fact that a product is at the end of its life cycle. This analysis is generally useful when transactional profit methods are used.

In such a case, an attempt should be made to reach a conclusion consistent with the arm's length principle that is satisfactory from a practical viewpoint to all the parties involved taking into account the facts and circumstances, the mix of evidence available and the relative reliability of the various methods under consideration.

What is meant by 'most appropriate method'? [Rule 10C(1)]

10A.3 ALP shall be determined by any of the 6 methods specified above but such method shall be the most appropriate method (MAM) having regard to the nature of transaction, or class of transaction, or class of associated persons or functions performed by such persons, etc. A comparability analysis must be performed in all cases in order to select and apply the most appropriate TP method.

For the purposes of section 92C(1), the most appropriate method (MAM) shall be the method which is best suited to the facts and circumstances of each particular international transaction or specified domestic transaction, and which provides the most reliable measure of an ALP in relation to the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction, as the case may be. However, it does not mean that all the TP methods should be analysed in-depth or tested in each case in arriving at the selection of MAM.

In this regard, it is pertinent to note that no one method is suitable in every possible situation, nor is it necessary to prove that a particular method is not suitable under the circumstances. It is also important to note that there is no prescriptive rule for establishing whether a particular method is the MAM or not.

According to ICAI's Guidance Note on Transfer Pricing, although it is difficult to prescribe general principles for choice of most appropriate method, the following broad categorisation may be considered as already indicated under each of the respective methods:—

(1)

CUP method may be used in case of loans, service fee, transfer of tangibles, sale and purchase of goods/ commodities, etc;

(2)

RPM is most useful in case of marketing operations of finished products, especially in case of distributors not performing significant value addition to the product;

(3)

CPM is normally used where raw materials or semi-finished goods are sold; where joint facility agreements or long-term buy-and-supply arrangements, or the provision of services are involved;

(4)

PSM is normally used in cases where the transactions involve provision of integrated services by more than one enterprise, e.g., one enterprise holds technology and the other enterprise holds the distribution network and both are the key intangibles for the overall success of the group; freight forwarders and supply chain specialists.

Outcome from ITAT

Despite the various measures adopted by the Indian Government, to provide for alternative dispute resolution mechanisms to the taxpayers, an overwhelming number of cases are still landing up before the ITAT. The ITAT too has recognized the requirement of specialized approach to resolve disputes pertaining to transfer pricing and have constituted special benches to address the same across several jurisdictions.

The ITAT has over the past couple of years passed several landmark judgments which has been valuable in respect of providing guidance to taxpayers on how to deal with their transfer pricing issues. The key take aways from these judgments, that are applicable to an IT/BPO company has been with regards to the application of turnover filter, treatment of comparables owning intangibles & brand, threshold limit for related party transactions, functional comparability, market risk etc. However in some cases, like the issue of adjustment for market risk for GICs, the ITAT has principally agreed to the issue and need for risk adjustment, but has not provided any clear direction in respect of the method to be followed.

The ITAT orders have proven to be an invaluable guidance for taxpayers. Although there are several judicial precedents set by the ITAT with respect to the benchmarking/comparability analysis, the Transfer Pricing Officers ("TPO") have not been forthcoming to implement the same in their orders on the reasoning that they have challenged the same before the higher appellate authorities. Hence, even if the taxpayer receives a favourable order from the ITAT for one year, the litigation continues for the subsequent years.

Key Issues/Challenges in the Indian Transfer Pricing Audit process:

Challenges Faced by the Captives/GICs

The Indian IT sector has completed seven rounds of transfer pricing audits and is on the verge of completing the eighth round. Although the TPOs have become more aggressive over the period and are identifying newer transfer pricing issues, the basic issues have remained the same over the years. The Indian Transfer pricing framework principally emphasizes on the 'comparability' analysis for determining the appropriate arm's length price. However, when compared with the international best transfer pricing practices, the Indian framework suffers from certain challenges.

The Indian Rules only allow the use of single year data for the determining the arm's length price of the comparables. Multiple year data, pertaining to not more than two years, can be used only if the taxpayer can prove that the multiple year data has had an impact on the margin earned by it.

Further the Indian regulation provide for the use of 'Arithmetic Mean' instead of the interquartile range to derive the arm's length margin. The arithmetic mean is affected by extreme values or outliers and thus fails as a measure of central tendency. When we adopt arithmetic mean to arrive at the arm's length margin, the presence of even one high margin/loss making comparable can result in a very high/low ALP, thereby distorting the analysis. On the other hand, the interquartile range is a more sophisticated descriptive statistic which eliminates the data points in the bottom and top quarter and is not affected by outliers. This increases the reliability and the robustness of the ALP.

Most GICs are captive delivery centers which receive a steady flow of work from their AEs and hence are shielded from the impacts of business cycle. In return they would typically earn a fixed mark-up every year. In contrast, an independent software developer would experience periodic boom and dip in their business, reflected in the variation in their margin/profitability. Thus to look at the margin of an independent comparable for a single year would not be a true reflection of its general profitability/performance. Use of multiple year data to determine the performance of third party comparables can help in accounting for the impacts of the vagaries of the business cycle and other market and economic factors. However, the same is not allowed as per the Indian Regulations.

The last seven4 years of Transfer Pricing audit experience shows that the TPO has consistently proposed an arm's length price in the range of 20% to 27% for the IT segment. A multiple year margin analysis (from 2001-02 to 2010-11) for all the comparables proposed by the TPO for the past seven years was undertaken. The results showed that the average ALP for the ten year period is similar to the average mark-up enjoyed by most GICs in the IT industry.

Further, the ALP for the ten year period was computed using arithmetic mean and inter-quartile range and the two results were compared. Whereas the ALP computed from arithmetic mean was 15.31%, the interquartile range gave an ALP of 13.97.

It is a subsidiary of X Ltd., a foreign company. XYZ Ltd. sold its registered patents to X Ltd., for Rs. 100 crores. The consideration for sale of patents has been determined based on a valuation report obtained from an independent valuer. The sale of patents is a unique transaction and XYZ or X Ltd. has not entered into similar transactions with third parties. Hence, no internal or external CUP is available. In such a case, XYZ Ltd. may select the Other Method as the most appropriate method and use the independent valuation report for comparability purposes.

Illustration 2 - An Indian company buys back its equity shares issued to its foreign AE. Indian company obtains a valuation report from an external firm identifying the fair market value of these shares. Indian company purchases the shares at the value determined in the valuation report. This value denotes a price that would have been charged if a third party would have bought the same shares. Hence, Indian company could use Rule 10AB and rely upon the valuation report to demonstrate this transaction to be arm's length.

Illustration 3 - An Indian company incurs hotel and travel expenses for the employees of its foreign AE visiting India for a global seminar. These expenses are paid by Indian company directly to third party vendors on behalf of foreign AE and recovered on a cost-to-cost basis from foreign AE. Further, such activity does not entail a service element for Indian company and, hence, does not necessitate a mark-up. Hence, Indian company may select the Other Method and rely upon such back-to-back arrangement to demonstrate this recovery transaction to be arm's length.

Illustration 4 - An Indian company deputes some of its employees to its foreign AE through secondment. Foreign AE takes these individuals onboard by issuing letter of employments and is responsible for payment of the salary of the employees. Indian company frequently facilitates payment of salaries to the overseas accounts of the seconded employees purely for administrative convenience. In this case, salary costs are reimbursed by foreign AE to Indian company on a cost-to-cost basis. Hence, Indian company may select the Other Method and rely upon such back-to-back arrangement to demonstrate transaction to be arm's length.

Illustration 5 - Another example where this method could be used is in cases of cost allocation arrangements where a taxpayer benefits from certain services provided by a central entity of the group and has to pay a portion of the total cost incurred by the service provider. These costs are generally allocated on the basis of allocation keys like headcount, time spent, revenues etc. and a third party outside the group may not have the capability to provide identical services. Hence, in the absence of comparable prices or transactions, Rule 10AB may be applied and the cost allocation arrangement could be justified appropriately.

Considerations to be taken while judging comparability of an international or specified domestic transaction with an uncontrolled transaction [Rule 10B(2)]

10A.13 As per OECD TP Guidelines, comparability analysis is at the heart of the application of the arm's length principle. Application of the arm's length principle is based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with the conditions that would have been made had the parties been independent and undertaking a comparable transaction under comparable circumstances. There are 2 key aspects in such an analysis, namely:—

(1)

Identify the commercial or financial relations between the AEs and the conditions and economically relevant circumstances attaching to those relations in order that the controlled transaction is accurately delineated; and

(2)

To compare the conditions and the economically relevant circumstances of the controlled transaction as accurately delineated with the conditions and the economically relevant circumstances of comparable transactions between independent enterprises.

Thus, the first aspect of the analysis is distinct from the second aspect of considering the pricing of that controlled transaction under the arm's length principle.

Before making comparisons with uncontrolled transactions, it is vital to identify the economically relevant characteristics (or comparability factors) of the commercial or financial relations as expressed in the controlled transactions. Therefore, such characteristics or factors can be broadly categorised as follows:—

(a)

Contractual terms of the transaction;

(b)

Functions performed by each of the parties to the transaction taking into account assets used and risks assumed (including how those functions relate to the wider generation of value by the MNE group to which the parties belong, the circumstances surrounding the transaction, and industry practices);

(c)

Characteristics of property transferred or services provided;

(d)

Economic circumstances of the parties and of the market in which such parties operate;

(e)

Business strategies pursued by the parties.

By virtue of their complex functional and risk profiles, their margins fluctuate heavily with the vagaries of the economy, thus making comparability analysis difficult and unreliable. Further, the financial results of the entrepreneur, being the ultimate fall-out of third-party business, often depend on external economic factors in the market and not on internal pricing policies.

The authors are of the view that the herald of safe harbour as a tool for reducing TP disputes in India is far flung from reality. Much of the disputes around contract service providers in the fields of IT, ITeS, KPO and R&D, arise due to the uniqueness of the Indian TP regulations in its use of arithmetic mean and a band around the mean, as against the use of median and inter-quartile range adopted by most other TP regimes.

The authors had earlier analysed8 comparable sets widely used for determination of arm's length prices for IT and ITeS companies in the TP assessments for fiscal year (FY) 2006-07, i.e. relevant to the assessment year 2007-08. The IT set comprised of 26 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 1.38% to 60.23%, with an arithmetic mean of 25.04%. Similarly, the ITeS set comprised of 27 companies with current year operating profitability in the form of operating profit/total cost, ranging from 13.55% to 113.49%, with an arithmetic mean of 30.24%.

Thus, any captive IT or ITeS company with an operating margin of less than 19% and 24% respectively, namely after considering the band of 5% around the arithmetic mean, as prevalent during the material time, would have failed to satisfy the arm's length test for FY 2006-07, as per the country-wide comparable benchmarking sets adopted by the Indian Revenue.

It may be pertinent to highlight that the lower quartiles of the same IT and ITeS sets were at about 14% and 12% respectively. Therefore, the use of inter-quartile range on the same comparables would have enabled captive taxpayers with an operating profitability of 15%, being the intuitive mark-up for most captive IT and ITeS companies, to comply with the arm's length standard. The analysis was re-run on the ITeS comparables used in the TP assessment cycle relating to FY 2007-08, i.e., relevant to the assessment year 2008-09. The lower limit of arm's length price, computed with reference to the 5% tolerable limit around the arithmetic mean, was again observed to be at 19%, while the lower quartile was at 9%.

These analyses vindicate that, but for the ingenuity of the Indian TP regulations, a large fraction of taxpayers falling within the bracket of 15% of operating profitability or even lower, would have remained unscathed, even if one were to otherwise accept the selection of comparables by the Indian Revenue for the IT and ITeS sets, which itself left enough room for debate. Therefore, the introduction of inter-quartile range and median would have better addressed the TP disputes in India and obviated the need for safe harbours, as the pre-dominant objective of introducing safe harbours is to reduce TP litigations in India.

Some may attribute the adoption of arithmetic mean by the Indian Revenue, for the purposes of computing the arm's length price, to the brevity of comparable data available in public databases in the formative years of transfer pricing in India, which inhibited the usage of quartiles. It is observed that ProwessTM, a public database widely used for the purposes of comparable benchmarking analyses in India, reported only 8,067 companies in the year 2002, as compared to 25,949 companies in 2011. Presently another database used for benchmarking analyses, namely Capita line PlusTM, provides data of around 1,000 additional companies over and above the companies provided in ProwessTM. Thus, brevity of data can no longer be the reason or cause for not adopting the more sophisticated approach of the inter-quartile range by the Indian Revenue, as several of the other developing economies, let alone the developed ones, have advocated the usage of inter-quartile range and median for the purposes of computing the arm's length range.

The safe harbour rates proclaimed by India are still not reasonable enough to entice large captive service providers, since opting for safe harbour rates in India might result in such taxpayers facing economic double taxation, as Revenue authorities of the headquarter countries are unlikely to accept the high mark-ups under the unilateral safe harbour rules of India. Furthermore, as the taxpayers adopting safe harbours would be precluded from seeking refuge of MAP, as expressly provided in the safe harbour regulations, the risk of double taxation at headquarter countries is aggravated.

Tribunals are more inclined (with a few exceptions) to include foreign exchange fluctuation as part of the operating activity. On the other hand, the OECD Guidelines emphasise that while the principle of accounting consistency is essential to be observed, the question of including the foreign exchange gain or loss as part of the cost base depends on whether the same arises from operating or non-operating (i.e. say, trading or investing) activities and the entity that assumes such foreign exchange risk.

The industry dimension A point of consideration, which does not seem to find place in most IT/ITeS rulings (perhaps as the argument is often not adduced in the course of the proceedings) is the treatment adopted by the Revenue authorities, while dealing with taxpayers rendering services to both "service" and "product" companies, spread across various industries. In the course of the economic analysis, no cognizance is given to the end recipient of the services, although there do exist differences in the supply chains of both "service" and "product" companies. Further, even the business and economic circumstances vary for both categories of companies, and the return earned is an immediate indicator of such differences.

In a perfect world, one would want the functional comparability to be viewed in the light of the industry considerations, since the same would help in arriving at a set, which best represents not only the functions undertaken by the taxpayer, but also the return one would expect, while operating in such an industry. However, the lack of financial data for comparable companies operating in a certain domain continues to be a key deterrent in such an analysis. It is for this reason that usually a broader comparability approach is adopted by both taxpayers as well as Revenue authorities, which thus results in arriving at a standard set of comparables companies, without considering either the industry domains in which the taxpayer operates or the business and commercial circumstances of such verticals.

Perhaps, another aspect, which ideally should be considered, prior to determining the arm's length result for the IT/ITeS sector is to additionally analyze whether the services rendered are in the nature of "support services" required for internal consumption and/or subsumed within the larger activities of the Group. In such situations fixing a stand-alone commercial value to such activities is difficult because neither the activity has any use being detached from the final solution, nor the solution itself would be completed without the said activity. Such a scenario will be witnessed when the Indian taxpayer renders services to its Group companies and the same are entirely consumed within the overall primary activity carried on by the Group. A dispassionate value chain analysis should go a long-way in clearing the picture on the true worth of any activity. Having said that, the overall risk-insulated motive of the captive service provider, and thereby its returns being based on risk profiling should be the accepted norm.

To further elaborate, under such a scenario, the service rendered is not a value driver or a source of core competence for the Group. Simply put, the rendition of the service does not augment the revenue potential of the MNC, but may only lead to gains in operating efficiency. Therefore, a market facing activity where the service is ultimately consumed by the end-customer (in whatever form) should invariably lead to the assertion of an arm's length profitability, as opposed to internal consumption of the service for the Group that could form the subject of a cost contribution or a typical safe harbour arrangement.

Mark-ups determined

Tribunals in India have, more often than not, adjudicated on the grievances surrounding comparability analysis specifically on filters applied, quantitative/qualitative analysis of comparables, the true nature of a limited risk service provider and finally on specific issues about comparables as may have been raised by the petitioner. One can safely say that the Tribunals, in their role as an adjudicator, have not commented or expressed an opinion on the level of the mark-up that ought to be applied. They have clearly not taken on the role of a negotiator or a policy maker (like a safe harbour threshold). This continues to be the domain of the Government and the taxman. However, based on certain Tribunal rulings, where principle based approach on comparability has been ascertained, the resultant mark-ups for the IT and ITeS sectors have been hovering in the range of 18-20 per cent and 23-25 per cent as against the 22-25 per cent and 25-30 per cent respectively determined at the TP audit level.

In this background it would be pertinent to mention that retrospective clarification in relation to the tolerance band of 5 per cent not being a standard deduction is rather retrograde and could be viewed as an unjust enrichment to the Indian Revenue authorities. Rather than being forward-looking by considering global practices of applying central tendency, the Government has resorted to empower the Revenue authorities to negotiate with a minor leeway. The fact that the Government has waited for a decade before providing any clarity to both taxpayers as well as the Revenue authorities, and more so after Tribunals adjudicated a standard deduction on the mean, that was the stated intent, is unfortunate and a source of heartburn among the ones who did not get away.

1. TYPICAL BUSINESS MODEL

Typically, Indian outbound IT companies have set up subsidiaries in overseas jurisdictions in order to market their services1. Generally, these companies follow the onsite-offshore model whereby a portion of the project is executed onsite at the client's premises by the subsidiaries and the remainder is offshored to software development centres in India. The typical functions performed by the overseas subsidiaries include the following:

i.

Marketing

ii.

Selling which includes negotiation and concluding of contracts with end customers

iii.

Entering into contracts with end customers for both, onsite and offshore work

iv.

Subcontracting the work to its Indian parent and carrying out onsite activities at client premises

It is relevant to note that the foreign subsidiaries of different Indian multinational groups may perform the above functions at varied levels of intensity i.e. some subsidiaries may perform all the above functions whereas others may perform a more limited function of marketing. Based on the intensity of the functions, the subsidiaries can be characterised either as marketing service providers or as distributors of services which in turn determine the manner of remunerating them. Depending on the intensity of functions, subsidiaries are remunerated as a percentage of the following:

revenue (gross profit), or

net margin of revenues, or

the local costs of subsidiaries (i.e. cost plus mark-up).

The balance revenue earned by overseas subsidiaries from end clients is paid to the Indian parent as remuneration for rendering offshore and related support services.

The Indian parent is significantly involved in driving the entire corporate strategy for the group, developing software products, undertaking R&D, supporting subsidiaries by providing offshore technical expertise and strategic guidance and the service delivery to end clients in relation to the work offshored by the subsidiary. At times, the Indian parent may have to provide a performance guarantee to the end clients of the overseas subsidiaries in order to guarantee the due and timely performance of the obligations agreed. Alternately, a comfort letter is also issued by the Indian parent stating that the overseas subsidiary is part of the same Indian group.

Further, the Indian parent companies also financially assist the subsidiaries by investing in the share capital, providing loans and financial guarantees for working capital or for the purpose of acquisition.

2. CHARACTERISATION OF OVERSEAS SUBSIDIARY AND INTER ALIA SELECTION OF TESTED PARTY AND PLI

Issue

Indian tax authorities, in the case of Indian outbound IT companies, have been typically contending that overseas subsidiaries carry out only marketing functions. Hence, the remuneration policy of percentage of revenue (gross profit) or net margin of revenue is not in line with the functions performed by them and subsidiaries should only be remunerated on a cost plus mark-up and the balance revenues should be passed on to the Indian parent.

Further, citing lack of reliable third-party data in the overseas jurisdiction, tax authorities prefer selecting the Indian parent as the tested party for benchmarking the arm's length margin.

In this regard, it is pertinent to note that the two critical elements of a transfer pricing analysis, viz. the FAR analysis and the economic analysis, cannot be isolated. Characterisation of the entities and inter alia selection of a tested party is the first step in any economic analysis and must find its 'connect' back with the FAR analysis.

While the concept of 'tested party' does not find any mention in Indian regulations, the concept has been laid down in the US regulations, OECD Guidelines as well as the recently released UN TP Manual.

23.4-4 Auditor must himself verify management assertion that RPTs are at Arm's Length; cannot blindly rely on internal audit/expert

Auditor cannot blindly rely on internal auditors and conclude that RPTs are at Arm's Length. Nor can they assume that RPTs are at arm's length in view of audit committee's approval.

NFRA's observations are as under:

'5.3-19 The Audit Firm states that "To evaluate management's substantiation of assertion that related party transactions were undertaken at arm's length:

(a)

We had noted that it was part of the scope of Internal Auditor to verify the compliance with Approved Framework and compliance with the provisions of Companies Act, 2013, in respect of related party transactions. We had also read Internal Auditor's reports wherein they had confirmed that all transactions entered with the related parties were at arm's length price and in normal course of business.

(b)

We had verified that all the transaction entered with related parties were authorised as per delegation of authority and verified that the same were approved by the Audit Committee.

(c)

We had independently benchmarked related party transactions to satisfy that the transactions were undertaken at Arm's length and in normal course of business."

5.3-20 It is clear from the above assertion of the Audit Firm that it relied on the internal auditor's report and audit committee approval to verify whether the related party transactions were at arm's length price. It is important to note that all the approvals of the audit committee were post facto approvals and were in non-compliance with the Companies Act, 2013. (Refer to Paras 5.1.50, 5.2.36 and 5.2.37 above for details)

5.3-21 Moreover, as stated by the Audit Firm that they independently benchmarked RPTs to satisfy that the transactions were undertaken at arm's length and in the normal course and has given reference of WP "IL&FS-Standalone Hardcopy Files Folder - 47_Memo on Arm's Length (Page No. W3.1 to W3.76)". If there are numerous adjustments, which individually appear not material but collectively appear to be material, the same would require to be adjusted. 10A.7-1 'Price charged or paid' do not refer to hypothetical/illusive price - What is to be taken as a comparable uncontrolled transaction is 'the price charged or paid.' It is the actual transaction of charging or paying the price in a comparable uncontrolled transaction which is to be considered for the purposes of determining the ALP under the CUP method. There is no reference to any hypothetical or illusive price which ought to have been charged or paid for the services rendered. Since the delegated legislation refers to 'the price charged or paid', there can be no question of substituting such actual price charged or paid with a notional or hypothetical price which could have been charged or paid—Bumi Highway (India) (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 132/69 SOT 30 (URO) (Delhi - Trib.). Also see, AWB India (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 50 taxmann.com 323/[2015] 152 ITD 770 (Delhi - Trib.).

Under CUP method, TPO should compare price declared by assessee with custom tariff rate at port of destination as it stood on day of contract of sale entered into between assessee and its AE. On the other hand, the TPO is going for Customs tariff rate relevant for a subsequent date. This method is not a proper one—Liberty Agri Products (P.) Ltd. v. 10A.7-2 WDV can never be a determining factor to determine ALP - Under CUP method, value of machinery purchased has to be compared with identified transaction in uncontrolled market and in view of specific provision in Rule 10B(1)(a), written down value cannot be a determining factor to decide arm's length price. The assessee purchased machinery from its Italian holding company. CUP method was adopted as the most appropriate method for determining ALP. The TPO adopted written down value of machinery in books of holding company for making adjustment. The Dispute Resolution Panel held that adopting the written down value as the arm's length price under the comparable uncontrolled price method was not justified. It was held that when the transaction was compared by taking comparable uncontrolled price method as the most appropriate method, the price charged or paid by the assessee for the property transferred needed to be compared in a comparable uncontrolled transaction or a number of such transactions, as identified. Therefore, it was obligatory on the part of the TPO to identify the comparable transaction in the uncontrolled transaction for the purpose of determining the arm's length price. When the machinery was sold, the buyer of the machinery would naturally look for the efficiency and life of the machi- nery after the purchase. Therefore, the written down value may be one of the factors to be taken into consideration for determining the value of the machinery. However, in view of the specific provision in Rule 10B(1)(a), the written down value cannot be a determining factor to decide the arm's length price. The value of the machinery has to be compared with identified transaction in the uncontrolled market—Asstt. CIT v. Interpump Hydraulics India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 50 ITR (Trib.) 43/[2017] 82 taxmann.com 57 (Chennai-Trib).

10A.7-3 Internal or external CUPM - There are generally two ways to apply the CUPM, namely:—

(a)

Internal CUP - In this, a company must find examples of comparable transactions it has made with the third (or independent) parties; or

(b)

External CUP - In this, a company may look to the pricing of comparable transactions that take place between the third (or independent) parties to the extent they exist.

Example of internal CUP - Company ABC resident in India manufactures a precision cutting machine which it sells at a price of $1 million to a UK subsidiary but at a price of $1.2 million to an independent UK enterprise. Here, the price charged by ABC to the independent UK enterprise is the internal CUP. The method directly and reliably reflects the arm's length price. Assuming all other factors of comparability such as contractual terms are the same, an amount of $0.2 million should be added to Company ABC's taxable income.
