Example of external CUP - Company PQR resident in India is trading in listed securities and holds stock which would raise $20 million on the NSE. It sells to an overseas associated enterprise the stock for $10 million. The quoted price of $20 million in NSE is external CUP. Application of the external CUP is appropriate here as it reliably reflects the arm's length price. A sum of $10 million should be added to Company PQR's assessable profits.

While the tax administration accepts both the internal CUP as well as external CUP but since it is very difficult for a company to find the external transaction which is almost comparable to their own, that is the reason why most companies prefer to apply the internal CUP. In other words, the use of an internal CUP is preferred to the use of an external CUP as all other things being equal, the circumstances of the controlled transaction are likely to mirror more closely those of the uncontrolled transaction.

Ordinarily the internal CUP method should be preferred over the external CUP method as it neutralizes several distinguishing factors, such as the local factors and the economies available or unavailable to the assessee in particular, having bearing over the comparison of price charged from unrelated parties and AE—Gharda Chemicals Ltd. v. DCIT [2010] 35 SOT 406 (Mum. - Trib.).

Where diamonds of similar description had been sold to both AEs and third party customers, prices of transactions with both AEs and third party customers could be compared and it was to be held that there was internal CUP method available in case of assessee—Livingstones v. Dy. CIT [2014] 41 taxmann.com 499 (Mum. - Trib.).

Where on assessee becoming agent of parent shipping company, erstwhile agent was appointed as sub-agent of assessee, price agreement between assessee and its sub agent could not be used as internal CUP for determining ALP—Hapag Lloys India (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2016] 66 taxmann.com 257 (Mum. - Trib.).

In Skoda Auto India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2009] 30 SOT 319 (Pune - Trib.), it has been held that since the transactions between the AEs did not satisfy the criterion of internal CUP and further there were no external comparables available as accepted by the assessee, thus, the authorities were rightly rejected the assessee's case that as per CUPM, the transactions that the assessee entered into with its parent company were at ALP. Also see,DCIT v. CMA CGM Global India (P.) Ltd. [2012] 28 taxmann.com 165/[2013] 55 SOT 20 (Mum. - Trib.).

10A.13.5-2 MNE GROUP SYNERGIES - Group synergies can arise as a result of combined purchasing power or economies of scale, combined and integrated computer and communication systems, integrated management, elimination of duplication, increased borrowing capacity, etc. Such group synergies are often favourable to the group as a whole and, therefore, may heighten the aggregate profits earned by group members depending on whether expected cost savings are realised and on competitive conditions.

In other circumstances, such synergies may be negative, as when the size and scope of corporate operations create bureaucratic barriers not faced by smaller and more nimble enterprises, or when one portion of the business is forced to work with computer or communication systems that are not the most efficient for its business because of group-wide standards established.

When synergistic benefits or burdens of group membership arise purely as a result of membership and without the deliberate concerted action of group members, such synergistic benefits of group membership need not be separately compensated or specifically allocated among members of that group. On the other hand, where corporate synergies arising from deliberate concerted group actions do provide a member of an MNE group with material advantages or burdens not typical of comparable independent companies, it is necessary to determine the nature of the advantage or disadvantage, the amount of the benefit or detriment provided, and how that benefit or detriment should be divided among members of the group.

If important group synergies exist and can be attributed to deliberate concerted group actions, the benefits of such synergies should generally be shared by members of the group in proportion to their contribution to the creation of the synergy. Therefore, comparability adjustments may be warranted to account for group synergies.

10A.13-6 Recognition of accurately delineated transaction - Every effort should be made to determine pricing for the actual transaction as accurately delineated under the arm's length principle. A tax administration should not disregard the actual transaction or substitute other transactions for it unless the exceptional circumstances discussed below apply.

Because non-recognition can be contentious and a source of double taxation, every effort should be made to determine the actual nature of the transaction and apply ALP to the accurately delineated transaction, and to ensure that non-recognition is not used simply because determining an ALP is difficult. Where the same transaction can be seen between independent parties in comparable circumstances, non-recognition would not apply. Importantly, the mere fact that the transaction may not be seen between independent parties does not mean that it should not be recognised. AEs may have the ability to enter into a much greater variety of arrangements than can independent enterprises, and may conclude transactions of a specific nature that are not encountered, and may do so for sound business reasons. The transaction as accurately delineated may be disregarded, and if appropriate, replaced by an alternative transaction where the arrangements made in relation to the transaction, viewed in their totality, differ from those which would have been adopted by independent enterprises behaving in a commercially rational manner in comparable circumstances thereby preventing determination of a price that would be acceptable to both of the parties taking into account their respective perspectives and the options realistically available to each of them at the time of entering into the transaction. It is also a relevant pointer to consider whether the MNE group, as a whole, is left worse-off on a pre-tax basis since this may be an indicator that the transaction viewed in its entirety lacks the commercial rationality of arrangements between unrelated parties.

The qualitative characteristics include the relevance, reliability, and comparability over time of financial information that is reported about the different groups of products and services of an enterprise and about its operations in particular geographical areas, and the usefulness of that information for assessing the risks and returns of the enterprise as a whole. 12. The predominant sources of risks affect how most enterprises are organised and managed. Therefore, the organisational structure of an enterprise and its internal financial reporting system are normally the basis for identifying its segments.

13. The definitions of segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities include amounts of such items that are directly attributable to a segment and amounts of such items that can be allocated to a segment on a reasonable basis. An enterprise looks to its internal financial reporting system as the starting point for identifying those items that can be directly attributed, or reasonably allocated, to segments. There is thus a presumption that amounts that have been identified with segments for internal financial reporting purposes are directly attributable or reasonably allocable to segments for the purpose of measuring the segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities of reportable segments.

14. In some cases, however, a revenue, expense, asset or liability may have been allocated to segments for internal financial reporting purposes on a basis that is understood by enterprise management but that could be deemed arbitrary in the perception of external users of financial statements. Such an allocation would not constitute a reasonable basis under the definitions of segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities in this Standard. Conversely, an enterprise may choose not to allocate some item of revenue, expense, asset or liability for internal financial reporting purposes, even though a reasonable basis for doing so exists. Such an item is allocated pursuant to the definitions of segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities in this Standard.

15. Examples of segment assets include current assets that are used in the operating activities of the segment and tangible and intangible fixed assets. If a particular item of depreciation or amortisation is included in segment expense, the related asset is also included in segment assets. Segment assets do not include assets used for general enterprise or head-office purposes. Segment assets include operating assets shared by two or more segments if a reasonable basis for allocation exists. Segment assets include goodwill that is directly attributable to a segment or that can be allocated to a segment on a reasonable basis and segment expense includes related amortisation of goodwill. If segment assets have been revalued subsequent to acquisition, then the measurement of segment assets reflects those revaluations.

16. Examples of segment liabilities include trade and other payables, accrued liabilities, customer advances, product warranty provisions, and other claims relating to the provision of goods and services. Segment liabilities do not include borrowings and other liabilities that are incurred for financing rather than operating purposes. The liabilities of segments whose operations are not primarily of a financial nature do not include borrowings and similar liabilities because segment result represents an operating, rather than a net-of-financing, profit or loss. Further, because debt is often issued at the head-office level on an enterprise-wide basis, it is often not possible to directly attribute, or reasonably allocate, the interest-bearing liabilities to segments.

17. Segment revenue, segment expense, segment assets and segment liabilities are determined before intra-enterprise balances and intra-enterprise transactions are eliminated as part of the process of preparation of enterprise financial statements, except to the extent that such intra-enterprise balances and transactions are within a single segment.

18. While the accounting policies used in preparing and presenting the financial statements of the enterprise as a whole are also the fundamental segment accounting policies, segment accounting policies include, in addition, policies that relate specifically to segment reporting, such as identification of segments, method of pricing inter-segment transfers, and basis for allocating revenues and expenses to segments.

Identifying Reportable Segments

Primary and Secondary Segment Reporting Formats

19. The dominant source and nature of risks and returns of an enterprise should govern whether its primary segment reporting format will be business segments or geographical segments. If the risks and returns of an enterprise are affected predominantly by differences in the products and services it produces, its primary format for reporting segment information should be business segments, with secondary information reported geographically. Similarly, if the risks and returns of the enterprise are affected predominantly by the fact that it operates in different countries or other geographical areas, its primary format for reporting segment information should be geographical segments, with secondary information reported for groups of related products and services.

20. Internal organisation and management structure of an enterprise and its system of internal financial reporting to the board of directors and the chief executive officer should normally be the basis for identifying the predominant source and nature of risks and differing rates of return facing the enterprise and, therefore, for determining which reporting format is primary and which is secondary, except as provided in sub-paragraphs (a) and (b) below:

This apart, under the entrepreneurial model for the outbound structures, the Indian entity assumes the role of the Group companies as mentioned aforesaid, carries out the "entrepreneurial activities", could possibly own the intangibles required for the final delivery of the services and will typically be exposed to the business and market risks related to its operations. Given the differences in the functional, asset and risk profiles, even the compensation for the aforesaid models vary based on the functional analysis. While the captive service providers are usually compensated through a fixed rate of return on cost or on a time & material basis, the returns of the entrepreneurs are always market linked. It would be pertinent to mention here that inevitably the compensation is only a derivate of the functions, assets and risks. The stable returns earned by the captive service providers are commensurate with the routine functions and limited risks borne by the captives whereas the returns in the entrepreneur model are also commensurate with the non-routine functions being performed. While fluctuating returns therefore have their highs and lows, the steady returns tend to follow the more consistent middle path, albeit tempered by the lesser risk that they assume in the course of their functions.

From the above discussion, it emerges that a comparison of the functional, asset and risk analysis is basic to any transfer pricing analysis. However, the TP audits and recent Tribunal rulings in India do not seem to be inclined towards appreciating the differences in characterization and risk profiles between a low risk contract service provider and a third-party entrepreneurial companies operating within the same sector.

Furthermore, to account for differences in the functions performed, assets owned and/or deployed and risks assumed, appropriate adjustments such for difference in risk profile, basis of depreciation or working capital position should be carried out between the tested party (i.e. captive service provider) and the uncontrolled third-party entrepreneur companies. Such adjustments help even out any differences between the tested party and comparables companies to arrive at an unbiased "adjusted arm's length price". Such price will better represent the mark-up appropriate for a risk insulated service provider.

Dealing with adjustments in the comparability analysis

The point in relation to the need for a working capital adjustment has been deliberated by various Tribunals, namely Vedaris Technology (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT3, TNT India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT4 and Genisys Integrating Systems (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT5. Therefore the necessity for the same can be considered to be a settled position. In all these instances, the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out working capital adjustment as the same has a material impact on the effective return that the tested party need to earn. Of course, the OECD guidelines endorse the adoption of the working capital adjustment wherever applicable. It is significant to note that working capital adjustment is an effective substitute for any adjustment that may be warranted towards imputed interest consequent to deferred payments arising out of receivables from Group companies.

With regard to the adjustment for equating the basis of capital-asset depreciation, it is observed that in the Indian context, the said adjustment has been more widely accepted and acknowledged for companies in the manufacturing sector as against the services sector. The general belief is that the manufacturing sector requires initial period of high capital investment, whereas the services sector can up its asset base as it renders services. The turnaround time for a services company to become functional is a shorter duration than for a manufacturing plant to start commercial operations. Though the differences in asset bases are varied, it is imperative to adjust the same having regard to the industry/functional activity.

Therefore, such dictums do not rule out the application of the depreciation adjustment in the services sector, since the depreciation adjustment helps even out differences in the depreciation policies adopted by the tested party as against the third-party comparable companies. Having said that, it is imperative to take cognizance of the facts of the case, since application of the depreciation adjustment is case specific and is dependent on the class of assets deployed and the intensity of usage of such assets.

The need for carrying out a risk adjustment is perhaps most critical in the Indian context, considering that a majority of the subsidiaries of the overseas MNEs operate as low/limited risk service providers, bearing less than normal business risks in the course of undertaking the routine non-entrepreneurial functions. Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform.

Transfer pricing determination is not primarily undertaken to re-write the character and nature of the transaction, though this is permissible under two exceptions. Chapter X and TP rules do not permit the Revenue authorities to step into the shoes of the assessee and decide whether or not a transaction should have been entered. It is for the assessed to take commercial decisions and decide how to conduct and carry on its business. Actual business transactions that are legitimate cannot be restructured. It is not uncommon for manufacturers cum exporters to enter into distribution and marketing agreements with third parties or incorporate subsidiaries in different countries for undertaking marketing and distribution of the products—CIT v. Cotton Naturals (I) (P.) Ltd. [2015] 55 taxmann.com 523/231 Taxman 401 (Delhi).

Since ultimate aim of transfer pricing exercise is to determine an accurate value of ALP for purpose of taxation, appellate authorities would not be barred from adopting a different method, from that adopted by assessee in the TP report, if latter is not found to be MAM—PCIT v. Matrix Cellular International Services (P.) Ltd. [2018] 90 taxmann.com 54 (Delhi). However, it is to be reiterated that the primary onus/burden to determine the ALP is that of the assessee by resorting to any of the methods prescribed u/s 92C(1) which needs to be most appropriate method (MAM) as per section 92C(2). Where such onus/burden is discharged by the assessee and the data used for determining the ALP is reliable and correct, there should normally be no intervention by the AO. Ordinarily, it is only where the assessee has not discharged the onus placed on him, or he has not determined the price of the international transaction in terms of the provisions, or the data used by him is not reliable, correct or appropriate, or the TPO finds evidence which discredits the data used by the assessee, or the methodology applied by him in arriving at ALP of the international transaction, the ALP declared by the assessee should be rejected and re-determined in terms of section 92C—Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2010] 192 Taxman 317 (Delhi).

The AO/TPO can overrule the assessee as to the method adopted and select the most appropriate method. The reasons for selecting or adopting a particular method would depend upon functional analysis, comparison, which requires availability of data of comparables performing of similar or suitable functional tasks in a comparable business. When suitable comparables relating to a particular method are not available and functional analysis or adjustments is not possible, it would be advisable to adopt and apply another method. Of course, justification and reasons must be stated and elucidated—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi).

The exercise of determining the ALP in respect of international transactions between the related enterprises is aimed to determine the price, which would have been charged for products and services, as nearly as possible, in case such international transactions were not controlled by virtue of them being executed between related parties. The object of the exercise is, thus, to remove the effect of any influence on the prices or costs that may have been exerted on account of the international transactions being entered into between related parties. It is, at once, clear that for the exercise of determining ALP to be reliable, it is necessary that the controlled transactions be compared with uncontrolled transactions which are similar in all material aspects—Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 60 taxmann.com 355/234 Taxman 573 (Delhi), SLP granted in CIT v. Rampgreen Solutions (P.) Ltd. [2016] 76 taxmann.com 287/[2017] 244 Taxman 153 (SC).

Key factors for determining the materiality in outsourcing contracts

(i)

An outsourcing arrangement shall be considered material if the estimated annual expenditure under an outsourcing contract is likely to exceed 5 % of the total expenditure incurred during preceding financial year on all outsourcing activities.

(ii)

Notwithstanding the above, an outsourcing arrangement shall be considered material if its disruption has the potential to significantly impact an Insurer's business operations, reputation or profitability.

(iii)

Without limiting their scope, the criteria for assessing the materiality of outsourcing arrangements should have regard to the following key factors:

(a)

significance of the activity being outsourced (e.g. in terms of contribution to revenue, capital allocations or importance to overall achievement of strategic and business objectives);

(b)

financial, reputational and operational impact on the Insurer of an Outsourcing Service provider's failure to adequately perform the outsourced activity;

(c)

potential impact on the Insurer`s continuing ability to meet its obligations to its Policyholders in the event of disruption of services of an outsourcing Service Provider;

(d)

consequences of outsourcing the activity on the ability and capacity of the Insurer to maintain internal controls and meet current as well as future changes to regulatory requirements;

(e)

cost of the outsourcing arrangement in terms of contractual expenditures relative to the Insurer's net assets and annual operating expenditures;

(f)

interrelationship of the outsourced activity with other activities within the Insurer;

(g)

aggregate exposure to a particular outsourcing service provider where the Insurer outsources multiple activities to the same outsourcing service provider;

(h)

degree of difficulty and time required to replace the Outsourcing Service provider or if necessary to bring the activity in-house

(i)

Availability of alternative outsourcing service provider in the market for the same service

(j)

Any other factor which will have a significant impact on the Insurer or the Policyholders not covered above.

Despite the need for an appropriate risk adjustment, typically it is observed that the field officers disallowed such adjustments to taxpayers, citing reasons of the "single customer risk" borne by the captive service providers, surpassing various other risks that the captive does not bear e.g. success/failure for the activities such entities perform. Although the need for a risk adjustment has been disregarded at the lower echelons of power, it is encouraging to note that the Tribunals in various instances have taken a contrary view on this matter. In the case of Intellinet Technologies6, the Bangalore Tribunal has observed the need for providing a risk adjustment. The Tribunal in the said ruling has taken cognizance of the principles of economic adjustments and emphasised the need to carry out risk adjustments, with a specific reference to the point that the single customer risk borne by the captive service providers is only an "anticipated risk". This apart, the ruling has remained silent on the methodology and approach to be adopted for undertaking a risk based adjustment.

In fact, it is observed that in several other decisions, although the Tribunals have adjudicated the need for carrying out a risk adjustment, there continues to remain a lack of clarity on the methodology to be adopted for undertaking the same. One may not fault the Tribunals for not setting an approach to such risk adjustment, since the topic itself is complex and desirous of a separate analysis. Many a company have attempted to demonstrate the basis of arriving at a risk based adjustment, however, the final word on it still remains elusive.

Having said that there are contrary views doing the rounds, specifically in the case of GE India Technology Centre7, wherein the Tribunal has placed the onus on the taxpayer to prove that the risk can be remotely controlled by the overseas parent. Further, the observations of the Bangalore Tribunal in the instance case are in line with the comments of the Indian tax administrators in the recent India chapter as part of the UN Manual. While the UN Manual appreciates that "risk" is an important element in the comparability analysis, it does not treat the risk bearing capacity of an enterprise as an independent element, but similar to the functions performed and assets deployed. Additionally, the UN Manual also mentions that the conduct of the parties should provide the key to determine whether the actual allocation of risk conforms to such contractual risk allocation. A mere agreement citing the contractual arrangement, along with hard evidences (like demonstrating the difference in risks profiling in various situations) may help the tested party to fortify their stand for a risk-based adjustment.

Outliers and the risk dimension

To reiterate, there do exist certain fundamental principles, where the Indian TP legislation deviate from the globally accepted best practices. The adoption of the arithmetical mean as a measure of central tendency in the Indian context as against the inter-quartile range or the median, which are the internationally accepted measures of central tendency, as they tend to eliminate outliers, and are better representatives of the industry averages is one such major exception. This coupled with the use of single year data for the purpose of comparability analysis, daunts taxpayers in the IT/ITeS sector and is the prime reason for the increasing disputes, particularly in this sector. The law, through a proviso, does provide for expanding the base of comparable data, going back up to two further years back from the year of the transaction, thereby allowing for a three-year comparability analysis. Though overseas approaches suggest a 5-year period for any comparability analysis, one may accept a 3-year period specifically for developing countries like India, which has been witnessing contrasting growth year-on-year. Incidentally, the IT/ITeS sectors have been through such tumultuous times over the past decade. However, from the field officers' perspective and indeed the Tribunals, the approach has been to rely on the so-called "contemporaneous data", a phase contained in the legislation but often misused for annual audits. This, along with the concept of mean, has meant that expected mark-up drives comparability selection, rather than the reverse.

The adoption of the arithmetical mean as the arm's length price, hitherto with a limited tolerance band, has its inherent limitations and poses its own set of challenges. Unlike the median and the inter-quartile range, the arithmetical mean tends to be influenced by extreme values and the results are therefore skewed towards either very high/loss making companies. It is for this reason that there exist huge variations in the profitability of comparables arrived at by the Indian Revenue authorities during the course of the audit process, vis-à-vis the ex-post comparability analysis performed by the taxpayer to defend their position. Given that the results so arrived at are not representative of the normal industry averages, consisting varied types of entities in varied stages of growth, there definitely exists an immediate need to provide taxpayers with certain leeway in the form of a risk based adjustment.

10A.13-5 Business strategies - Business strategies would take into account many aspects of an enterprise, such as innovation and new product development, degree of diversification, risk aversion, assessment of political changes, input of existing and planned labour laws, duration of arrangements, and other factors bearing upon the daily conduct of business. It could also include market penetration schemes (such as to increase its market share, charging price lower than its competitors).

10A.13.5-1 CONSISTENT LOSSES - When an AE consistently realises losses while the MNE group as a whole is profitable, the facts could trigger some special scrutiny of TP issues. Of course, AEs can sustain genuine losses, whether due to heavy start-up costs, unfavourable economic conditions, inefficiencies, or other legitimate reasons. How- ever, an independent enterprise would not be prepared to tolerate losses that continue indefinitely. Recurring losses may be justified for a reasonable period in some cases as a business strategy to set especially low prices to achieve market penetration. If the pricing strategy continues beyond a reasonable period, a TP adjustment may be appropriate. For example, an MNE group may need to produce a full range of products and/or services in order to remain competitive and realise an overall profit, but some of the individual product lines may regularly lose revenue. One member of the MNE group might realise consistent losses because it produces all the loss-making products while other members produce the profit-making products. An independent enterprise would perform such a service only if it were compensated by an adequate service charge. Therefore, one way to approach this type of TP problem would be to deem the loss enterprise to receive the same type of service charge that an independent enterprise would receive under arm's length principle.

Where assessee-company having imported gold bars from its AE, converted same into jewellery and sold same back to AE, since assessee was a simple job worker, CUP was to be regarded as most appropriate method for determining ALP—Kailash Jewels (P.) As far as reimbursement of labour expenses, overhead expenses and consultancy charges incurred by the assessee were concerned, which were reimbursed by AE to the assessee, CUP method would be most appropriate method as no mark up was involved in same. Further, it was beyond any doubt that project receipts were from KMRCL which was a Government body and, hence, margins earned by the assessee was bound to be comparatively lower to reflect lower level of business risk involved. Moreover, comparables selected for analysis also included companies that performed additional functions while being engaged in providing comparable services. In such a case, TNMM could not be regarded as most appropriate method to determine ALP of international transactions entered into between two parties. Accordingly, impugned addition was to be set aside and matter was to be remanded back to TPO with a direction to adopt CUP method as Most Appropriate Method for determination of ALP for international transactions in question—Lee Harris Pomeroy Architects PC v. Dy. CIT [2015] 64 taxmann.com 444 (Kol. - Trib.).

Where the CUP method and any other TP method can be equally applied reliably, then the CUP method is to be preferred over any other method. Greater weight should be given to evidence provided by price-based methods if this is available. If no comparable can be found, other traditional transaction methods will have to be used.

Where assessee had followed CUP method for determining ALP, which was a standard method, it could not be discarded in preference over transactional profit methods unless revenue authorities were able to demonstrate fallacies in application of such method—Kailash Jewels (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2015] 59 taxmann.com 473/[2016] 156 ITD 685 (Delhi - Trib.).

Where assessee sold its old machines to its AE abroad and adduced CUP data in respect of said transaction, since said data had been found to be acceptable in considering five transactions of sales as being in consonance with arm's length price, it could not be disregarded in case of other three transactions merely because of resultant loss—Perma Pipe India (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2016] 65 taxmann.com 319 (Mum. - Trib.).

Since isobutyl benzene (IBB) was a generic chemical product and so far as prices of generic products were concerned, CUP method, on basis of database built on inputs like customs data, was reasonably acceptable. DCIT [2016] 68 taxmann.com 158 (Mum. - Trib.). Further it has been held that so far as CUP comparability is concerned, differences in size, geographical location etc. cannot be reason enough to discard comparables, unless it is shown that such factors influence conditions in market in which respective parties to transactions operate.

10A.7-6 CUPM, when not suitable - CUP method held not justified to be MAM where intra AE transactions were fundamentally different in character, in economic circumstances and contractual terms and these could not be compared with independent transactions entered into by the assessee—PCIT v. 2.3 Classification issues

A quick perusal of the definitions of these different categories23 indicates that a classification of services on these grounds may be notoriously complicated and require a level of technical expertise in the field of IT that cannot be expected from TPOs. The table below provides an indicative list of possible overlaps: The overlap and the ensuing absurdities may be illustrated by an example. Administering the 'payroll' of a foreign principal is classified explicitly as 'ITES'. However, pension management, employees' health benefits management or retirement benefits management are not strictly 'payroll' and could well be read as 'human resources services'. As a result, companies that manage payroll of current employees satisfy a 20% brightline test; but companies who manage compensation payable to employees after retirement are forced to prove a 25% margin. Similarly, a company that collates data on potential clients of the foreign principal and then 'cold calls' them may be said to be involved in 'data integration', as well as 'business analytics'/'market research'(KPO). On what basis the TPO will distinguish these categories is not clear from the rules.

As the definitions are exhaustive, and not inclusive, some activities that are typically considered as outsourcing processes may fall outside the rules. For example, review of transactional and litigation documents and preparation of due diligence reports are typical KPO activities.24 Yet, these activities are not captured by the term 'legal databases' listed under ITES, or by any of the categories under knowledge process outsourcing.

Further, IT companies often provide ITES and KPO services as a cluster under the same contract. Asking them then to allocate their income to different heads may be impractical.

2.4 Conceptualization and Design

Another aspect of the definition of eligible transactions in the software sector that may run into problems is the fact that the rules exclude research functions that fall within the scope of 'conceptualization' and 'design'.25 In the same breath, they define research services to include seemingly high end activities like the "development of new theorems" or the "development of information technology"26; but also require them to be low end activities that do not involve conceptualisation and design. This definition seems to be poised at a paradox that can be read pedantically to exclude traditional contract research services. For instance, requirement analysis, software testing or minor adaptation to suit local needs are usually outsourced on contract27, but they may easily be bracketed as 'conceptualisation and design'. Requirement analysis which involves enlisting the needs of the client-base from the software, is particularly susceptible as it precedes the code-writing stage. Software testing and subsequent reports that are used to make improvements in the product are also vulnerable to classification as 'conceptualization and design'. Minor adaptation to local needs may easily be bracketed under 'conceptualization and design' if these words are interpreted broadly.

2.5 Insignificant Risk

The rules also prescribe that the eligible assessee rendering ITES, KPO or research services undertake 'Insignificant Risk' to be eligible for safe harbour.28 While the definition per se seems to be consistent with the international understanding that safe harbours be extended to low-end activities, a United Nations appraisal of the practice of TPOs in India indicates that officers require extensive documentation before they accept such a submission.29 Most cases where MNEs have raised arguments as to insignificant risk have been rejected on the grounds of inadequate documentation, and assessees have been classified as firms undertaking substantial risk. There is a danger that TPOs will refuse to recognise that assessees are undertaking insignificant risk under the new rules on the grounds that such a contention was previously rejected before the rules were notified.

Finally, the rules require the Foreign Principal to provide the funds or capital and other economically significant assets including intangibles for research.30 As the criticism of the OECD rules on the same lines indicate31 there is a risk that TPOs will read this pedantically as to exclude transactions where the assessee provides some insignificant intangibles. Industry experts widely hold such a reading to be untenable on the grounds that companies providing contract research services usually have some significant intangibles on their own- such as know-how that they may have developed through experience. Indeed, the problem may be exacerbated by the requirement that capital and funds be provided by the foreign principal. This may lead to the assessee being excluded from the scope of the provisions on slim grounds such as borrowing in its own name from a bank.

In Capgemini(2013)17 the ITAT observed that the "classification was on the basis of classification made by Dun & Bradstreet. However, it is found that Dun & Bradstreet had made the classification according to size of the company i.e. large, small and medium. The classification was not made on the basis of margin and there is no empirical evidence to suggest that margin is directly related to turnover." Further, in Willis Processing(2013)18 the ITAT took the same view of the turnover classification as taken by the author in the preceding paragraph and stated that "as per the classification on the basis of turnover from Rs. 10 million to Rs. 2 billion, an entity having Rs. 10 million can be compared with an entity having Rs. 2 billion turnover; but at the same time, an entity having Rs. 2 billion turnover cannot be compared with the entity having Rs. 2.01 billion turnover. Thus, the classification gives unrealistic result as two entities having difference of Rs. 10 million cannot be compared. In our view for the purpose of comparing the profit margin of functionally similar entities, the classification of such slab range is not practically workable."

Thus the aforementioned cases not only rejected the application of the concept of economies of scale to service companies but also struck at the very basis of the turnover filter by breaking the link assumed to be existing between turnovers and margins.

Turnover Filters: The way forward

Does the strong criticism of the turnover filter in the immediately preceding paragraph mean that the turnover filter must be rejected altogether? No - such a measure would be too drastic and uncalled for. Infact, despite the criticism, the turnover filter continues to be applied, though with greater diligence. What is the way forward in establishing an objective, logical and fair use of the turnover filter?

The decision of the High Court of Delhi in Chrys Capital(2015)19 serves in this regard as a guiding light at the end of a tunnel. The High Court observed that "Quantitative and qualitative filters/criteria have been used in different cases to include or exclude comparables. The intuitive logic for excluding big companies from the list of comparables while undertaking the FAR [functions, assets employed and risks undertaken] analysis of a smaller company is attractive, given that such big companies provide services to diverse clientele, perform multifarious functions, often assume risks and employ intangible assets which are specially designed, unlike in the case of smaller companies. The bigger companies have an established reputation in the segment, are well known and employ economies of scale to a telling end. On the other hand, these obvious - and apparent features should not blind the TPO from the obligation to carry out the transfer pricing exercise within the strict mandate of Section 92C and Rules 10A to 10E."

Taking a cue from this decision in Chrys Capital(2015)20, one may proceed with the understanding that determining the arm's length price in India is based on choosing the most appropriate method and conducting a comparability analysis. Where a comparable meets each of the standards enumerated in Rule 10B(2) and the differences between the potential comparable and the taxpayer, if any, can be appropriately eliminated under Rule 10B(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 then the comparable gets a thumbs up in the comparability analysis. Any application of a quantitative filter must not result in the bypassing of this qualitative analysis on the basis of assumed 'the intuitive logic' described in Chrys Capital(2015)21 above. A similar view was also taken in Capgemini (2013)22 and Willis Processing(2013)23.

Thus, taking the liberty of making some suggestions, turnover filters must be applied -

Firstly, by keeping in mind that the purpose to be achieved by the turnover filters as by any quantitative filter is to reduce the effort involved in having to go through a large number of potential comparables during the qualitative analysis, and not as an alternative to conducting a thorough qualitative analysis in accordance with Rules 10B(2) and 10B(3) wherein comparability is tested on a large number of factors and which form the basis of comparability under the Indian transfer pricing regulations.

Secondly, on the basis of the facts of each case; rigid classifications as being cast text stone must be avoided in order to prevent judgments such as the one in McAfee Software(2015)24 (discussed above) where as many as seven companies were excluded as comparables by the ITAT on a very technical application of the turnover filters without any comprehensive comparability analysis.

Thirdly, keeping in mind the grind involved in shifting through the large number of companies with relatively smaller turnovers, a lower turnover filter is desirable. It is also required because smaller turnovers are often suggestive of one of the three situations that the company is in reducing stage, the company is a start-up or the company is winding up. Each of these three situations are avoidable for the purposes of comparability. Thus, a lower turnover filter is a necessity.

10A.13-4 Economic/Market Circumstances - ALP may vary across different markets even for transactions involving similar or same property or services, therefore, to achieve comparability requires that the markets in which the independent and associated enterprises operate do not have differences that have a material effect on price or that appropriate adjustments can be made. It is essential to identify the relevant market(s) taking into account of available substitute goods or services.

Economic circumstances that may be relevant to determining market comparability include the geographical location, size of the markets, extent of competition in the markets and the relative competitive positions of buyers and sellers, availability of substitute goods and services, levels of supply and demand in the market as a whole and in particular regions, consumer purchasing power, nature and extent of Government regulation of the market, costs of production (including costs of land, labour and capital), transport costs, level of market (retail or wholesale), date and time of transactions, and so forth.

10A.13.4-1 GOVERNMENT POLICIES - There are circumstances in which a taxpayer will consider an ALP must be adjusted to account for Government interventions such as price controls (even price cuts), interest rate controls, controls over payments for services or management fees, subsidies to particular sectors, exchange control, anti-dumping duties, etc. As a general rule, these interventions should be treated as conditions of the market in the particular jurisdiction, and in the ordinary course, they should be taken into account in evaluating the taxpayer's TP in that market.

A special problem arises when a jurisdiction prevents or blocks the payment of an amount which is owed by one AE to another. For example, exchange controls may effectively prevent an AE from transferring interest payments abroad on a loan made by another AE located in a different jurisdiction. This circumstance may be treated differently by the two jurisdictions, i.e., borrower jurisdiction may or may not regard the untransferred interest as having been paid, and the lender's jurisdiction may or may not treat the lender as having received the interest. Perhaps one way to deal is to apply the arm's length principle viewing the intervention as a condition affecting the terms of the transaction.

Another problem is that often independent enterprises would not enter into such a transaction in which payments were blocked. In such cases, where application of arm's length principle is unclear, one possibility is to treat the payment as having been made between the AEs on the assumption that an independent enterprise in a similar circumstance would have insisted on payment by some other means. An alternative approach would be to defer both the income and the relevant expenses of the taxpayer. However, in any case, a taxpayer should not be permitted to treat the blocked payments due from an AE differently from blocked payments due from an independent enterprise.

10A.13.4-2 LOCATING SAVINGS AND OTHER LOCAL MARKET FEATURES - In determining how location savings are to be shared between the AEs, it is necessary to consider existence of location savings, amount of such location savings, extent to which such savings are retained by the MNE group or passed on to the customers/supplies, and where location savings are not fully passed on, the manner in which independent enterprises operating under similar circumstances would allocate any retained net locating savings.

Other features that may give rise to comparability concerns that are not directly related to savings include purchasing power and product preferences of the households in that market, the degree of competition in the market, local country infrastructure, relative availability of a pool of trained or educated workers, proximity to profitable markets. In such cases, the most reliable approach for assessing whether comparability adjustments are required will be to refer to data regarding comparable uncontrolled transactions in that geographical market between independent enterprises performing similar functions, assuming similar risks and using similar assets.

10A.2-1-1-1 SET-OFFS OR ADJUSTMENTS ARE NOT BARRED - As per OECD TP Guidelines, ideally, in order to arrive at the most precise approximation of arm's length conditions, the arm's length principle should be applied on a transaction-by-transaction basis. However, there are often situations where separate transactions are so closely linked or continuous that they cannot be evaluated adequately on a separate basis. An example may include some long-term contracts for the supply of commodities or services, or rights to use intangible property and such transactions should be evaluated together using the most appropriate arm's length method. Another example where a taxpayer's transactions may be combined is related to portfolio approaches. While some separately contracted transactions between AEs may need to be evaluated together in order to determine whether the conditions are arm's length, other transactions contracted between such enterprises as a package may need to be evaluated separately. An MNE may package as a single transaction and establish a single price for a number of benefits such as licences for patents, know-how, and trademarks, the provision of technical and administrative services, and the lease of production facilities. This type of arrangement is often referred to as a package deal. In some cases, it may not be feasible to evaluate the package as a whole so that the elements of the package must be segregated. In such cases, after determining separate TP for the separate elements, the tax administration should nonetheless consider whether in total the TP for the entire package is arm's length.

Aggregation (or segregation) of various or all international transactions, whether essential in a given case, held to be entirely fact dependant exercise which is to be viewed having regard to the nature of transaction and surrounding circumstances—Gruner India (P.) Ltd. v. DIT [2017] 77 taxmann.com 311 (Delhi). Where advertisement revenue was directly co-related to channel viewership and sale of advertisement airtime increased with number of cricketing events, both distribution business segment and advertisement sale segment being closely linked had rightly been aggregated for ALP purposes—CIT v. ESPN Software India Ltd. [2017] 87 taxmann.com 323/[2018] 252 Taxman 171 (Delhi). In PCIT v. Almatis Alumina (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 202/286 Taxman 378 (Cal.), it has been held that where segmental results are available, adjustment can only be made on the basis of individual transaction and not on aggregation basis.

An intentional set-off is one that AEs incorporate knowingly into the terms of the controlled transactions. It occurs when one AE has provided a benefit to another AE within the group that is balanced to some degree by different benefits received from that enterprise in return. These enterprises may indicate that the benefit each has received should be set-off against the benefit each has provided as full or part payment for those benefits so that only the net gain or loss (if any) on the transactions needs to be considered for the purposes of assessing tax liabilities. Intentional set-offs may vary in size and complexity. Such set-offs may range from a simple balance of two transactions to an arrangement for a general settlement balancing all benefits accruing to both parties over a period. Independent enterprises would be very unlikely to consider the latter type of arrangement unless the benefits could be sufficiently accurately quantified and the contract is created in advance. Otherwise, independent enterprises normally would prefer to allow their receipts and disbursements to flow independently of each other, taking any profit or loss resulting from normal trading. Recognition of intentional set-offs does not change the fundamental requirement that for tax purposes, the transfer prices for controlled transactions must be consistent with the arm's length principle. It would be a good practice for taxpayers to disclose the existence of set-offs intentionally built into two or more transactions between AEs and demonstrate that, after taking account of the set-offs, the conditions governing the transactions are consistent with the arm's length principle. It may be necessary to evaluate the transactions separately to determine whether they each satisfy the arm's length principle. However, if the transactions are to be analysed together, care should be taken in selecting comparable transactions.

15. Insurers shall ensure compliance with the following additional principles where outsourcing service providers are the related parties or group entities of Insurers or Insurance Intermediaries registered with the Authority.

(a)

With the objective of avoiding potential conflict of interest, Insurers shall endeavor that the related Parties or group entities of Insurers or Insurance Intermediaries registered with the Authority shall ordinarily not be engaged for outsourcing any of the activities.

Insurers shall not outsource any activity that leads to potential conflict of interest with the functions of the Insurer or with the functions of Insurance Intermediaries.

However, it is generally useful to examine data from both the year under consideration and prior years since the use of past year's data will show whether a taxpayer's reported loss on a transaction is part of a history of losses on similar transactions, the result of particular economic conditions in a prior year that increased costs in the subsequent year, or a reflection of the fact that a product is at the end of its life cycle. This analysis is generally useful when transactional profit methods are used. Step 2 - Broad-based analysis of the taxpayer's circumstances:—'Broad-based analysis' can be defined as an analysis of the industry, competition, economic and regulatory factors and other elements that affect the taxpayer and its environment, but not yet within the context of looking at the specific transactions in question. This step helps to understand the conditions in the taxpayer's controlled transaction as well as those in the uncontrolled transactions to be compared, in particular, the economic circumstances of the transaction.

In principle, the information relating to the conditions of comparable uncontrolled transactions undertaken or carried out during the same period of time as the controlled transaction is expected to be the most reliable information to use in a comparability analysis since it reflects how independent parties have behaved in an economic environment that is the same as the economic environment of the taxpayer's controlled transaction.

Step 3 - Understanding the controlled transaction(s) under examination (or review):—The examination is based, in particular, on a functional analysis in order to choose the tested party (where needed), the selection and application of the MAM to the circumstances of the case, the financial indicator that will be tested (in the case of transactional profit methods), and to identify the significant comparability factors that should be taken into account.

Step 4 - Review of existing internal comparables (if any):—Internal comparables may have a more direct and closer relationship to the transaction under review than external comparables and access to such information may also be both more complete and less costly. The financial analysis may be easier and more reliable as it will presumably rely on identical accounting standards and practices for the internal comparable and for the controlled transaction. On the other hand, internal comparables are not always more reliable and it is not the case that any transaction between a taxpayer and an independent party can be regarded as a reliable comparable for controlled transactions carried on by the same taxpayer.

In POS Hyundai Steel Manufacturing (P.) Ltd. v. CIT(A) [2021] 125 taxmann.com 383 (Mad.), it has been held that in TP analysis, only in the absence of internal comparables, external comparables will be taken for comparability purpose using TNMM.

Step 5 - Determination of available sources of information on external comparables where such external comparables are needed taking into account their relative reliability:—A common source of information is commercial database which have been developed by editors who compile accounts filed by companies with the relevant administrative bodies and present them in an electronic format suitable for searches and statistical analysis (sometimes cost-effective way of identifying external comparables) subject to certain identified limitations. Another source may be foreign (or non-domestic) comparables where there are insufficient data available at the domestic level and/or in order to reduce compliance costs where several entities of an MNE group have comparable functional analysis. Another source may be information which is undisclosed to the taxpayers, i.e., tax administrators may have information available to them from examinations of other taxpayers or from other sources of information that may be not disclosed to the taxpayer.

Published data available from stock or commodity exchanges could also form basis of prices in both uncontrolled and controlled transactions—CIT v. Cargill Food India Ltd. [2017] 88 taxmann.com 470 (Delhi). However, ALP could not be determined on the basis of Indian published prices under the New Exchange Control Policy—CIT v. Oracle India (P.) Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 45/241 Taxman 253 (Delhi).

Step 6 - Selection of the MAM and depending on the method, determination of the relevant financial indicator.

Step 7 - Identification of potential comparables (i.e., determining the key characteristics to be met by any uncontrolled transaction in order to be regarded as potentially comparable based on relevant factors identified in Step 3):—There are basically two ways in which the identification of potentially comparable third party transactions can be conducted, i.e., additive approach and deductive approach.

21. For most enterprises, the predominant source of risks and returns determines how the enterprise is organised and managed. Organisational and management structure of an enterprise and its internal financial reporting system normally provide the best evidence of the predominant source of risks and returns of the enterprise for the purpose of its segment reporting. Therefore, except in rare circumstances, an enterprise will report segment information in its financial statements on the same basis as it reports internally to top management. Its predominant source of risks and returns becomes its primary segment reporting format. Its secondary source of risks and returns becomes its secondary segment reporting format.

22. A 'matrix presentation' — both business segments and geographical segments as primary segment reporting formats with full segment disclosures on each basis — will often provide useful information if risks and returns of an enterprise are strongly affected both by differences in the products and services it produces and by differences in the geographical areas in which it operates. This Standard does not require, but does not prohibit, a 'matrix presentation'.

23. In some cases, organisation and internal reporting of an enterprise may have developed along lines unrelated to both the types of products and services it produces, and the geographical areas in which it operates. In such cases, the internally reported segment data will not meet the objective of this Standard. Accordingly, paragraph 20(b) requires the directors and management of the enterprise to determine whether the risks and returns of the enterprise are more product/service driven or geographically driven and to accordingly choose business segments or geographical segments as the primary basis of segment reporting. The objective is to achieve a reasonable degree of comparability with other enterprises, enhance understandability of the resulting information, and meet the needs of investors, creditors, and others for information about product/service-related and geographically-related risks and returns.

25. The data place of the ψsixty-fifth percentile is = 7*0.65 = 4.55.

Since this is not a whole number, the next higher data place, i.e.; the value at the fifth place would have at least sixty-five per cent of the values below it. The sixty-fifth percentile is therefore value at fifth place, i.e., 10.57%.

The arm's length range will be beginning at 8.2% and ending at 10.57%.

Therefore, if the transaction price of the international transaction or the specified domestic transaction has OP/OC percentage which is equal to or more than 8.2% and less than or equal to 10.57%, it is within the range. The transaction price in such cases will be deemed to be the arm's length price and no adjustment shall be required.

The data place of median is calculated by first computing the total number of data point in the data set * (50/100). In this case it is 7 * 0.5 = 3.5.

Since this is not a whole number, the next higher data place, i.e.; the value at the fourth place would have at least fifty per cent of the values below it (median).

The median is the value at fourth place, i.e., 9%. Therefore, the arm's length price shall be considered as 9% and adjustment shall accordingly be made.

Where safe harbours are adopted unilaterally, care should be taken in setting safe harbour parameters to avoid double taxation, and the jurisdiction adopting such should generally be prepared to consider modification of the safe harbour outcome in individual cases under MAP to mitigate the risk of double taxation.

(3) Safe harbours may also increase the risk of double non-taxation when adopted unilaterally. If a unilateral safe harbour permits taxpayers to report income below arm's length levels in the jurisdiction providing the safe harbour, taxpayers would have an incentive to elect application of the safe harbour. In such a case, there would be no assurance that the taxpayer would report income in other jurisdictions on a consistent basis or at levels above arm's length levels based on the safe harbour. Moreover, it is unlikely that other tax administrations would have the authority to require that income be reported above arm's length levels. While the burden of under-taxation in such situations would fall exclusively upon the jurisdiction adopting the safe harbour, and should not adversely affect the ability of other jurisdictions to tax arm's length amounts of income, double non-taxation would be unavoidable and could result in distortions of investment and trade.

(4)

Safe harbours potentially open avenues for inappropriate tax planning. Enterprises may have an incentive to modify their transfer prices in order to shift taxable income to other jurisdictions (especially low tax ones). This may also possibly induce tax avoidance to the extent that artificial arrangements are entered into for the purpose of exploiting the safe harbour provisions. If a safe harbour were based on an industry average, tax planning opportunities might exist for taxpayers with better than average profitability.

(5)

It may also raise issues of equity and uniformity since by implementing a safe harbour, one would create 2 sets of distinct rules in the TP area. Preferential tax treatment under safe harbour regimes for a specific category of taxpayers could potentially entail discrimination and competitive distortions.

10TA.1-3 Recommendations on use of safe harbour provisions [OECD TP Guidelines] - Where jurisdictions adopt safe harbours, willingness to modify safe harbour outcomes in MAP to limit the potential risk of double taxation is advisable. It is important to observe that the problems of non-arm's length results and potential double taxation and double non-taxation, inter alia, arising under safe harbours could be largely eliminated if safe harbours were adopted on a bilateral or multilateral basis by means of competent authority agreements between jurisdictions. Therefore, the use of bilateral or multilateral safe harbours under the right circumstances should be encouraged.

Tax administrations in each jurisdiction should carefully weigh the benefits of, and concerns regarding, safe harbours, making use of such provisions where they deem it appropriate. Properly designed safe harbour provisions, applied in appropriate circumstances, can help to relieve some of the burdens such as complexity, time-consuming nature and costliness and provide taxpayer with greater certainty.

It should also be recognised that a safe harbour provision does not bind or limit any tax administration in any way other than that administration that has expressly adopted for it.

The Rationale for the Rate Prescribed:

The operational margin (PBDIT) of 20-30% fixed by the Committee has been widely decried by the Industry as unjustified.32 A number of problems with the Committee's methodology is immediately apparent. The data on which the committee based its decision is not publicly available. Further, the data the committee uses pertain to the A.Y 2008-09.33 Not only is this old, but it also predates the financial crisis and the consequences it had on outsourcing margins. Analysis points to the fact that the operations considered are those bearing negligent risk, and it is implausible that they earn such a broad mark-up. The sector-wise segmentation of the mark-up also seems unjustified on the grounds that the risk profile of the sectors is the same. In addition, what the Rules consider to be activities that are higher on the value chain may also be low-end activities. 34 While the term "Knowledge Process Outsourcing" seems to signify more complex services, experts point out that in reality "human resource" services may mean employee database management; while "engineering and design" may mean converting paper drawings into electronic forms. Thus, a 25% mark-up is not in tune with commercial reality.35 Moreover, the increase in margins from 20 to 22% with the increase in scale may be consistent with the traditional understanding of economies of scale, however, the logic may be misplaced in the low-risk, routine services industry. As the scale increases, the customer may expect a discount for volume which may lower the mark-up. Salaries, which constitute a bulk of the costs of such industries would increase as more people must be recruited to cater to industry demands. As a result, the idea that volume would significantly improve margins may be misguided.

The available data do not corroborate the figure fixed by the Committee. Though studies of the IT/ITES sector in India indicate margins close to or exceeding 20% are frequently reported, importing such data wholesale must be treated with great caution. Such data is based on the performance of the industry leaders like Infosys, Wipro, TCS etc. who often develop their own software products, provide complex services and undertake substantial risk.36 Companies covered by the rules are those that undertake 'insignificant risk', and they cannot be asked to abide by such high benchmarks.

In addition, the Committee accepts that captive centres in developing economies like Philippines or China who offer roughly the same location savings, earn 10%-14% margins.37 No reasons are offered to suggesting that Indian firms enjoy a distinct advantage over these countries, and hence earn higher margins.

More relevant indicators may be found in the ITAT decisions that consider the appropriate profit level indicator of companies with a similar risk profile. Such decisions usually accept margins around 12-15% for software development and ITES Services (as indicated in the table below) and criticise the department's pegging at 20% as unreasonable.

3. Auto-Industry: Unintentional Exclusions

The rules extend a safe harbour to auto component manufacturers and exporters. However, they insist that the assessee export at least 90% of their components to Original Equipment Manufacturers. Original Equipment Manufacturers procure sub-parts from Tier 1 manufacturers and then manufacture more sophisticated components, or assemble various sub-parts. They onsell their wares to automakers, who inturn assemble the final product and sell it to customers.38

The language of the rules complicates the understanding of the scope of the definition. The rules define the eligible international transaction as 'manufacture and export' of auto components. However, they define the 'eligible assessee' as a person, ninety per cent or more of whose turnover is in the nature of sales to an Original Equipment Manufacturer.39

By omitting the qualification that an eligible assessee's turnover must be from sales to an overseas OEM, the rules support the interpretation that an assessee who primarily sells to a domestic OEM, with some negligible sales to a non-resident OEM is covered by the definition. This is because the assessee still satisfies the condition of earning 90% of its turnover from OEMs, and has still engaged in the eligible international transaction of 'manufacture and export' of auto components.

Further OEMs constitute about 30% of the clientele of the auto components industry.40 However, it is unclear how many component industries supply exclusively to OEMs as to meet the stringent threshold of the rules. Around 30% of the clientele of the Auto Component Industry is made up of Tier 1 manufacturers who in turn supply to OEMs, and the rest is divided between Aftermarket sales and Tier II clientele. Excluding firms who supply to such manufacturers is not based on any sound distinction.

A quick perusal of the data indicates that the rate of profitability fixed for auto manufacturers is closer to commercial reality than in the case of the IT sector. An analysis of the Confederation of Indian Industries reports a 10-12% margin for auto-component manufacturers, and includes a number of SMEs in its analysis.41

14.2-2 Third person or HQ may place orders or make payment on behalf of service receiver

Para 5.3.4 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012 states as follows - Occasionally, a person may be the person liable to make payment for the service provided on his behalf to another person. For instance, the provision of a service may be negotiated at the headquarters of an entity by way of centralized sourcing of services whereas the actual provision is made at various locations in different taxing jurisdictions (in the case of what is commonly referred to as a multi-locational entity or MLE). Here, the central office may act only as a facilitator to negotiate the contract on behalf of various geographical establishments. Each of the geographical establishments receives the service and is obligated to make the payment either through headquarters or sometimes directly. When the payment is made directly, there is no confusion. In other situations, where the payment is settled either by cash or through debit and credit note between the business and fixed establishments, it is clear that the payment is being made by a geographical location. Wherever a fixed establishment bears the cost of acquiring, or using or consuming a service through any internal arrangement (normally referred to as a "recharge", "reallocation", or a "settlement"), these are generally made in accordance with corporate tax or other statutory requirements. These accounting arrangements also invariably aid the MLE's management in budgeting and financial performance measurement. Various accounting and business management systems are generally employed to manage, monitor and document the entire purchasing cycle of goods and services (such as the ERP-Enterprise Resource Planning System). These systems support and document the company processes, including the financial and accounting process, and purchasing process. Normally, these systems will provide the required information and audit trail to identify the establishment that uses or consumes a service.

It should be noted that in terms of proviso to section 66B, the establishments in a taxable and non-taxable territory are to be treated as distinct persons. Moreover, the definition of "location of the receiver" clearly states that "where the services are "used" at more than one establishment, whether business or fixed, the establishment most directly concerned with the use of the service" will be the location. Thus, the taxing jurisdiction of service, which is provided under a 'global framework agreement' between two multinational companies with the business establishment located outside the taxable territory, but which is used or consumed by a fixed establishment located in the taxable territory, will be the taxable territory.

14. Product/Service Profitability Analysis

14.1 The unit product or service profits are driven by two major components viz. cost per unit and selling price per unit. The cost auditor should analyse if the business belongs to the sellers' market or buyers' market. This would facilitate the assessment of impact of changes in selling prices and changes in costs on the profitability or otherwise of the products or services. While the selling price is a single number, the cost is the sum total of different elements. The cost auditor must ensure that the basis use to allocate indirect costs is consistently adopted by the company.

14.2 In case of services, the unit of measurement is very important and hence carefully selected. Further, due to the diverse nature of services, it is essential to exercise care in analyzing the profitability thereof especially when the services provided are not standard. Many times, there is a combined contract for sale of product along with the service & maintenance contract. In such cases, the cost auditor should bifurcate the sales and costs for each portion and then compute and comment on their respective profitability.

14.3 Care should be taken in splitting the joint costs in case of joint products and by products. The method adopted for separation of costs should be checked to ensure correctness and consistency.

14.4 It would help to separately identify the costs of production, selling & marketing and handling customer services.

14.5 The cost auditor is expected to provide a thorough evaluation to bring out the products and/or services that are contributing more or less to the overall company performance. For convenience purpose, the products and/or services could be classified in groups with similar risk-return profiles. This classification may be different from the 'product groups' in the cost audit report annexures.

14.6 The analysis should separately appraise profitability of newly introduced products or services and also their proportion to the total profits of the organisation. The cost auditor should incorporate the profitability analysis of products discontinued during the period.

14.7 The term "profitability" should be taken with an extended meaning to include, apart from the concept of accounting profit, the ROI analysis as well. It would be useful to analyse profitability of products/services in domestic and export market. Care should be taken to isolate reasons for the changes in the profitability percentages. Similarly, if significant, profitability on sales to the related parties may be separately highlighted.

14.8 The report should specifically highlight the top five and the bottom five products. This will help the company to understand which products or services are contributing to the performance and which are ones that are non-performing. Based on this the suitable corrective actions may be suggested.

♦ Sales and production records

♦ Reconciliation with CENVAT records

33.1-7 Contract for some work or consultancy etc. is not manpower supply service

Deputing officers from one company to other - It is normal practice to depute employees/officers from one company to other. The salary is debited to the other company. This is manpower recruitment and supply service and service tax is payable - CBEC letter No. 137/35/2011-ST dated 13-7-2011 [Clarification in respect of employees deputed by ONGC to DGH (Directorate General of Hydrocarbon) but principle applies to all deputations]

Services provided outside ambit of employment for a consideration would be a service. For example, if an employee provides his services on contract basis to an associate company of the employer, then this would be treated as provision of service - Para 2.9.1 of CBEC's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Secondment/deputation of employee to another group company - It is not uncommon to second/assign an employee to another group company (also termed as 'deputation'). In secondment deputation seconded/deputed employee remains under legal employment of one enterprise but performs functions for another enterprise (usually a group company). The salary is usually paid by company which has seconded/deputed the employee and the salary (including proportionate social security benefits) is debited to the account enterprise where the employee is working.

In case of international companies, the foreign enterprise pays part of the salary directly in foreign account of the employee, which is debited to the Indian company. Balance part of salary is paid by Indian company directly to the seconded/deputed employee in Indian Rupees. Income tax TDS under section 195 of Income Tax Act will apply in respect of salary paid to the employee. This can be treated as the 'Service Permanent Establishment' [service PE] of foreign enterprise in India - a view expressed in DIT v. Morgan Stanley Co. (2007) 162 Taxman 165 = 292 ITR 416 (SC) and Centrica India Offshore P Ltd. In re (2012) taxman 545 = 19 taxmann.com 214 (AAR). Hence, withholding tax may apply when the part of salary is remitted outside India to the foreign enterprise (though the foreign enterprise is debiting only actual salary without any mark-up).

Issue is whether such secondment/deputation (whether within India or outside India) is 'manpower supply service'. Safe course is of course to take a view that it is manpower supply service. However, there is distinction between 'manpower service' and 'manpower supply service'. In 'manpower service', the salary of manpower is includible, while in case of 'manpower supply service', only charges (mark-up) for deputing/seconding such employee should be includible.

Transfer of employees between group entities

B59. The fourth issue relates to group share-based payment arrangements that involve employees of more than one group entity. For example, a parent might grant rights to its equity instruments to the employees of its subsidiaries, conditional upon the completion of continuing service with the group for a specified period. An employee of one subsidiary might transfer employment to another subsidiary during the specified vesting period without the employee's rights to equity instruments of the parent under the original share-based payment arrangement being affected. If the subsidiaries have no obligation to settle the share-based payment transaction with their employees, they account for it as an equity-settled transaction. Each subsidiary shall measure the services received from the employee by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments at the date the rights to those equity instruments were originally granted by the parent as defined in Appendix A, and the proportion of the vesting period the employee served with each subsidiary.

B60. If the subsidiary has an obligation to settle the transaction with its employees in its parent's equity instruments, it accounts for the transaction as cash-settled. Each subsidiary shall measure the services received on the basis of grant date fair value of the equity instruments for the proportion of the vesting period the employee served with each subsidiary. In addition, each subsidiary shall recognise any change in the fair value of the equity instruments during the employee's service period with each subsidiary.

B61. Such an employee, after transferring between group entities, may fail to satisfy a vesting condition other than a market condition as defined in Appendix A, e.g. the employee leaves the group before completing the service period. In this case, because the vesting condition is service to the group, each subsidiary shall adjust the amount previously recognised in respect of the services received from the employee in accordance with the principles in paragraph 19. Hence, if the rights to the equity instruments granted by the parent do not vest because of an employee's failure to meet a vesting condition other than a market condition, no amount is recognised on a cumulative basis for the services received from that employee in the financial statements of any group entity.
